title: Block 1: Foundations and graph crimes
text:
How we see data
Our visual system did not evolve to read graphs. Some visual features are detected before conscious attention engages: a red dot among grey dots, a single triangle in a sea of circles, an unusually large shape in a field of small ones. This is called pre-attentive processing (Healey and Enns, 2012). If you encode important information as a feature the eye picks up automatically, readers see it without having to search. Encoding the same information as a subtle change in line style or a slightly different shade requires the reader to look for it.

title: Block 1: Foundations and graph crimes
text:
Game: spot it
The facilitator shares one tab at a time. Each hides one odd point among 80. Type found in the chat the moment you see it (no scrolling ahead!).


Colour
Shape
Colour and shape, mixed up


































Watch the chat: the colour target gets a flood of “found”s almost instantly, the shape target a moment later. In the third tab the odd point is the only grey triangle, and no single feature gives it away, so everyone has to check points one by one. This is the cost of making readers combine features (a conjunction search).

title: Block 1: Foundations and graph crimes
text:
Game: guess the value
Each round shows five values. A is always the same. Your job: what percentage of A is B? Post your guess in the chat before you check it in the box. One round at a time, no peeking at the next tab.


Round 1
Round 2
Round 3
Round 4











B is what % of A?  (within 5 points counts)










B is what % of A? 










B is what % of A? 










B is what % of A? 





What just happened?

The answers were 62%, 38%, 45% and 71%. Look back at the chat: most people find Round 1 easy, get scattered on Round 2, scatter further on Round 3 (people judge circles by width, not area, so they overestimate small ones), and are close to guessing on Round 4.
You have just played a version of Cleveland and McGill’s (1984) experiment (Rounds 3 and 4 go beyond what they tested). People read the same ratio most accurately as position on a common scale, then length, angle, area, colour lightness and colour hue. Mackinlay (1986) extended the ranking to categorical data: position is still best, but colour hue rises to second. Shape is weaker but useful as a redundant cue.

title: Block 1: Foundations and graph crimes
text:
The encoding hierarchy








The practical rule is: assign your most important variable to the highest-ranked encoding available to you. For two continuous variables, both go to position (a scatter plot). For a continuous variable grouped by a category, position handles the continuous variable and colour hue handles the category, with shape added redundantly for accessibility.


Colour
Shape
Both




penguins_complete |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm,
             colour = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 2.5) +
  colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(x = "Body mass (g)",
       y = "Flipper length (mm)",
       colour = "Species") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")










penguins_complete |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm,
            shape = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 2.5) +
  labs(x = "Body mass (g)",
       y = "Flipper length (mm)",
       shape = "Species") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")










penguins_complete |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm,
             colour = species, shape = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 2.5) +
  colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(x = "Body mass (g)",
       y = "Flipper length (mm)",
       colour = "Species",
       shape = "Species") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")










Two continuous variables to position (rank 1), one categorical to colour hue (rank 2 for categorical data), with shape added as a redundant cue. The figure works on a colour monitor, in greyscale print, and for a reader with colour vision deficiency. Treat this as the minimum for every figure.

title: Block 1: Foundations and graph crimes
text:
Colour as a tool
Colour hue is the second-most powerful encoding for categorical data, and it is pre-attentive, so readers pick it up without searching. It is also the encoding most often misused. Three palette types exist, each for a different data structure:







Palette type
Data structure
Example use



Qualitative
Discrete groups with no inherent order
Species, treatment arm


Sequential
Continuous, running in one direction from a minimum
Gene expression, density


Diverging
Continuous, with a meaningful midpoint
Log fold-change, temperature anomaly











Using the wrong type for the data structure is one of the most common errors. A sequential palette applied to categorical data implies an ordering that does not exist. A categorical palette applied to a continuous variable conceals the ordering that does exist.
The package colorspace (Zeileis et al., 2020) provides palette generators for all three types with documented design rationale, and is the project default for palette construction. The Dark2 palette ships directly:

# Categorical (Dark2): for discrete groups with no order
colorspace::swatchplot(
  colorspace::qualitative_hcl(8, palette = "Dark2")
)







The same package provides scale_*_discrete_qualitative(), scale_*_continuous_sequential(), and scale_*_continuous_diverging() functions that integrate directly with ggplot2. Prefer these over manual hex vectors.
Quick check: which palette type?

Treatment arm (control, drug A, drug B): 
Qualitative
Sequential
Diverging

Change in body mass after a season, where 0 = no change: 
Qualitative
Sequential
Diverging

Number of eggs per nest: 
Qualitative
Sequential
Diverging

title: Block 1: Foundations and graph crimes
text:
Accessibility
Roughly 8% of men have some form of colour vision deficiency (Sharpe et al., 1999); red-green is by far the most common. Using red and green to distinguish two groups will fail for a non-trivial fraction of any audience. The Okabe-Ito palette was designed to remain distinguishable under deuteranopia and protanopia (Okabe and Ito, 2008), and the viridis palette family is perceptually uniform under colour vision deficiency and in greyscale.
Beyond palette choice, the main rule is redundant encoding: never let colour be the only cue distinguishing groups. Use shape redundantly for points, linetype redundantly for lines, and direct labelling wherever it is legible (we will cover direct labelling in Block 4).
The colorBlindness package gives you the verification step. colorBlindness::cvdPlot() produces, by default, a four-panel simulation: the original (“normal vision”), deuteranopia, protanopia, and a desaturated (greyscale) version. This lets you see whether the figure still works when colour fails. Extra “enhanced” panels can be requested through its layout argument; note that it does not simulate tritanopia.

fig <- penguins_complete |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm, colour = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") +
  theme_minimal()

colorBlindness::cvdPlot(fig)







Tip



After the workshop, run cvdPlot() on three or four figures from your own thesis chapter or recent paper. Be honest about which ones fail.

title: Block 1: Foundations and graph crimes
text:
Data-ink ratio
Tufte (1983) introduced data-ink ratio: the proportion of a figure’s visual elements that actually encode data, as opposed to decoration, borders, gridlines, shadows, and three-dimensional effects that exist for their own sake. High data-ink ratio means most of the visual complexity of the figure carries information.
The default ggplot2 theme_grey() already fails this test: a grey panel background and white gridlines exist purely as decoration. Move to theme_minimal(), theme_classic(), or a project-specific theme function as your default.






Warning



Avoid theme_grey() (the ggplot2 default) in any figure intended for human consumption. Set theme_minimal(base_size = 12) or theme_classic(base_size = 12) as your project baseline.

title: Block 1: Foundations and graph crimes
text:
Graph crimes
A figure that violates these principles distorts what the data actually say. Five recurring crimes are worth recognising on sight:










Truncated bar chart axes. A bar encodes magnitude as length from a baseline. If the axis does not start at zero, the visual ratio between bars is no longer the data ratio.

Manipulating the y-axis. Compressed or expanded vertical ranges can make tiny effects look enormous or hide real effects.

Cherry-picking time ranges. Choosing a window of time that supports a story while ignoring the surrounding data.

Wrong chart for the data. Pie charts for many categories; line charts for unordered categorical data; dual y-axes pretending two arbitrary scales are commensurable.

Convention violations. Inverted colour scales (light = high); inverted y-axes; latitude on the x-axis. Readers bring expectations, and figures that violate them mislead.

A bonus crime: spurious correlation. Two variables with a strong correlation may have no causal relationship at all. Showing a strong correlation without acknowledging the confounders is a misrepresentation of evidence.
Warm-up: graph crimes tribunal


Graph crimes tribunal


You are the jury. For each figure below, post a one-line verdict in the chat in the form crime → sentence (e.g. “truncated axis → start at zero”). Is the crime one of distortion (the visual misrepresents the data) or omission (the figure leaves out something the reader needs)?
Three minutes, then the facilitator reads out the best (and harshest) sentences.




Example 1
Example 2
























Bonus. Look closely at the error bars.










The verdicts



Example 1: guilty of distortion. The y-axis starts at 80, so Japan’s 84 looks twice the height of Spain’s 82 when the real difference is under 3%. The 15-colour legend adds nothing the axis labels could not. Sentence: start the axis at zero, or show points on a sensible range, and drop the legend.

Example 2: guilty of distortion. The axis starts at 120, so a $123M opening looks almost nothing next to $177M. Sentence: bars from zero, or a dot plot with labelled values.

Bonus: guilty of everything. The “error bars” are the capital letter T typed above each bar. They show no variability at all, on top of a dynamite plot that hides the raw data. Sentence: plot the raw points with a real interval.


🏆 Challenge: crime scene investigation


Crime scene investigation (solo race, 12 minutes)


The code below was found at a crime scene. It uses chickwts, a dataset built into R: the weight of chicks after six weeks on one of six feed supplements. Copy it into RStudio and run it. There are at least eight graph crimes in it.


Investigate (4 min). Post each crime in the chat as you spot it. The first person to post a new crime gets the point, so be quick, and don’t repeat one already posted.

Rehabilitate (8 min). Rewrite the code into an honest, accessible figure in your own RStudio.

Report. Post a screenshot of your fixed figure in the chat. The facilitator shares the best few on screen, and you score yourself against the case file below.

Scoring: 1 point per crime you were first to post, 2 more for each crime fixed in your figure. Highest score chooses which figure the facilitator shows first.

chickwts |>
  group_by(feed) |>
  summarise(mean_weight = mean(weight), se = sd(weight) / sqrt(n())) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = feed, y = mean_weight, fill = feed)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean_weight - se, ymax = mean_weight + se), width = 0.2) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(150, 350)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = rainbow(6)) +
  labs(x = "feed", y = "mean_weight") +
  theme_grey()





Case file: the crimes and a rehabilitated figure



Dynamite plot. Bars of means hide the 71 individual chicks.

Truncated axis. The bars start at 150 g, so horsebean looks a fraction of casein’s weight; the real ratio is about half.

Undefined error bars. They are ± 1 SE, but nothing says so.

Rainbow palette. Not colour-blind safe (red vs green), and the lightness jumps around.

Redundant legend. Colour repeats the x-axis, so the legend is pure eye-travel.

Unordered categories. Alphabetical order hides the ranking.

Variable names as labels. “mean_weight” with no units.

theme_grey(). The grey panel fails the data-ink test.


chickwts |>
  mutate(feed = fct_reorder(feed, weight, .fun = median)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = weight, y = feed)) +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.15, alpha = 0.6, colour = "grey45") +
  stat_summary(fun = median, geom = "point", shape = 23,
               size = 3.5, fill = "#D95F02") +
  labs(x = "Chick weight at six weeks (g)", y = "Feed supplement",
       caption = "Points: individual chicks. Diamonds: medians.") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())







Every chick is visible, the feeds are ranked, there is one colour with a job (the median), the axis has units, and no legend is needed. Because these are points rather than bars, the axis does not need to start at zero.

title: Block 2: Choosing the right figure
text:
The chart-type table
Before anything else, the structure of your data determines the chart type. Variable count and variable type narrow the choice. The table below is a guide rather than a rule: your scientific question may demand something else, but you should be able to justify it.
A few rules are worth memorising: no pie charts (use a labelled proportion); no 3D effects of any kind; no dual y-axes (use two panels instead); no dynamite plots (bar charts of means with error bars) where raw data are available, so show a raincloud or strip plot instead (Weissgerber et al., 2015).

title: Block 2: Choosing the right figure
text:
Descriptive vs explanatory framing
Every figure communicates at two levels: it presents the data, and it makes an argument. The framing of the title and the legend determines which level the reader engages with first.
A descriptive title states what the figure shows in neutral language: “Body mass of three penguin species in the Palmer Archipelago”. The reader is shown the data and invited to interpret.
An explanatory title states what the figure means: “Gentoo penguins are substantially heavier than Adelie and Chinstrap”. The reader is told the conclusion and invited to verify it from the data.
Neither is wrong. The choice is determined by the audience. Journal figures and lab reports use descriptive framing because the reader is expected to bring their own judgement and the figure legend below carries the necessary methodological detail. Talks, posters, and public engagement use explanatory framing because the reader has limited time, attention, or technical background to derive the conclusion themselves.

title: Block 2: Choosing the right figure
text:
Audience design
The same finding becomes a different figure for different audiences. The table below summarises the design choices that should change with context:









Element
Journal / lab report
Poster
Talk
Public engagement



Title above figure
No
Yes (explanatory)
Yes (explanatory)
Yes (explanatory)


Figure legend below
Yes (four elements)
Optional, abbreviated
No
No


Direct labelling
Where it does not break convention
Yes
Yes
Yes


Highlighting (grey out non-focal groups)
No
Yes

Yes

Sparingly
Yes

Yes


Statistical detail
Precise p-values where shown
Abbreviated
One key result
None or one sentence


Base font size
12pt (floor)
16–20pt
14–18pt
14–18pt


Raw data shown
Always where n permits
Always
Always
Where it clarifies


Interactivity (hover, zoom)
Supplementary only
No
No
Yes, on the web



Every figure must stay honest and accessible whatever the audience. What changes are the design choices needed to communicate with that audience.

title: Block 2: Choosing the right figure
text:
Interactive figures
On a web page, a lab website, or a Quarto HTML report, the reader can interact with a figure. ggiraph turns a ggplot into an interactive one with almost no new code: swap geom_point() for geom_point_interactive(), add a tooltip (what appears on hover) and a data_id (what gets highlighted together), and wrap the plot in girafe(). Hover over a penguin below:

library(ggiraph)

p <- penguins_complete |>
  ggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour = species,
             tooltip = paste0(species, " (", sex, ")\n",
                              body_mass_g, " g, ", island),
             data_id = species)) +
  geom_point_interactive(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = "Body mass (g)", colour = "Species") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

girafe(ggobj = p,
       options = list(opts_hover_inv(css = "opacity:0.15;")))





Because data_id = species, hovering on one penguin highlights its whole species and fades the rest: the highlighting row of the audience table, under the reader’s control. Interactivity is a bonus, never a requirement. A figure must still work as a static image, because PDFs, printouts and most journal pages cannot hover.
🏆 Game: guess the audience


Same data, four audiences


You have one finding:

Gentoo penguins are substantially heavier than Adelie and Chinstrap penguins

🏆 Guess the audience (solo, 12 minutes). Draw your secret audience by running sample(1:4, 1), and don’t tell anyone which number you got:

Journal figure (specialist reader, no time pressure)
Conference poster (3 seconds to attract, 2 minutes to engage)
Seminar slide (audience cannot control viewing time)
Museum infographic (non-specialist, no assumed technical knowledge)

Build the best figure of the finding for your audience from penguins_complete, using the audience table above. Don’t put the audience in the title! Post a screenshot in the chat. The facilitator shows each figure on screen in turn and everyone posts their guess (1–4). You score a point for every correct guess about your figure. If nobody can place your figure, it was not designed for any particular audience. (Large group? The facilitator shows 4–6 entries picked at random, so the game fits in the time. Small group? Build two figures for two different audiences, so there are enough to guess.)
Bonus: if you got the museum, make it interactive with ggiraph. What would a visitor want to see when they hover?

title: Block 3: Themes and scales
text:
Themes
Once a figure is built, two parts of ggplot2 control how it looks: themes (how the non-data elements appear) and scales (how the data axes are formatted). Getting both right changes how your figures look without changing what they show. This block sets up patterns we use throughout Block 4.
A complete theme controls every non-data visual element: panel backgrounds, gridlines, text styling, axis ticks, margins, legend appearance. ggplot2 ships several complete themes; we have already used theme_minimal() in earlier examples. The ones worth knowing:
The base_size argument sets the text size for every text element in the figure proportionally. Setting theme_minimal(base_size = 12) once is preferable to setting axis.text = element_text(size = 12) and twelve similar lines: every text element will scale together when you change base_size for a different audience.

title: Block 3: Themes and scales
text:
Theme
When to use



theme_minimal()
Default for most figures. Clean panel, retained gridlines, no panel border.


theme_classic()
Traditional scientific look. Axis lines, no gridlines, no panel border.


theme_bw()
Black-and-white panel with thin border and gridlines.


theme_void()
Strip everything. Useful for maps and bespoke composed layouts.


theme_grey()
The ggplot2 default. Do not use this. The grey panel background fails the data-ink test.




Local modifications with theme()
The theme() function makes local modifications on top of any complete theme. Inside theme(), every named argument is a visual element of the figure and takes an element_*() function:


element_text() for text elements (titles, axis labels, legend text)

element_rect() for rectangular backgrounds (panel, plot, legend, strip)

element_line() for lines (gridlines, axis lines, tick marks)

element_blank() to remove an element entirely

ggtext::element_markdown() for rich text in titles and labels (introduced in Block 4)

A representative set of modifications, applied to a complete theme:

penguins_complete |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = flipper_length_mm, colour = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(title = "Penguin bill and flipper dimensions",
       x = "Bill length (mm)",
       y = "Flipper length (mm)",
       colour = "Species") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),          # remove minor gridlines
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold"),    # bold axis labels
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold",     # bold title at 1.2 × base_size
                              size = rel(1.2)),
    legend.position = "bottom",                  # legend below
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA)
  )







The rel() function sets a size relative to base_size. rel(1.2) means “1.2 times the base text size”, which adjusts automatically when you change base_size. Use rel() for any text size you set inside theme(); use absolute sizes only when you need to override the relationship.
A project theme function
If you make the same theme modifications in every script, wrap them in a function. Here we make a simple custom theme_project():

theme_project <- function(base_size = 12) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      axis.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = rel(1.1)),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey40"),
      legend.position = "bottom",
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
      strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
    )
}

Every figure in the project that uses theme_project() now follows your house style. Change the function and every figure updates, without editing individual scripts. Save the function in R/functions/plot_functions.R and source it at the top of any script that produces figures.
Theme demonstration: same data, four themes
The case for moving away from theme_grey() is more persuasive shown than argued. The figure below renders the same scatter plot four times: once with the ggplot2 default, once with theme_minimal(), once with theme_classic(), and once with our custom theme_project(). Look at each in turn and ask which one most clearly serves the data.

base_fig <- penguins_complete |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = flipper_length_mm, colour = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Flipper length (mm)", colour = "Species")

p_grey    <- base_fig + theme_grey(base_size = 11)    + labs(title = "theme_grey(): DEFAULT, AVOID")
p_minimal <- base_fig + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + labs(title = "theme_minimal()")
p_classic <- base_fig + theme_classic(base_size = 11) + labs(title = "theme_classic()")
p_project <- base_fig + theme_project(base_size = 11) + labs(title = "theme_project()")

(p_grey + p_minimal) / (p_classic + p_project) 













Note



Reflection: data-ink (Block 1). For each panel, which elements carry information and which are noise? The grey panel of theme_grey() encodes nothing; minor gridlines may or may not, depending on whether readers need precise values. Remove anything that does not encode data, until removing more would damage readability.


The theme_project() panel is the most restrained of the four. It removes the grey background and the minor gridlines, bolds the axis titles for slight emphasis, and moves the legend from the right-hand side to below the panel, where it does not compete with the data for the reader’s attention. Each of these choices can be defended on data-ink grounds.
Audience-appropriate base_size
The audience table in Block 2 specified base font sizes for different reading contexts. Translated into theme_project() calls:


Audience

base_size argument



Journal / lab report

theme_project(base_size = 12) (floor)


Conference poster
theme_project(base_size = 18)


Seminar talk
theme_project(base_size = 16)


Public engagement
theme_project(base_size = 16)









Warning



Setting individual text element sizes (axis.text = element_text(size = 14)) without adjusting base_size leaves other text elements at the default. The result is a figure with mismatched text sizes that looks unbalanced. Always change base_size first; tweak individual elements only as deliberate exceptions.


Just for fun: ThemePark
Themes are where ggplot2 lets you have fun. The ThemePark package (by Matthew B. Jané and contributors) has themes inspired by films and TV: Barbie, Oppenheimer, Star Wars, Zelda, Lord of the Rings, Hogwarts houses and more. It is on GitHub rather than CRAN:

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("MatthewBJane/ThemePark")

Each theme comes with matching colour scales. Most of them (scale_color_barbie() and friends) are continuous gradients, so map a continuous variable to colour:

library(ThemePark)

fun_fig <- penguins_complete |>
  ggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour = bill_length_mm)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = "Body mass (g)", colour = "Bill (mm)")



Barbie
Oppenheimer
Star Wars
Zelda












































Fun, but put on your Block 1 glasses. In Oppenheimer the darkest points almost vanish into the dark panel, so the highest values are the hardest to see. Star Wars has the same problem in reverse: its gradient runs from pale to dark olive, so the longest bills sink into the black panel, while the huge bold gold text shouts louder than the data. Neither theme hides any data, yet both make it harder to read.
There is no magic inside. Print a theme function to see how it is built:

theme_starwars

It is a single theme() call made of element_text(), element_rect() and element_line(), the same building blocks as theme_project(). So any of these themes can be fixed with your own theme() and scale_*() layers added on top.


🏆 The Ugly-Off (10 minutes)


Round 1: make it hideous (4 min, on your own). Let R pick your starting theme:

sample(ThemePark::themepark_themes$theme, 1)

Apply it to fun_fig, then use theme(), element_*() and scale_*() to make the ugliest figure you can that is still honest: every data point visible, axes truthful, labels readable in principle. Clashing fonts, garish backgrounds, rotated text and tick marks the size of bananas are all fair game. Post a screenshot in the chat; vote for your favourite with a 😂 reaction.
Round 2: the rescue (4 min). The winner of Round 1 pastes their code in the chat. Everyone races to rescue that monster by adding layers after theirs (no deleting lines!) until every point is visible, the labels are readable and the colours are accessible. Post your rescued version; the winner of Round 1 picks the best rescue.


The rule “add layers, don’t delete” is deliberate: later layers win, so a good theme() call can rescue almost anything. If you drew starwars, the solution below shows one rescue.


Solution

One rescue for Star Wars: a gradient that runs from dim to bright (so the largest values stand out against black, not into it), and calmer text.

fun_fig +
  theme_starwars() +
  scale_colour_gradient(low = "grey35", high = "#FFE81F") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  theme(axis.title = element_text(size = 13),
        axis.text  = element_text(size = 11))







Layers added later win, so your scale replaces the default gradient and your theme() overrides only the text sizes; everything else from theme_starwars() stays.

title: Block 3: Themes and scales
text:
Scales
Where themes control the non-data parts of the figure, scales control how the data axes are rendered. Axes are position encodings, the most accurate visual channel in the encoding hierarchy from Block 1. Yet the breaks and labels ggplot2 chooses by default often undermine that accuracy by placing ticks at awkward intervals or formatting numbers in ways that obscure them. The scales package gives you the tools to fix this.
Pretty breaks
The default break algorithm sometimes places ticks at awkward intervals. scales::breaks_pretty() and scales::breaks_extended() produce better-looking breaks at round numbers.

penguins_complete |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#0072B2", colour = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = scales::breaks_extended(6)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = scales::breaks_extended(5),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))
  ) +
  labs(x = "Body mass (g)", y = "Count") +
  theme_project()







The expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05)) argument adds no padding at the bottom (so bars sit on the axis) and 5% padding at the top (so the tallest bar does not touch the upper edge). This is the convention for bar charts and histograms.






NotePrecise breaks





The scales package treats your n argument as a target, not a guarantee. The algorithm optimises jointly over simplicity, coverage, density and legibility, and it will return fewer breaks than requested if “nicer” round numbers score better at a lower count.
If you want exact breaks, set them manually:

penguins_complete |>
  ggplot(aes(x = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#0072B2", colour = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(3000, 6000, by = 500)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 25, 5),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))
  ) +
  labs(x = "Body mass (g)", y = "Count") +
  theme_project()










Label functions
Number formatting matters. Thousands separators, percentage signs, properly formatted p-values, and currency prefixes are all small touches that distinguish a polished figure from a draft. The scales package provides label functions for each:






Function
Use



scales::label_number()
Generic number formatting; arguments include big.mark, accuracy, prefix, suffix



scales::label_comma()
Thousands separator (shorthand for label_number(big.mark = ","))


scales::label_percent()
Multiplies by 100 and adds %



scales::label_currency()
Currency; the prefix argument supports any symbol (e.g. "£"). Replaces the superseded label_dollar()



scales::label_scientific()
Scientific notation for very large or very small numbers


scales::label_log()
Log-scale labels formatted as 10^n



scales::label_pvalue()
P-values with < for very small values


scales::label_wrap()
Wrap long category labels across multiple lines




penguins_complete |> 
  count(island) |> 
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = prop, y = fct_reorder(island, prop))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#0072B2") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = scales::breaks_extended(n = 5),
    labels = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 1),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))
  ) +
  labs(x = "Proportion of sampled penguins", y = NULL) +
  theme_project()







Mapping the category to y and the value to x gives horizontal bars directly, so there is no need for coord_flip() (now superseded), and the scale you format is simply the one the values are mapped to (scale_x_continuous() here). Two improvements over the default: the proportion axis labels render as 30% rather than 0.3, and the breaks sit at sensible round percentages rather than at arbitrary values like 0.275. Both changes happen entirely in the scale_* call; the data are not modified.
Demonstration: before and after
The figure below shows the same data twice: first with ggplot2 defaults, then with theme_project() and scales::label_*() applied. The data are identical; only the styling has changed.

base_data <- penguins_complete |> 
  count(island) |> 
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n))

p_default <- base_data |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = island, y = prop)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Island", y = "prop", title = "Default theme and scales") +
  theme_grey()

p_improved <- base_data |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_reorder(island, prop), y = prop)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#0072B2") +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = scales::breaks_extended(n = 5),
    labels = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 1),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))
  ) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Proportion of sampled penguins",
       title = "theme_project() and scales::label_percent()") +
  theme_project()

p_default + p_improved







Three concrete changes between the panels: the y-axis labels render as percentages, the bars are ordered (by fct_reorder) rather than alphabetical, and the grey panel background is gone. The data-ink ratio has improved without altering a single number.
Log scales
When a variable spans more than two orders of magnitude, transform to log. The scales package handles both breaks and labels:

scale_y_continuous(
  transform = "log10",
  breaks = scales::breaks_log(n = 5),
  labels = scales::label_log()
)

label_log() formats the labels as 10^1, 10^2, and so on, the standard notation for log-scaled data. The figure should also state the log transformation in either the axis title or the legend so the reader does not misread the scale as linear.






Note



Why this matters. A figure with theme_project() and formatted labels reads as finished; one with theme_grey() and default labels reads as a draft, however good the analysis.

title: Block 4: Extensions in action
text:
Distributions with ggdist
The base ggplot2 grammar covers most chart types but makes several common visualisation tasks awkward. The extension packages below fill the gaps:
Statistical annotation (significance brackets, p-value labels on figures) is not covered in this workshop. The principled approach is to fit a model with emmeans or equivalent and use ggpubr::stat_pvalue_manual() to render the contrasts. In a half-day workshop on visualisation principles, we leave statistical annotation to the wider statistical training in your programme.
Each segment is short: a problem and a worked example to run along with the facilitator (the In your own time tasks are for after the session). Keep moving, because the block ends with a 🏆 capstone challenge where you race to recreate a published-style figure from scratch, on data you have not seen. There is a bonus after that: making a multi-panel figure interactive.
The default way to summarise a continuous variable across groups is a boxplot. A boxplot is informative but lossy: it shows quartiles and outliers but conceals the shape of the underlying distribution. Bimodality, skew, and gaps in the data all vanish.
The raincloud plot (Allen et al., 2021) addresses this by combining three layers: a half-density (the “cloud”) to show distribution shape, a slim boxplot for summary statistics, and jittered points (the “rain”) for the raw data. ggdist::stat_halfeye() provides the cloud half.
penguins_complete |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species, colour = species)) +
  ggdist::stat_halfeye(
    adjust = 0.5,
    justification = -0.2,
    .width = 0,
    point_colour = NA,
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.12,
    outlier.shape = NA,
    alpha = 0.5,
    linewidth = 0.4,
    colour = "grey20"
  ) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.08, alpha = 0.4, size = 1.2) +
  colorspace::scale_fill_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") +
  colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Body mass (g)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
Three things to notice. First, the cloud, the box, and the points are three separate layers stacked in a specific order: clouds at the back, box in the middle, points on top. Second, justification = -0.2 shifts the cloud off the centre line so the box and points sit beside it rather than underneath. Third, the boxplot’s outlier points are hidden with outlier.shape = NA because all the raw data are already shown as jittered points; leaving them on would double-count.

title: Block 4: Extensions in action
text:
In your own time


Horizontal raincloud with point intervals


Modify the worked example to flip the orientation (raincloud horizontal rather than vertical) and to use ggdist::stat_pointinterval() instead of the boxplot. stat_pointinterval shows the median and a range; work out from the documentation which range it shows by default.




Solution


penguins_complete |> 
  ggplot(aes(y = species, x = body_mass_g, fill = species, colour = species)) +
  ggdist::stat_halfeye(
    adjust = 0.5,
    justification = -0.2,
    .width = 0,
    point_colour = NA,
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  ggdist::stat_pointinterval(
    .width = c(0.5, 0.95),
    point_size = 2.5
  ) +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.08, alpha = 0.2, size = 1.2, shape = 21) +
  colorspace::scale_fill_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") +
  colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(x = "Body mass (g)", y = NULL) +
  theme_project(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

title: Block 4: Extensions in action
section: Accessible colour with colorspace and colorBlindness
text:
Accessible colour with colorspace and colorBlindness
Two packages put the Block 1 principles into practice: colorspace builds the palette and colorBlindness checks it. Use them together, because a palette you have not checked leaves accessibility to chance.

fig <- penguins_complete |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = flipper_length_mm,
             colour = species, shape = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8, size = 2) +
  colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Flipper length (mm)",
       colour = "Species", shape = "Species") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

# Inspect under simulated colour vision deficiency
colorBlindness::cvdPlot(fig)







The four-panel grid shows: the original, deuteranopia, protanopia, and a desaturated (greyscale) version. The figure passes if all groups remain distinguishable in all four panels. If any panel fails (typically deuteranopia or protanopia for red-green sensitive figures), strengthen the redundant encoding (shape or linetype), choose a more separated palette, or fall back to direct labelling.
This is the encoding hierarchy from Block 1 in practice: position handles the two continuous variables (rank 1), colour hue handles the categorical (rank 2 for categorical data), and shape is added as a redundant cue so that the figure does not depend on colour alone. Shape is a weaker encoding on its own, but as a backup it is what keeps the groups apart in the greyscale panel.
In your own time


Redundant encoding under simulated CVD


Build a scatter plot from penguins_complete using only bill_length_mm and bill_depth_mm, colour mapped to species, and without shape mapped redundantly. Run colorBlindness::cvdPlot(). Now add shape = species to the mapping and rerun. Compare the two outputs honestly. Which encoding survives the desaturation test?




Solution


# Without redundant shape encoding
fig_no_shape <- penguins_complete |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, colour = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8, size = 2) +
  colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") +
  theme_project(base_size = 12)

colorBlindness::cvdPlot(fig_no_shape)

# With redundant shape encoding
fig_with_shape <- fig_no_shape +
  aes(shape = species) +
  labs(colour = "Species", shape = "Species")

colorBlindness::cvdPlot(fig_with_shape)

The figure with redundant shape encoding survives the desaturated panel because the shape carries the species information when the colour information collapses. The figure without redundant encoding becomes unreadable in greyscale.

title: Block 4: Extensions in action
section: Direct labelling with ggrepel and ggtext
text:
Direct labelling with ggrepel and ggtext
A figure legend separates the colour key from the data: the reader’s eye has to travel from the data layer to the legend and back, holding a mapping in working memory. Direct labelling puts the group name on the data itself, so the eye reads the label as part of the data. For talks, posters, and public engagement, direct labelling is almost always clearer.
The problem is that labels placed at data points overlap each other. ggrepel::geom_text_repel() and ggrepel::geom_label_repel() solve this by moving labels iteratively until they no longer collide, with connector lines preserved. The example below uses geom_label_repel(), which draws each label on a small background box.

# Label location: one label per species at the species centroid
label_data <- penguins_complete |> 
  group_by(species) |> 
  summarise(x = median(bill_length_mm),
            y = median(flipper_length_mm),
            .groups = "drop")

penguins_complete |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = flipper_length_mm, colour = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) +
  ggrepel::geom_label_repel(
    data = label_data,
    aes(x = x, y = y, label = species, colour = species),
    size = 5,
    fontface = "bold",
    label.size = 0,
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Flipper length (mm)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")







ggtext is the companion package for rich text: it allows markdown formatting inside titles, axis labels, and legend entries, and supports inline colour. This is what lets you write a title like "**Gentoo** penguins are <span style='color:#5F96C2;'>**substantially heavier**</span> than Adelie and Chinstrap" directly. To enable rich text on a theme element, set it to ggtext::element_markdown().

penguins_complete |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species)) +
  ggdist::stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5, justification = -0.2,
                       .width = 0, point_colour = NA, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5,
               colour = "grey20") +
  colorspace::scale_fill_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(
    title = "<span style='color:#5F96C2;'>**Gentoo**</span> penguins are substantially heavier than <span style='color:#C87A8A;'>**Adelie**</span> and <span style='color:#6B9D59;'>**Chinstrap**</span>",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Body mass (g)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        plot.title = ggtext::element_markdown(size = 13, lineheight = 1.2))







Inline colour in the title removes the need for a separate legend entirely. The hex codes in the title are the three Dark2 colours used for the fills (colorspace::qualitative_hcl(3, palette = "Dark2") returns them), so the colours in the title match the fills in the data, and the reader makes the mapping in a single saccade.
These techniques put the direct labelling and highlighting rows of the audience table from Block 2 into practice. Reach for direct labels and inline-coloured titles when designing for posters, talks, or public engagement, where the reader cannot afford the eye-travel to a separate legend.
In your own time


Highlight one species in a rich-text title


Take the rich-text title in the worked example and modify it so that only Gentoo is highlighted in colour (in #5F96C2, its Dark2 fill), and the other two species names appear in plain text. Then add a subtitle that gives the sample sizes for each species. The subtitle should also be rich text, so you will need to set plot.subtitle = ggtext::element_markdown() in theme().




Solution


n_species <- count(penguins_complete, species)

penguins_complete |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species)) +
  ggdist::stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5, justification = -0.2,
                       .width = 0, point_colour = NA, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5,
               colour = "grey20") +
  colorspace::scale_fill_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(
    title = "<span style='color:#5F96C2;'>**Gentoo**</span> penguins are substantially heavier than Adelie and Chinstrap",
    subtitle = paste0("*Pygoscelis* spp., Palmer Archipelago (n = ",
                      paste(n_species$n, n_species$species, collapse = ", "), ")"),
    x = NULL,
    y = "Body mass (g)"
  ) +
  theme_project(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        plot.title = ggtext::element_markdown(size = 13, lineheight = 1.2),
        plot.subtitle = ggtext::element_markdown(size = 10, colour = "grey40"))

title: Block 4: Extensions in action
text:
Multi-panel composition with patchwork
For panels showing the same chart type for different subsets of the data, use facet_wrap() or facet_grid(). For panels showing different chart types or different aspects of one analysis, use patchwork.
Three defaults apply for patchwork compositions: collect legends into a single shared legend, tag panels with uppercase letters, and use an explicit design = string for the layout. The string is self-documenting; you can rearrange the layout by editing the letters without rewriting the composition call.

pal <- colorspace::qualitative_hcl(3, palette = "Dark2")
names(pal) <- levels(penguins_complete$species)

p1 <- penguins_complete |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species)) +
  ggdist::stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5, justification = -0.2,
                       .width = 0, point_colour = NA, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal, name = "Species") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Body mass (g)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  guides(fill = "none")

p2 <- penguins_complete |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm,
             fill = species, shape = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal, name = "Species") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(21,22,23), name = "Species") +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Bill depth (mm)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

p3 <- penguins_complete |> 
  count(species, island) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = island, y = n, fill = species)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge2(preserve = "single")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal, name = "Species") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  guides(fill = "none")

# Edit the letter grid below to rearrange panels.
# Letters refer to plots in the order they are added (A = p1, B = p2, C = p3).
layout <- "
AB
CC
"

p1 + p2 + p3 +
  patchwork::plot_layout(design = layout, guides = "collect") +
  patchwork::plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        plot.tag = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12))













Noteguides





When you combine plots with patchwork and set guides = "collect", patchwork gathers legends from every panel and merges any it considers identical.
“Identical” is strict: the guides must share the same aesthetic, scale, breaks and title. If your panels encode the same grouping variable through different aesthetics (say fill in one panel and colour plus shape in another) or through different scales, patchwork treats them as distinct and shows one legend per panel rather than a single shared key.

First, decide which single legend should represent the shared variable across all panels, and choose the panel whose legend carries the most visual encoding, since that legend can serve as a complete key for the others.
Second, suppress the legends on the remaining panels with guides(<aesthetic> = "none").

Without step two you get this. The three panels below use different aesthetics and scales and none of them suppresses its legend, so patchwork collects three separate legends:

q1 <- penguins_complete |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species)) +
  ggdist::stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5, justification = -0.2,
                       .width = 0, point_colour = NA, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5) +
  colorspace::scale_fill_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Body mass (g)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

q2 <- penguins_complete |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm,
             colour = species, shape = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Bill depth (mm)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

q3 <- penguins_complete |> 
  count(species, island) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = n, fill = island)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  colorspace::scale_fill_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Set 2") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

# Edit the letter grid below to rearrange panels.
# Letters refer to plots in the order they are added (A = q1, B = q2, C = q3).
layout <- "
AB
CC
"

q1 + q2 + q3 +
  patchwork::plot_layout(design = layout, guides = "collect") +
  patchwork::plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        plot.tag = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12))










The & operator applies its right-hand side to every subplot already in the composition, so use it for global theme settings like legend position and tag formatting. The + operator applies only to the most recently added subplot.






Tip



Try later. Change the layout string so that panels A and C are stacked on the left and panel B occupies the full right column ("AB\nCB\n").


Use multi-panel composition for figures that combine several aspects of one analysis into a single figure. A typical journal “Figure 1” with three panels labelled A, B, C is almost always a patchwork composition, not a facet_wrap(). The layout string makes the composition easy to edit: if a reviewer asks you to rearrange the panels, you change the letters rather than rewrite the code.
In your own time


Rearrange the patchwork layout


Take the three-panel composition from the worked example. Change the layout string so that panel A spans the entire top row, and panels B and C share the bottom row. Then change tag_levels = "A" to tag_levels = "i" (lowercase Roman numerals) and observe the change. Finally, change tag_levels to c("A", "i") for nested tagging and see what happens.




Solution


layout <- "
AA
BC
"

p1 + p2 + p3 +
  patchwork::plot_layout(design = layout, guides = "collect") +
  patchwork::plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        plot.tag = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12))

# With lowercase Roman numeral tags
p1 + p2 + p3 +
  patchwork::plot_layout(design = layout, guides = "collect") +
  patchwork::plot_annotation(tag_levels = "i") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        plot.tag = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12))

# Nested tagging is for compositions of compositions; with a single
# layer of subplots, c("A", "i") behaves the same as "A".

title: Block 4: Extensions in action
text:
🏆 Capstone challenge: recreate this figure
Time to put the whole block together on data you have not seen. CO2 is built into R: CO2 uptake by 12 grass plants from Quebec and Mississippi, half of them chilled overnight, each measured at seven CO2 concentrations. Here is your target:










Recreate the figure: how far can you get? (solo race, 15 minutes)


Everyone starts at Bronze. Post 🥉, 🥈 or 🥇 in the chat each time you clear a tier. The first Gold screenshot wins. Stuck? Post your error message in the chat; anyone who helps fix it gets a shout-out.

🥉 Bronze: panel B. Raw points for each Treatment, dodged by Type, with a median bar, in the two Type colours. Hint: position_jitterdodge() and stat_summary(geom = "crossbar").
🥈 Silver: panel A. One line per plant, colour by Type, linetype by Treatment, and direct labels instead of a colour legend. Hint: group = Plant, and ggrepel on a small data frame of line ends.
🥇 Gold: the full figure. Both panels side by side (A twice as wide), tagged A and B, with the coloured rich-text title and proper sub/superscripts in the axis titles. Hint: patchwork, plot_annotation() and ggtext::element_markdown().





Solution: Bronze


co2_pal <- c(Quebec = "#1B9E77", Mississippi = "#D95F02")

CO2 |>
  ggplot(aes(Treatment, uptake, colour = Type)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.15, dodge.width = 0.6),
             alpha = 0.6) +
  stat_summary(fun = median, geom = "crossbar", width = 0.25,
               position = position_dodge(0.6), linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = co2_pal) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)




Solution: Silver and Gold

The full code for the target figure. Silver is target_a; Gold adds the composition at the end.

co2_ends <- CO2 |>
  filter(conc == max(conc)) |>
  summarise(uptake = mean(uptake), .by = Type) |>
  mutate(conc = 1000)

target_a <- CO2 |>
  ggplot(aes(conc, uptake, colour = Type, group = Plant, linetype = Treatment)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 1.2) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(
    data = co2_ends, aes(conc, uptake, label = Type, colour = Type),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, nudge_x = 80, direction = "y", hjust = 0,
    fontface = "bold", segment.colour = NA) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = co2_pal, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1250), breaks = seq(0, 1000, 250)) +
  labs(x = "Ambient CO<sub>2</sub> (mL L<sup>-1</sup>)",
       y = "CO<sub>2</sub> uptake (µmol m<sup>-2</sup> s<sup>-1</sup>)",
       linetype = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(axis.title.x = ggtext::element_markdown(),
        axis.title.y = ggtext::element_markdown(),
        legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

target_b <- CO2 |>
  ggplot(aes(Treatment, uptake, colour = Type)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.15, dodge.width = 0.6),
             alpha = 0.6) +
  stat_summary(fun = median, geom = "crossbar", width = 0.25,
               position = position_dodge(0.6), linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = co2_pal, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

(target_a + target_b + plot_layout(widths = c(2, 1))) +
  plot_annotation(
    tag_levels = "A",
    title = "Chilling cuts CO<sub>2</sub> uptake in <span style='color:#D95F02'>**Mississippi**</span> grasses far more than in <span style='color:#1B9E77'>**Quebec**</span> ones",
    theme = theme(plot.title = ggtext::element_markdown(size = 13)))

title: Block 4: Extensions in action
section: Bonus: linked, interactive panels with ggiraph
text:
Bonus: linked, interactive panels with ggiraph
Block 2 introduced ggiraph for a single plot. It also works on a whole patchwork composition, and that is where it gets fun: give every panel the same data_id, and hovering in one panel highlights the same group in all of them.

library(ggiraph)

i1 <- penguins_complete |>
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, colour = species,
             data_id = species,
             tooltip = paste0(species, ": ", body_mass_g, " g"))) +
  geom_jitter_interactive(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Body mass (g)")

i2 <- penguins_complete |>
  ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, colour = species,
             data_id = species,
             tooltip = paste0(species, ": ", bill_length_mm, " × ", bill_depth_mm, " mm"))) +
  geom_point_interactive(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Bill depth (mm)")

i3 <- penguins_complete |>
  count(species, island) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = island, y = n, fill = species,
             data_id = species, tooltip = paste0(species, " on ", island, ": ", n))) +
  geom_col_interactive(position = position_dodge2(preserve = "single")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Count")

linked <- (i1 + i2) / i3 &
  colorspace::scale_fill_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") &
  colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") &
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) &
  theme(legend.position = "none")

girafe(ggobj = linked, width_svg = 8, height_svg = 6,
       options = list(opts_hover(css = "stroke:black;stroke-width:1.5px;"),
                      opts_hover_inv(css = "opacity:0.15;")))





Hover over any Gentoo point or bar and watch the other two panels follow. (Panel A is a strip of raw points rather than a boxplot: geom_boxplot_interactive() tags each box by its group number, not its species, so it would not link up.) The recipe is the same one you already know: interactive geoms, a shared data_id, then girafe(). Everything else (the patchwork layout, & for shared settings, the Dark2 palette) is unchanged from the static version.






Tip



Try later. Add opts_selection(type = "single") to the options list and click a group instead of hovering. Then save the figure for a lab website with htmlwidgets::saveWidget(girafe(ggobj = linked), "linked_penguins.html").

title: Block 5: Saving figures correctly
text:
ggview for canvas-size preview
The on-screen plot pane is rarely the same physical size as the saved figure. A font that looks correct at 10pt in the RStudio plot pane can look quite different in the saved PDF, because the plot pane is sized to your window, not to the saved file, while the PDF is drawn at the dimensions you specify. This is the single most common source of “the figure looks fine on my screen but is unreadable in the manuscript” problems.
Two extensions and one habit solve this.
ggview (Domin, 2025) adds a canvas() layer to the plot. The preview then renders at the dimensions the file will be saved at, so what you see is what you save.
fig <- penguins_complete |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species)) +
  ggdist::stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5, justification = -0.2,
                       .width = 0, point_colour = NA, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5) +
  colorspace::scale_fill_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Body mass (g)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  ggview::canvas(width = 7, height = 5, units = "in", dpi = 300)

# Print displays the figure at the canvas size
print(fig)

# save_ggplot uses the canvas dimensions
ggview::save_ggplot(
  fig,
  here::here("outputs", "figures", "fig01_body_mass.png")
)
For one-off iteration, canvas() is lighter than the older camcorder package, which auto-saves every plot to disk. Use camcorder only when you specifically want a session-wide recording or a GIF of your iteration history.

title: Block 5: Saving figures correctly
text:
The ragg graphics device
ggsave() is the interface for writing figures; under the hood it calls a graphics device to do the rendering. For raster output (PNG, JPG, TIFF), ragg::agg_png is the modern recommended device because it renders text with better antialiasing and accesses system fonts without extrafont or showtext. (If you track figures in git, note that a PDF changes on every save, because it embeds a creation date.)
To set ragg as the plot pane backend in RStudio (≥1.4), go to Tools → Global Options → General → Graphics → Backend: AGG. For Quarto documents, set knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev = "ragg_png") in the setup chunk.

title: Block 5: Saving figures correctly
text:
The two-format default
Save publication figures in two formats:


PDF for inclusion in LaTeX manuscripts and final journal submission. A vector format that scales to any size, and the default for serious typesetting.

PNG at 300 dpi via ragg::agg_png for slides, posters, and quick previews.


ggplot2::ggsave(
  filename = here::here("outputs", "figures", "fig01_body_mass.pdf"),
  plot = fig,
  width = 7,
  height = 5,
  units = "in"
)

ggplot2::ggsave(
  filename = here::here("outputs", "figures", "fig01_body_mass.png"),
  plot = fig,
  width = 7,
  height = 5,
  units = "in",
  dpi = 300,
  device = ragg::agg_png,
  bg = "white"
)

bg = "white" is a safe default for PNG output. Without it, ggsave() takes the background from the theme’s plot.background, so bg = "white" guards against themes with a blank background, such as ThemePark or custom themes. Those would otherwise give a transparent PNG, which displays badly in many viewers.






Warning



Always specify width, height, units, and dpi explicitly. Never rely on ggsave() defaults. The defaults rarely match the dimensions of the figure you actually want.








Note



Interactive figures (the ggiraph examples from Blocks 2 and 4) are web pages, not images, so ggsave() cannot write them. Save them as HTML with htmlwidgets::saveWidget(girafe(ggobj = fig), "fig.html"), and always save a static PDF/PNG of the same plot as well, for the manuscript.


Next, Block 6 shows how to write the legend that goes with a saved figure.

title: Block 6: Writing figure legends
text:
The four elements
A figure in a journal or lab report is not finished until its legend is. The legend lets a reader understand the figure without going back to the main text, which is the third of the three questions for every figure (Block 7): is the figure self-contained?
Write a legend as four elements, in this order:
Most bad legends fail in one of two ways: they are too vague (leaving out details the reader needs), or they put the wrong kind of thing in an element (a result where a description belongs, or a plot name where a definition belongs).

title: Block 6: Writing figure legends
text:
Descriptive sentence. What the figure shows, stated neutrally, in the past tense. A description, not a result.

Methods and sample. Where the data came from (with a citation), the sample size for each group, and any exclusions.

Statistical model and result. The test, the test statistic with its degrees of freedom, the p-value (exact, or bounded such as p < 0.001), and any adjustment for multiple comparisons. Leave this element out if the figure is purely descriptive: never invent a test to fill it.

Visual components defined. Every layer on the figure (density, box, points, error bars, colours, shapes) explained.

title: Block 6: Writing figure legends
text:
Game: legend triage
The facilitator puts each fragment on screen. Post your verdict in the chat, then check it here.






Fragment
Your verdict



“Body mass of three penguin species in the Palmer Archipelago, Antarctica.”

Good
Bad: a result, not a description
Bad: too vague or missing details
Bad: names the plot but defines nothing


“Gentoo penguins are heavier.”

Good
Bad: a result, not a description
Bad: too vague or missing details
Bad: names the plot but defines nothing


“n = 342.”

Good
Bad: a result, not a description
Bad: too vague or missing details
Bad: names the plot but defines nothing


“Shows a raincloud plot.”

Good
Bad: a result, not a description
Bad: too vague or missing details
Bad: names the plot but defines nothing


“ANOVA showed differences (p < 0.05).”

Good
Bad: a result, not a description
Bad: too vague or missing details
Bad: names the plot but defines nothing





Why?



“n = 342” gives only the total. The reader needs the sample size for each group, the data source and any exclusions.

“ANOVA showed differences (p < 0.05)” names a test, but gives no test statistic, no degrees of freedom and only a threshold rather than the p-value.

“Shows a raincloud plot” tells the reader what kind of plot it is, but not what the cloud, the box or the points mean.

title: Block 6: Writing figure legends
text:
🏆 Challenge: legend repair









Figure 1. Gentoo penguins are heavier. Data from a survey (n = 342). Species differed significantly (p < 0.05). Shows a raincloud plot.



Legend repair (solo race, 10 minutes)


The legend above breaks every rule. Rewrite it as a four-element legend for this figure.
What you need to know:

The data are body masses from the Palmer Penguins dataset (Horst, Hill and Gorman, 2020). Penguins with no recorded body mass were excluded.
A one-way ANOVA of body mass on species was fitted, with Tukey-adjusted pairwise contrasts.
Work out the sample sizes and the ANOVA result yourself:


legend_data <- palmerpenguins::penguins |>
  tidyr::drop_na(body_mass_g)

count(legend_data, species)

anova(lm(body_mass_g ~ species, data = legend_data))

Post your legend in the chat. Scoring: one point for each element that is present and correct, and a bonus point if every visual layer (cloud, box, points) is defined. The facilitator reads out the best one.




Solution: a four-element legend


Figure 1. Body mass (g) of three penguin species (Pygoscelis adeliae, P. antarcticus and P. papua) in the Palmer Archipelago, Antarctica. Data are from the Palmer Penguins dataset (Horst, Hill and Gorman, 2020); penguins with no recorded body mass were excluded, giving 151 Adelie, 68 Chinstrap and 123 Gentoo individuals. A one-way ANOVA showed that body mass differed between species (F(2, 339) = 343.6, p < 0.001); pairwise contrasts were Tukey-adjusted. The shaded region shows a kernel density estimate of each distribution; the box shows the interquartile range with the median as a horizontal line; points are individual penguins, jittered horizontally.

The four elements are, in order: the descriptive sentence; the source, exclusions and sample sizes; the test and its result; and the definitions of the cloud, box and points. Note that the legend still describes: the conclusion (“Gentoo are heavier”) belongs in the main text or, for a talk or poster, in an explanatory title (Block 2).







Note



In the Quarto session you will put a legend like this into a figure’s fig-cap option, so the caption travels with the figure and can be cross-referenced in your text.

title: Block 6: Writing figure legends
section: Block 7: Three questions for every figure
text:
Block 7: Three questions for every figure
Every figure you produce, in every context, should answer three questions. If it cannot, it is not finished.

Does the visual impression match the data? Honest axes, appropriate encoding, no distortion. The reader should reach the same conclusion from the figure that they would reach from the underlying numbers.
Who is the audience and does the design serve them? Complexity, annotation density, and font size calibrated to the reader. A journal figure, a poster figure and a public engagement figure each need a different design.
Is the figure self-contained? Labels, units, a legend that defines every visual layer, and ideally the script that produced it, so a future reader (including yourself) can reconstruct what you did and why.

Final check: true or false?

A bar chart of means may start its y-axis at any value, as long as it is labelled. 
TRUE
FALSE

Colour should never be the only cue that distinguishes groups. 
TRUE
FALSE


theme_barbie() is fine for a journal figure if the reviewers like pink. 
TRUE
FALSE

An interactive ggiraph figure can replace the static figure in a PDF manuscript. 
TRUE
FALSE

Setting base_size scales every text element in the figure together. 
TRUE
FALSE

A figure legend should state the main conclusion in its first sentence. 
TRUE
FALSE

title: Block 6: Writing figure legends
text:
Take-home exercise
Your homework is to apply everything from the workshop to your own data. The aim is to produce one publication-ready figure from your own dataset, using the techniques from Blocks 1 to 7.


Take-home: one publication-ready figure


Choose a dataset from your own research with at least one continuous variable, one categorical grouping, and a sample size of at least thirty observations. Produce one publication-ready figure that applies the principles and extensions from this workshop:


Block 1. Variable types determine the chart. Honest axes. Accessible palette via colorspace. The encoding hierarchy applied: most important variable to position, most important categorical to colour hue with shape redundantly.

Block 2. Audience-appropriate framing: pick journal/lab report unless you have a specific other audience in mind. Descriptive title.

Block 3. A theme_project() (or equivalent) applied; scales formatted with scales::breaks_pretty() and an appropriate scales::label_*() function for the units.

Block 4. At least one extension used appropriately (raincloud distribution display, direct labelling with ggrepel or ggtext, or multi-panel composition with patchwork).

Block 5. Save the figure as both PDF and PNG using ragg::agg_png for the PNG; verify with colorBlindness::cvdPlot() before saving.

Block 6. Write a four-element legend for it.

Block 7. Check it against the three questions.



A skeleton to adapt

# !! PARTICIPANT: replace the data load with your own file.
my_data <- readr::read_csv(here::here("data", "my_data.csv"))

# Source the project theme function defined in Block 3
# (paste theme_project() into R/functions/plot_functions.R first)
source(here::here("R", "functions", "plot_functions.R"))

# Build the figure using the patterns from Blocks 1-4.
# Example structure (modify to match your variables and audience):
my_figure <- my_data |>
  tidyr::drop_na(<your_continuous_var>, <your_grouping_var>) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(x = <your_grouping_var>,
                               y = <your_continuous_var>,
                               fill = <your_grouping_var>)) +
  ggdist::stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5, justification = -0.2,
                       .width = 0, point_colour = NA, alpha = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5) +
  colorspace::scale_fill_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = scales::breaks_pretty(n = 6)
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "<Variable name (unit)>") +
  theme_project(base_size = 12) +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "none")

# Verify accessibility before saving
colorBlindness::cvdPlot(my_figure)

# Save in both formats
ggplot2::ggsave(
  filename = here::here("outputs", "figures", "my_figure.pdf"),
  plot = my_figure,
  width = 7, height = 5, units = "in"
)
ggplot2::ggsave(
  filename = here::here("outputs", "figures", "my_figure.png"),
  plot = my_figure,
  width = 7, height = 5, units = "in",
  dpi = 300, device = ragg::agg_png, bg = "white"
)







Tip



If your figure passes colorBlindness::cvdPlot() and the legend would let someone understand it without the manuscript text, you have met the standard. If either fails, fix it before submitting.








Note



These rules as an AI skill. Everything in this workshop, from the chart-type and audience tables to the accessibility check and the two-format save, can be written down once for an AI assistant to follow. Day 4 does exactly that: the instructions-and-skills block provides pub-figures, a skill that packages these conventions with a fuller version of theme_project(), and shows you how to test whether an assistant actually follows them.

title: Block 1: Quarto
text:
Learning outcomes
By the end of this session, you will be able to:

Create a Quarto document from scratch
Render documents to HTML and PDF
Include figures and tables with proper captions
Control figure size and placement
Reference figures and tables dynamically
Install and use a Quarto extension or journal template
