title: Block 1: GitHub
text:
The mental model
You do not need to understand Git’s internals to use it well, but you do need one mental model.
A Git repository (or repo) is a project folder whose change history Git tracks. Within it, a file passes through three states:


Untracked / modified. You create or edit a file. Git sees that it has changed but does nothing with it yet.

Staged. You add the file to the staging area, marking it for inclusion in the next snapshot.

Committed. You commit the staged changes, writing a permanent, labelled snapshot into the repository’s history.

The everyday loop is therefore modify → add → commit, repeated whenever you reach a natural stopping point. A good habit is to commit each time you complete a discrete task, so that each commit corresponds to one coherent change.







Figure 1: The local Git workflow: modify, stage (add), commit.




These actions exist both as buttons in the RStudio Git pane and as terminal commands. The two are equivalent; this workshop uses the RStudio interface, but the terminal forms are shown alongside so you can recognise them.






NoteThe same actions at the command line



git add <file>     # stage a file for the next commit
git commit -m "A short, descriptive message"   # snapshot the staged files


Local versus remote
Everything above describes the local workflow, where the repository lives only on your machine. A local repository can also be connected to a remote repository hosted on a server. This workshop uses GitHub; GitLab is a common alternative.
Two further actions move commits between local and remote. You push to send your local commits up to the remote, bringing the two into agreement. When a collaborator pushes their commits, your local copy becomes outdated, and you pull to bring those commits down.







Figure 2: Push sends local commits to the remote; pull retrieves remote commits.










NoteThe same actions at the command line



git push    # upload local commits to the remote
git pull    # download remote commits to the local repo

title: Block 1: GitHub
text:
One-time setup
Before creating your first repository, three things must be in place: Git must be installed, Git must know who you are, and Git must be able to authenticate to GitHub on your behalf. You do this once per machine.
Install Git and create a GitHub account

Install Git on your machine.
Create a free account at github.com.







Note



You can confirm that RStudio can see your Git installation under Tools → Global Options → Git/SVN, where the path to the Git executable should be shown.


Introduce yourself to Git
Git labels every commit with a name and email. Set these once, using the usethis package:

library(usethis)
use_git_config(
  user.name  = "Jane Doe",
  user.email = "jane@example.org"
)

Use the email associated with your GitHub account. The equivalent at the command line is:






Note



git config --global user.name 'Jane Doe'
git config --global user.email 'jane@example.org'


Authenticate with a Personal Access Token
GitHub no longer accepts account passwords for Git operations; it uses a Personal Access Token (PAT) instead. The recommended workflow for R users keeps you inside R and stores the token in your operating system’s credential manager rather than in any file.
Step 1: generate a token. This opens a GitHub page with sensible scopes pre-selected. Give the token a descriptive name, set an expiry, and generate it. Leave the page open and copy the token to your clipboard.

usethis::create_github_token()

Step 2: store the token. This registers the token with your OS credential store, from which usethis, gh and gert retrieve it automatically. Paste the token when prompted.

gitcreds::gitcreds_set()

Step 3: verify. Either of these confirms that a valid, discoverable token is in place and reports its scopes:

usethis::gh_token_help()
usethis::git_sitrep()







WarningDo not store your token in a tracked file



Earlier guidance sometimes suggested saving the PAT in a plain-text file or in .Renviron. The current recommendation from the usethis maintainers is to store it only in the OS credential manager via gitcreds_set(), and to treat the token like a password. On Windows and macOS the credential manager persists the token indefinitely, so you should not need to re-enter it. If you have a legacy GITHUB_PAT line in .Renviron, delete it, as it can interfere with the credential-store approach.

title: Block 1: GitHub
text:
Create a repository (GitHub first)
There are several ways to start a repository. The “GitHub first” approach (create the remote repository, then clone it locally) is the most reliable, because GitHub configures the link between local and remote for you, which avoids a common class of setup errors.
Create the remote repository

Log in at github.com.
Click the + (Create something new) in the top-right corner, then New repository.

Choose a template: leave as No template.

Owner: your account. Repository name: e.g. my-first-repo.

Description: a short, human-readable summary.

Visibility: Public.

README, .gitignore and licence: leave all of these off (you will configure everything from R).
Click Create repository, then copy the repository URL from the Quick Setup page.
Clone into RStudio
In RStudio: File → New Project → Version Control → Git. Paste the repository URL into the “Repository URL” field, choose a parent folder, and click Create Project.
The resulting folder is simultaneously a Git repository, a clone linked to your GitHub remote, and an RStudio Project. RStudio also adds a .gitignore file listing files Git should not track (for example .Rhistory).






Tip



Open .gitignore and read it. Adding a filename here keeps that file local and prevents it from ever being pushed to GitHub. This is useful for large data, cached output, or anything sensitive.

title: Block 1: GitHub
text:
The solo local cycle
This section covers the modify → add → commit loop entirely on your own machine.






WarningInstall packages first, but never inside a script



The exercise below uses tidyverse and palmerpenguins. Install them once at the console with install.packages(c("tidyverse", "palmerpenguins")), or renv::install() if you use renv. Never place install.packages() inside a script or Quarto document, as it would re-download the packages on every run. Note the package is palmerpenguins, with a trailing s.




Track some changes



Create a new .qmd file.
Add a setup chunk that loads the packages:


---
title: "analysis"
format:
  html:
    embed-resources: true
---

```{r}
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
```

Save the file.









Note



For HTML output, you need to embed resources if you want to share a single file; otherwise, things like images are kept in a separate folder.


See what has changed
The RStudio Git pane lists every file that has been added, modified or deleted since the last commit. An icon indicates the kind of change:







Figure 3: Modified file.











Figure 4: New, untracked file.











Figure 5: Deleted file.




Right-click a file and choose Diff to see line-by-line changes:







Figure 6: The diff window highlights additions (green) and deletions (red).




Added text is shown on a green background and removed text on red. If you have a colour-vision deficiency, the line numbers in the two left-hand columns indicate which side each change belongs to.
Stage and commit
A commit is a labelled snapshot of your project at a moment in time. Git gives each commit a unique identifier and records who made it and when.


Commit your changes



In the Git pane, tick the checkbox beside the file to stage it.
Click Commit, write a descriptive message (phrase it as what the change does, e.g. “Add setup chunk loading tidyverse and palmerpenguins”), and confirm.









Tip



You can stage files selectively, but most of the time you will stage everything that has changed since the last commit.


Commits are stored locally. The Git pane shows how many commits your local repo is ahead of the remote.







Figure 7: The Git pane indicates how far ahead of the remote you are.

title: Block 1: GitHub
text:
The solo remote cycle
Push


Push your commits


Click Push (the green up-arrow) in the Git pane. Nothing appears on GitHub until you push.


Refresh your repository page on GitHub: the committed files now appear. Click Commits to browse the history; each entry lets you inspect the project’s state at that point and view the file differences.
Make a change on GitHub, then pull
You can also edit directly on GitHub. Your local copy is then out of date, and you must pull the change down to it.


Add a README and pull it



On the repository main page, click Add a README.
Write a short description (READMEs are written in Markdown).
Click Commit changes…, enter a commit message in the dialog, and click Commit changes.
Back in RStudio, click Pull (the blue down-arrow). The README should appear among your local files.









WarningPull before you start, to avoid merge conflicts



Changes made on GitHub exist only on the remote until you pull them. If you edit a file locally while your copy is out of date, you risk a merge conflict: Git cannot reconcile two incompatible versions of the same lines and asks you to resolve it by hand. To avoid this, pull at the start of every session before doing anything else. The message is usually “Already up to date”, but the habit is worth keeping.

title: Block 1: GitHub
text:
Working with branches
A branch is an independent line of development. Branches let you work on a new analysis, a manuscript section, or a bug fix without disturbing the stable main branch. When the work is ready, you merge it back into main.
Create a branch on GitHub


Create a branch



On the repository page, click the branch drop-down (showing main).
Type a new branch name, e.g. new-plot, and press Enter to create it.








Figure 8: Creating a branch from the GitHub web interface.






Work on the branch in RStudio

Click Pull to retrieve the new branch.
In the Git pane, use the branch drop-down (next to New Branch) to switch to new-plot. This is “checking out” the branch.
Work proceeds exactly as before: stage, commit, push. Commits go to new-plot and leave main untouched until you merge.



Add a figure on the branch


Add a chunk that produces a figure, then commit and push it to new-plot.

```{r}
#| label: fig-penguins
#| fig-cap: "Body mass against flipper length, by species."
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)

pal <- c(
  "Adelie"    = "#FF8C00",
  "Chinstrap" = "#A034F0",
  "Gentoo"    = "#159090"
)

penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = species)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal) +
  theme_minimal()
```


Merge via a pull request
Back on GitHub, your pushed branch is offered for comparison. Merging it into main is done through a pull request (PR), which records the proposed change and lets it be reviewed before integration.


Open and merge a pull request



Click Compare & pull request.
On the next page, click Create pull request.










Figure 9: Opening a pull request.




GitHub compares main with new-plot and confirms whether the two can be merged without conflict.







Figure 10: GitHub reports a clean, mergeable pull request.




Click Merge pull request, then Confirm merge. Once merged, delete the branch with Delete branch, since its changes now live in main. Finally, return to RStudio, switch back to main, and Pull so your local main includes the merged work.







Figure 11: Deleting a branch after its changes are merged.










NoteDo I need branches?



If you are working alone, branches are optional. You can work directly on main and push whenever you like. If you are working with others, branches are essential for keeping work organised and avoiding conflicts.
Keep branches short-lived and focused. You must resolve any merge conflicts by hand, and that is far simpler when a branch contains one small, coherent change.

title: Block 1: GitHub
text:
Collaborating on a repository
Collaboration takes one of two forms, depending on whether you have write access.
With write access (typical for a team you belong to), you clone the repo and use the workflow above directly. GitHub checks your permissions when you push. The only additional requirement is communication: avoid two people editing the same file at once, which is the usual source of merge conflicts.
Without write access (typical when contributing to a stranger’s project, for example fixing a bug in an open-source package), you fork the repository. A fork is a personal copy under your own account, to which you have full access. You work in the fork as normal (modify, add, commit, push) and then open a pull request to propose your changes to the original. The owner may accept, reject, or request changes.







Figure 12: A fork is a personal copy of another user’s repository.




Exercise: contribute to someone else’s repository


Fork, edit, and open a pull request



Log in at github.com (sign up with your institutional email if you do not have an account).
Search for the repository Philip-Leftwich/5023Y-Happy-Git.
Open it and review its structure.

Fork the repository.
Copy the clone URL and create a new RStudio Project via New Project → Version Control → Git.
Open some_cool_animals.qmd and its rendered output.
Add your name at the top of the document.
Add a new section with your favourite animal: an image and a few facts.
Render the document to update the output.

Stage → Commit → Push all files.
On GitHub, refresh to confirm the files have updated.





Open the pull request



On your fork, find the banner saying your branch is ahead of the original, open the Contribute menu, and choose Open a pull request.
On the comparison page, click Create pull request.
Add a title and description, then click Create pull request again to submit.



The repository owner receives a notification and can review, comment on, and choose whether to merge your contribution.

title: Block 1: GitHub
text:
General workflow habits






Tip




Pull at the start of every session, to retrieve the current state from GitHub before doing any work. This is the single most effective habit for avoiding conflicts.
Commit and push in small, meaningful increments, often. You may make many commits in a session; always push before you finish.
Treated this way, your GitHub repository becomes the authoritative master copy of your project.

title: Block 1: GitHub
text:
Publishing and reuse
A profile README
A profile README is displayed at the top of your GitHub profile page and lets you introduce yourself: your work and interests, contributions you are proud of, and how others can engage with your projects.







Figure 13: A profile README displayed on a GitHub profile.




Useful guides:

https://dev.to/ruppysuppy/beautify-your-github-profile-like-a-pro-5093
https://docs.github.com/en/account-and-profile/setting-up-and-managing-your-github-profile/customizing-your-profile/managing-your-profile-readme
Releases, tags, and a DOI
A tag marks a specific commit as a fixed point, such as a version release, a manuscript submission, or any other milestone. Unlike a branch, a tag does not move as new commits are added, so it permanently records the exact state of your project at that moment. See GitHub’s guide to managing releases.
Once a project is a well-organised repository, generating a permanent DOI is close to a one-click process through Zenodo or Figshare. Each release can carry its own DOI, letting you cite distinct stages (a preprint and a peer-reviewed version, for example) in your papers.







Figure 14: A Zenodo DOI badge for a GitHub release.










TipA note on template repositories



When you created your first repository you were told to leave Choose a template as No template. A template repository is an existing repository whose files and folder structure GitHub copies as the starting point for a new one, which is useful when you repeatedly create projects with the same layout (a standard folder structure, a licence, a .gitignore, and so on). You did not need one here, but once your own projects settle into a consistent shape, marking a repository as a template can save setting it up by hand each time. See GitHub’s guide to creating a template repository.
Do not confuse this with the project and document templates offered inside RStudio and Quarto, which are a separate mechanism.

title: Block 1: GitHub
text:
Glossary








Term
Definition



clone
A copy of a repository on your own computer, still linked to the remote so changes can be pushed and pulled to keep them synced.


commit
An individual, labelled change to a set of files. Git assigns each commit a unique ID and records who made it and when.


commit message
Short text accompanying a commit that describes the change it introduces.


fork
A personal copy of another user’s repository under your own account, from which you can open pull requests back to the original.


Git
An open-source system for tracking changes in files; the technology GitHub is built on.


Markdown
A lightweight text format for writing prose with simple structural markup (links, lists, headings).


pull
Fetching commits from the remote and merging them into your local copy.


push
Sending your committed changes from the local repo to the remote.


README
A text file describing a repository’s contents; usually the first thing a visitor reads.


repository (repo)
The basic unit of GitHub: a project folder containing all files and their full revision history.


Quarto
A publishing system that interleaves Markdown prose with executable code chunks (including R) to render many output formats.


personal access token (PAT)
A token used in place of a password for Git operations over HTTPS.

title: Block 1: GitHub
text:
Further reading


Happy Git and GitHub for the useR, Jenny Bryan et al. — the definitive reference for the workflow taught here.

title: Block 1: GitHub
text:
Bonus exercise: resolving merge conflicts
Practise handling merge conflicts in a collaborative setting using this NCEAS exercise. You will need a partner.

title: Block 2: GitHub Automations
text:
Bridging Block 1 and Block 2
In Block 1 you built a repository (the my-first-repo clone) containing a Quarto document that loads tidyverse and palmerpenguins and produces a figure of body mass against flipper length. That figure was developed on the new-plot branch and merged into main. Block 2 now adds two automated checks to that same repository, so the work here extends what you already have rather than starting afresh.
Before continuing, confirm three things:

title: Block 2: GitHub Automations
text:
You are on the main branch.
You have pulled the merged work, so the figure code is present in your local main.
Your Quarto file has a known name. Rename it to analysis.qmd if it does not already match, since every task below refers to that name.

Set up renv in your penguins repository
Block 2 assumes your project tracks its dependencies with renv, which Block 1 did not set up. Initialise it now, once, at the console:

renv::init()

renv::init() creates the project library, writes the renv.lock file and, in RStudio, restarts R so that the project library takes over. You do not need to run renv::snapshot() straight afterwards, because init() has already done it. The lockfile records the packages your code uses. renv finds them by scanning your project’s scripts and Quarto documents for library() calls and pkg::fn() usages, so here it records tidyverse and palmerpenguins because analysis.qmd loads them. Packages that are merely installed, or loaded at the console, are not recorded. Commit renv.lock, .Rprofile and the renv/ folder through the Git pane before proceeding. The .Rprofile file is what switches renv on whenever R starts in this project, so it needs to be committed too.






Note



With renv.lock committed, the “Before you start” checks below will pass rather than report a missing lockfile. Everything in this block now operates on your penguins repository: the hook guards its lockfile, and the Action renders its document.


What you will learn
By the end of this tutorial you will have two automated checks running in your penguins project, and your penguins document published on the web:

A git hook that runs on your machine every time you commit, checking that your renv.lock file is up to date.
A GitHub Actions workflow that runs on GitHub’s servers every time you push, automatically rendering your penguins Quarto document and storing the output for download.
A GitHub Pages site that publishes your rendered penguins document at a public web address.

The hook and the workflow need no manual triggering. All three connect directly to the project workflow you established in Block 1.
The mental model: two gates, two purposes
Before writing any code, it is worth understanding what these tools are and why you would use both.
A git hook is a script that fires automatically when a specific git event occurs: in this case, when you run git commit. It runs on your own machine, before the commit completes. If the script fails, the commit is blocked and you see an error message explaining why. This makes hooks ideal for catching problems before they leave your machine.
GitHub Actions is a set of instructions stored in your repository that GitHub’s servers execute automatically when a specified event occurs: in this case, when you push. In practice, “GitHub’s servers” means a brand-new computer with nothing installed: no R, no packages, no files. GitHub provides that computer, downloads your repository onto it, and follows your instructions step by step. This is what is meant by a “clean environment”: there are no local settings, no previously installed packages, and no assumptions about your machine. If your code works there, it does not depend on anything that exists only on your machine.
The two tools do different jobs. The hook catches problems locally before they are committed. Actions verifies that your code works in a clean environment after they are pushed. Together they form two checkpoints:
You write code
↓
git commit 
↓
[HOOK: renv check]
↓
git push 
↓
[ACTIONS: render Quarto]
A note on YAML
The GitHub Actions workflow file is written in YAML (rhymes with “camel”). YAML is a format for writing structured configuration; think of it as a way of expressing a nested list using indentation rather than brackets. You do not need to learn YAML deeply for this tutorial; the file is fully annotated and you only need to make small edits to adapt it to your project. The one rule that matters: indentation is significant. Use spaces, not tabs, and keep the indentation consistent with the examples shown.
A note on r-lib/actions
The R community maintains a library of pre-built GitHub Actions specifically for R users, available at https://github.com/r-lib/actions. These cover common tasks such as installing R, restoring renv packages, and running checks. Rather than writing these steps from scratch, you can use them in your workflow file with a single line. This tutorial uses two of them: setup-r and setup-renv. When you are ready to go further, the r-lib/actions repository contains a full set of examples for other tasks.

title: Block 2: GitHub Automations
text:
Before you start
You should be working in the penguins repository from Block 1, on the main branch, with the merged figure code present and your Quarto file named analysis.qmd. You should also have run renv::init() as set out in the bridge above, and committed renv.lock, .Rprofile and the renv/ folder.
Check that renv.lock is committed. In RStudio, open the Git pane (usually in the top-right panel). In Positron, open the Source Control view from the Activity Bar on the left. If renv.lock appears in the list of changed files, it has not been committed yet. If it does not appear, it is already committed and you are ready to proceed.
If renv.lock is not yet committed, run the following in R and then commit the result using the Git pane:

renv::snapshot()

Check your branch name. In RStudio’s Git pane, your current branch name is shown at the top. In Positron, it is shown in the status bar at the bottom left. If it says main, you are ready to proceed. If it says master or something else, note the name, because you will need to substitute it in the workflow file in Part 2.
Confirm your penguins Quarto document. Your project should contain analysis.qmd, the document carrying the body-mass-against-flipper-length figure you built in Block 1. If you have not renamed it yet, do so now so that the tasks below match.

title: Block 2: GitHub Automations
section: Part 1: Your first hook (checking renv synchronisation)
text:
Part 1: Your first hook (checking renv synchronisation)
Why this matters
renv tracks your project’s package dependencies in renv.lock. When your code starts using a new package, or you update or remove one, renv.lock must be updated with renv::snapshot() to reflect the change. If you forget, anyone who restores from your lockfile — including yourself on a new machine, or GitHub Actions — will get a different set of packages. This is one of the most common reproducibility failures in R projects and one of the easiest to prevent automatically.
How the hook works
Every time you run git commit, the hook calls renv::status(). If your installed packages and renv.lock are out of sync, the commit is blocked and you are told to run renv::snapshot(). If they are in sync, the commit proceeds normally. You do not interact with the hook directly; it runs on its own.
Setting up the hook with usethis
The usethis package provides a function that creates the hook file and sets the correct file permissions in a single R call, with no terminal commands required.
First, install usethis into this project, even if you already have it elsewhere. Now that renv is active, R only looks in the project library, so a copy you installed for other projects is not visible here:

install.packages("usethis")

Create a file called scripts/hooks/pre-commit.sh containing the following:
#!/usr/bin/env bash

echo "--- Checking renv synchronisation..."
"Rscript" --no-save --no-restore-data -e '
  if (!isTRUE(renv::status()$synchronized)) {
    message("\nrenv is out of sync with renv.lock.\nRun renv::snapshot() then commit again.\n")
    quit(status = 1)
  }
  message("renv check passed.")
'






Warning



This script assumes Rscript is available on your system PATH, which is the default on macOS and Linux. On Windows, R is not always added to the PATH. If the hook fails with a “command not found” error, replace Rscript in the script above with the full path to your installation:

file.path(R.home("bin"), "Rscript") # find your Rscript.exe

For example, "/c/Program Files/R/R-4.6.1/bin/x64/Rscript". Adjust the version number to match your installed version of R.
#!/usr/bin/env bash

echo "--- Checking renv synchronisation..."
"/c/Program Files/R/R-4.6.1/bin/x64/Rscript" --no-save --no-restore-data -e '
  if (!isTRUE(renv::status()$synchronized)) {
    message("\nrenv is out of sync with renv.lock.\nRun renv::snapshot() then commit again.\n")
    quit(status = 1)
  }
  message("renv check passed.")
'



usethis::use_git_hook(
  hook   = "pre-commit",
  script = readLines("scripts/hooks/pre-commit.sh") |> paste(collapse = "\n")
)

usethis::use_git_hook() writes the script into .git/hooks/pre-commit and makes it executable. You do not need to use the terminal for any of this.

What is .git/? Every git repository contains a hidden folder called .git/ that stores git’s internal data: your commit history, configuration, and hooks. You will not normally interact with it directly. It does not appear in RStudio’s Files pane because it is hidden; you can see it in your operating system’s file explorer if you enable hidden files.

Watch the hook block a commit
We will now deliberately trigger the hook on your penguins repository so you can see it work. Your existing figure colours the points by species; suppose you decide to format the body-mass axis with thousands separators, which the scales package provides. Using scales in your document without snapshotting is the kind of mismatch the hook is designed to catch.


Watch the hook block a commit (this commit is meant to fail)


This task deliberately triggers the hook so you can see it work. The first commit attempt is supposed to be blocked. That is the demonstration, not an error on your part.


Install scales at the console (a package you have not yet snapshotted):

install.packages("scales")   # or renv::install("scales")



Edit the figure chunk in analysis.qmd to use it. For example, load the package and format the y-axis:
```{r}
#| label: fig-penguins
#| fig-cap: "Body mass against flipper length, by species."
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
library(scales)

pal <- c(
  "Adelie"    = "#FF8C00",
  "Chinstrap" = "#A034F0",
  "Gentoo"    = "#159090"
)

penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = species)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  theme_minimal()
```
Save the file.

Your document now uses scales (via library(scales)), but renv.lock does not record it: you have not snapshotted. That is what puts the project out of sync. Stage the file in the Git pane and attempt to commit.
The commit is blocked. The hook reports that renv is out of sync and tells you to run renv::snapshot().
Run renv::snapshot() at the console to record scales in the lockfile. Stage the updated renv.lock alongside your other changes and commit again. This time it succeeds.



The point to take from step 3 is that the block was caused by code that uses a package missing from renv.lock, not by the install itself. renv’s default ("implicit") snapshot only records packages your code uses, so installing scales and never using it would not trip the hook; adding library(scales) (or a scales::label_comma() call) without snapshotting does.






WarningBypassing the hook



Occasionally you will need to commit despite the hook, for instance when it raises a false positive or you must record an urgent change. The --no-verify flag skips the hook for a single commit, leaving it in place for the next one:
git commit --no-verify -m "your message"
Keep this for occasional use: a hook you bypass by habit checks nothing. RStudio’s Commit button has no equivalent tick box, so a bypass must be done at the terminal, which adds a useful bit of friction.








NoteRemoving the hook permanently



If you want to disable the check altogether, delete or rename the hook file at .git/hooks/pre-commit in your operating system’s file explorer (it is hidden by default). A deleted hook can only be restored by recreating it with usethis::use_git_hook(), so prefer --no-verify for one-off cases and reserve removal for when you no longer want the check at all.

title: Block 2: GitHub Automations
section: Publishing to the web with GitHub Pages
text:
Publishing to the web with GitHub Pages
GitHub Pages serves web pages at a public URL of the form https://your-username.github.io/your-repo/. With no Action and no configuration file, you can publish your rendered penguins document by committing the HTML and letting Pages serve it. This is the simplest way to put your analysis on the web. Pages does not render Quarto; it only serves files that already exist in your repository. So the process is: render index.qmd to index.html locally, commit that HTML, and point Pages at it. Pages looks for a file named index.html at the repository root as the default page, which is why the document must be named index.qmd.






Warning



Anything published to Pages is publicly visible on the open web, including the rendered document and any data shown in it. Do not publish a repository containing data you would not want public.




Publish your penguins analysis to the web


Rename analysis.qmd to index.qmd in RStudio’s Files pane. The index name is what Pages needs, and the rest of this tutorial uses index.qmd from here on. Render it locally. In the terminal:
quarto render index.qmd
This produces index.html in your project root.
On GitHub.com, open your repository’s Settings, click Pages in the left sidebar, and under Build and deployment → Source select Deploy from a branch. Set Branch to main and the folder to / (root), then Save.
Commit and push. git add -A stages every change, including the removal of analysis.qmd, so Git records the rename rather than leaving the old file behind. If you use the Git pane instead, tick analysis.qmd, index.qmd and index.html before committing.
git add -A
git commit -m "docs: publish penguins analysis to Pages"
git push
Visit https://your-username.github.io/your-repo/. The first build can take a minute or two. Confirm the body-mass-against-flipper-length figure appears.








Note



Because Pages serves the committed index.html, you must re-render and re-commit it whenever you change index.qmd; the site does not update on its own. Part 2 shows how a GitHub Action can render the document for you, and committing output back to the repository shows how to have it commit index.html on every push, so the published page stays current without manual steps.

title: Block 2: GitHub Automations
section: Part 2: Your first GitHub Action (rendering the penguins document)
text:
Part 2: Your first GitHub Action (rendering the penguins document)
Why this matters
Rendering your penguins document on GitHub’s clean servers achieves two things. First, it confirms that the document renders correctly using only the packages in renv.lock, catching the common situation where something works on your machine but fails elsewhere. Second, it produces a rendered HTML file that anyone with access to the repository can download, without needing R or Quarto installed.
usethis::use_github_action()
The usethis package provides use_github_action(), which sets up common GitHub Actions workflows with a single R function call. Running it without arguments shows you the available options:

usethis::use_github_action()

This opens an interactive menu. The built-in options are primarily aimed at R package developers (running checks, computing test coverage, building documentation sites). For an analysis project with a Quarto document, none of the built-in templates fits directly, so we will write the workflow file manually. However, use_github_action() is worth knowing about: as your use of GitHub grows, it provides a fast path to common workflows without writing YAML from scratch. The r-lib/actions repository (https://github.com/r-lib/actions) lists all available options and their corresponding use_github_action() calls.
Step 1: Give the workflow only the permissions it needs
Each workflow run gets a temporary token (GITHUB_TOKEN) that controls what it may do to your repository. Rather than granting write access to every workflow through the repository settings, declare what this workflow needs with a permissions: key in the workflow file itself. The rendering workflow below only reads your files and uploads an artefact, so it asks for contents: read. You do not need to change anything under Settings → Actions. The one workflow later in this tutorial that pushes to the repository asks for contents: write in its own file.
Step 2: Pin your R version, then create the workflow file
Because this workflow restores your exact packages from renv.lock, it must run on the R version those packages were recorded under. Find yours by running R.version.string at the console and note the number, for example 4.6.1.
Create the following folder structure in your project. You can do this in RStudio’s Files pane: New Folder → .github, then inside that New Folder → workflows.
.github/
  workflows/
    render-quarto.yml
Open render-quarto.yml and paste the following. It restores the exact package versions recorded in the renv.lock you built in Part 1, so the document renders against the same packages you used locally. Every section is explained in the comments.
# The name shown in the Actions tab on GitHub.
name: Render penguins analysis

# When to run this workflow.
# 'push' means: every time you push commits to GitHub.
# Adjust the branch name below if yours is not 'main'.
on:
  push:
    branches: ["main"]

# Least privilege: this workflow only needs to read the repository.
permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  render:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Step 1: Download your repository files onto GitHub's machine.
      - name: Check out repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v7

      # Step 2: Install R. Set the version to match your renv.lock,
      # i.e. the number from R.version.string on your machine.
      - name: Set up R
        uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2
        with:
          r-version: "4.6.1"   # set to YOUR version from R.version.string
          use-public-rspm: true

      # Step 3: Install renv and restore the exact packages from renv.lock.
      # Because this reads renv.lock, there is no package list to maintain
      # here: it is the same lockfile your hook guards in Part 1.
      - name: Set up renv
        uses: r-lib/actions/setup-renv@v2
        env:
          RENV_CONFIG_PAK_ENABLED: "true"

      # Step 4: Install Quarto so we can render the document.
      - name: Install Quarto
        uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2

      # Step 5: Render the penguins document.
      - name: Render Quarto document
        run: quarto render index.qmd

      # Step 6: Save the rendered output so you can download it.
      - name: Upload rendered output
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: rendered-analysis
          path: index.html
          retention-days: 7
Because setup-renv restores from renv.lock, and your lockfile now contains tidyverse, palmerpenguins, and scales from Part 1, there is no packages: block to edit. This is the advantage of the renv approach: the workflow’s package list and your project’s package list cannot drift apart, because they are the same file.






Warning



The workflow file refers to index.qmd and index.html. If your Quarto file has a different name, change both the .qmd and .html references everywhere they appear, including the upload path. A mismatch produces a failure whose cause is not obvious from the log.








Note



The @v2 and @v7 suffixes pin each action to a major version, which protects you from unexpected breaking changes. These major versions are occasionally superseded; if a workflow begins to fail after working previously, check the action’s repository for a newer version.








WarningMatch the R version





If the r-version you pin differs from the version recorded in renv.lock, setup-renv may rebuild packages from source, which makes the first run noticeably slower and can occasionally fail on a package that needs system libraries. Setting r-version from your own R.version.string, as Step 2 instructs, avoids this.
A workflow that does not depend on renv or on a specific R version looks like this:
# The name shown in the Actions tab on GitHub.
name: Render penguins analysis

# When to run this workflow.
# 'push' means: every time you push commits to GitHub.
# Adjust the branch name below if yours is not 'main'.
on:
  push:
    branches: ["main"]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  render:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    # This repository still contains renv's .Rprofile, which would otherwise
    # activate renv (and its project library) whenever R starts.
    # Turning the autoloader off makes R use the packages installed below.
    env:
      RENV_CONFIG_AUTOLOADER_ENABLED: "false"

    steps:
      # Step 1: Download your repository files onto GitHub's machine.
      - name: Check out repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v7

      # Step 2: Install R. 'release' tracks the current release version,
      # so there is no version number to maintain here.
      - name: Set up R
        uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2
        with:
          r-version: "release"
          use-public-rspm: true

      # Step 3: Install the packages your document needs.
      # List every package loaded in index.qmd here.
      - name: Install R packages
        uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r-dependencies@v2
        with:
          packages: |
            any::palmerpenguins
            any::tidyverse
            any::scales

      # Step 4: Install Quarto so we can render the document.
      - name: Install Quarto
        uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2

      # Step 5: Render the penguins document.
      - name: Render Quarto document
        run: quarto render index.qmd

      # Step 6: Save the rendered output so you can download it.
      - name: Upload rendered output
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: rendered-analysis
          path: index.html
          retention-days: 7
Note the RENV_CONFIG_AUTOLOADER_ENABLED line. Your repository still contains the .Rprofile that renv::init() created, and without that line R would activate renv on start-up and look for packages in the renv project library (which this workflow never restores) rather than the ones it installs.



Step 3: Commit and push
Save the file, then commit and push using the Git pane or terminal:
git add .github/workflows/render-quarto.yml
git commit -m "chore: add Quarto rendering workflow"
git push
Note that the pre-commit hook will run before this commit. It will pass because you have not changed any packages since your last snapshot in Part 1.
Step 4: Watch the workflow run

Go to your repository on GitHub.com
Click the Actions tab in the top navigation bar
You will see a workflow run listed, named Render penguins analysis

Click on it, then click the render job
Each step expands to show its output as it runs

A green tick next to a step means it passed. A red cross means it failed and the job has stopped. The workflow typically takes three to five minutes on first run because packages are being restored; on subsequent runs, caching makes the renv step much faster.
Step 5: Download the rendered output
When the run completes with a green tick:

Scroll to the bottom of the run page
Under Artifacts, click rendered-analysis

A zip file downloads containing index.html


This is your penguins document, rendered on GitHub’s servers from the exact package versions in your lockfile, without any action on your part beyond pushing a commit.
Reading a failure
Failures are normal, particularly on first run. Click on the red cross next to the failing step to see the full log. The four most common causes are:
renv.lock is not committed
This project does not contain a lockfile.
Have you called `snapshot()` yet?
Fix: run renv::snapshot() locally, commit renv.lock, and push again.
A package used in the document is not in renv.lock
Error in library(somepackage) : there is no package called 'somepackage'
Fix: install the package locally, run renv::snapshot(), commit the updated renv.lock, and push. This is the situation Part 1’s hook is designed to prevent before the commit ever leaves your machine.






Note



renv finds the packages your project uses by scanning your scripts and Quarto documents for both library() calls and pkg::fn() usages, so dplyr::filter() counts as using dplyr just as library(dplyr) does. Either way, if the package is used but you forgot to snapshot, it is missing from renv.lock, setup-renv does not install it, and the render fails with “there is no package called” (for pkg::fn(), the message comes from loadNamespace()). The fix is the same: run renv::snapshot() locally, commit renv.lock, and push.


The Quarto document contains a code error
The log will show the R error message from inside the document, with a line number. Fix: correct the code locally, render the document in RStudio or Positron to confirm it works, commit, and push.
The workflow does not appear in the Actions tab
The trigger branch name in the workflow file does not match your actual branch. Fix: open the workflow file and change "main" to your branch name, commit, and push.

title: Block 2: GitHub Automations
section: How the two tools work together
text:
How the two tools work together
With both in place, your penguins workflow now looks like this:







Event
What fires
What it catches



git commit
Pre-commit hook
renv out of sync with renv.lock



git push
GitHub Actions
Render failures; missing packages; clean-environment problems



The hook catches the most common problem before it is committed. Actions catches problems that are invisible in your local environment and produces output anyone can download. Neither replaces the other.

title: Block 2: GitHub Automations
section: Going further: running code on a schedule
text:
Going further: running code on a schedule
So far, the workflow has been triggered by a push. That is useful for testing, but for many analytical tasks a scheduled run is more appropriate: a report that refreshes every morning, or a data file that is updated weekly, without you having to do anything.
GitHub Actions supports scheduled runs using what are called cron jobs. A cron expression is a compact way of specifying a time schedule. Replace the on: push: trigger in your workflow file with the following:
# Run every day at 9:00am UTC
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 9 * * *'
The five fields in a cron expression represent, in order: minute, hour, day of month, month, and day of week. An asterisk means “every”. So 0 9 * * * means: at minute 0 of hour 9, every day of every month. By default the time is in UTC, which is one hour behind British Summer Time (and the same as UK time in winter), and four to five hours ahead of US Eastern Time depending on daylight saving. To use local time instead, add a timezone: key with an IANA time-zone name under the cron line:
# Run every day at 9:00am UK time, all year round
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 9 * * *'
      timezone: "Europe/London"
The syntax is not intuitive to read or write from memory. The website crontab.guru translates cron expressions into plain English and lets you build expressions interactively. It is worth bookmarking.
Some useful examples:


Cron expression
When it runs



0 9 * * 1
Every Monday at 9:00am UTC


0 8 1 * *
The first day of every month at 8:00am UTC


*/30 * * * *
Every 30 minutes


0 9 * * 1-5
Weekdays at 9:00am UTC



You can also combine a schedule with a push trigger, so the workflow runs both when you push and on a timer:
on:
  push:
    branches: ["main"]
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 9 * * 1'

title: Block 2: GitHub Automations
section: Going further: committing output back to the repository
text:
Going further: committing output back to the repository
The workflow in Part 2 uploads the rendered document as a temporary artefact, which GitHub deletes after seven days and which requires a manual download to access. An alternative is to have the workflow commit the rendered file back into the repository directly, making it a permanent part of your commit history and accessible at a fixed URL.
Pushing needs write access, so first change the workflow’s permissions: block from contents: read to:
permissions:
  contents: write
Then add the following step after the render step, replacing the upload-artifact step:
      - name: Commit rendered output to repository
        run: |
          # Set the git identity for this commit. This is GitHub's own
          # Actions bot account, so the commit shows as made by github-actions[bot].
          git config user.name "github-actions[bot]"
          git config user.email "41898282+github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com"

          # Stage the rendered file.
          git add index.html

          # Commit it. The || handles the case where nothing has changed:
          # if there is no new output, git commit would normally fail with
          # an error. The || tells bash: if the left side fails, run the
          # right side instead — in this case, just print a message and
          # continue without failing the workflow.
          git commit -m "chore: update rendered analysis" || echo "No changes to commit"

          # Push the commit back to GitHub. No || here: if the push fails,
          # the workflow should fail so that you find out.
          git push
This pattern suits scheduled workflows: the workflow runs on a timer, re-renders the document with current data, and pushes the updated HTML back to the repository automatically. In bash, the || operator means “or”: it separates a command from a fallback to run if the first command fails. Use it only where failure is harmless (nothing to commit), never on the push itself.
Note that this approach writes to your repository’s main branch directly, which adds commits generated by GitHub Actions to your history. Whether this is desirable depends on your project; for a solo analyst it is usually fine.

title: Block 2: GitHub Automations
text:
Going further: projects without renv
The workflow in Part 2 uses r-lib/actions/setup-renv@v2, which requires a committed renv.lock file. If you encounter a project or tutorial that does not use renv, you will see a different approach: r-lib/actions/setup-r-dependencies@v2, which installs packages listed explicitly in the workflow file:
- name: Install packages
  uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r-dependencies@v2
  with:
    packages: |
      any::ggplot2
      any::dplyr
      any::quarto
This is less reproducible than renv because it installs the latest available version of each package rather than the exact version you used locally. For your own projects (such as the penguins repository you have built here), renv and setup-renv is the better choice. For adapting workflows from others who do not use renv, setup-r-dependencies is what you will encounter.

title: Block 2: GitHub Automations
text:
Where to go next
The r-lib/actions repository (https://github.com/r-lib/actions) contains example workflows for a wide range of R tasks. Each example includes its usethis::use_github_action() call where one exists. The patterns you have learned here transfer directly: adjust the trigger, swap the render step, change what is uploaded.
Render only on pull requests rather than every push, to keep the per-push feedback loop fast:
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: ["main"]

title: Block 1: AI-assisted R programming
text: Prerequisites

title: Block 1: AI-assisted R programming
text:
A GitHub account, an IDE (RStudio or Positron), and the Git, renv and testthat skills from earlier sessions.

Claude Code, the workshop’s main tool, installed and checked before the day: follow Setting up Claude Code. It needs a Claude Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise seat, or a Console account.

Posit Assistant works as an alternative; each page says where it differs.

GitHub Copilot (Copilot Free is enough) for the inline completions in Block 2.
Your institution’s permission to use these tools, and, near research data, your ethics approval and data agreements. Block 4 covers this.

title: Block 1: AI-assisted R programming
text:
Learning outcomes
By the end of the day you will be able to:

Explain what a large language model is and why the model choice matters.
Use inline completion and know what context it sees.
Debug your own code with AI, and know when AI helps most.
Choose how much an agent may do, and know every route by which your data leave your machine.
Write an AGENTS.md instruction file and a skill, and test that they load.
Protect files with a permission rule, and detect any change with git.
Have an agent clean data against a codebook you own, and check it with tests.
Use AI as a code reviewer, and grade it against a known answer.
Have an agent refactor code under a characterisation testA test that checks new code reproduces the saved output of the original code exactly. It shows the output is unchanged, not that it is correct., with the reference in your hands.
Check an AI translation, report results without typed numbers, and leave with a documented, tested repository.

title: Block 1: AI-assisted R programming
text:
Materials
You work in your own copy of a workshop template repository (its layout), forked before the day.






TipReference: how the day is made forgiving





The repository holds a synthetic voles dataset, scripts, and three things that make the day forgiving:


Tests that wait. Each test in tests/ skips until its block is done; at 16:00 they run together as one suite.

Checkpoint branches. block5-done, block7-done and block9-done: if you fall behind, switch to the next one from the Git pane’s branch menu and carry on. Nobody needs to finish every exercise.

Built-in protections. The raw data, the checks and the references are protected before you start.

Block 8 also uses the project folder from https://osf.io/jgeq9/ that you reviewed on Day 2.



Verification is the workshop’s only non-negotiable, and it is what lets you automate with confidence: once you can check an agent’s work quickly and independently, you can hand it more of the work. Every exercise ends with that check.

title: Block 1: AI-assisted R programming
section: The thread through the day: Check · Reproduce · Record
text:
The thread through the day: Check · Reproduce · Record
Every block applies three habits, and ends with a box saying what it added:


Check. Treat what an AI produces as a claim, and verify it independently: the data, a test, a reference you hold, the Git pane’s diff, or your own knowledge of the biology.

Reproduce. The code runs in a fresh R sessionAn R session with nothing loaded from earlier work: Session > Restart R in RStudio or Positron (with “never save .RData” set, as on Day 1), callr::rscript() from the console, or Rscript in the terminal. Code that only works in your current session depends on something you did not record. with the package versions in the lockfileThe renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment., and nothing changed that you did not see.

title: Block 1: AI-assisted R programming
text:
Block 1: framing
This block gives you the two words you will use all day, what a large language model is, and why its context window matters. It ends with a short discussion and a quiz.
⏱ ~15 minutes: presentation, a short discussion and a quiz.

title: Block 1: AI-assisted R programming
text:
Framing and mental models
Two words recur all day. An assistantAny AI tool that helps you write or understand code, from inline completion to a chat window. In this course “assistant” is the general word; “agent” is used when the tool acts on your files. is any AI tool that helps you write or understand code. An agentAn assistant that can read across a project’s files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises. is an assistant that acts: it reads your project and, if you let it, edits files and runs commands. Claude Code and Posit Assistant are agents; a chat window that only answers is not. To see how one works inside, the self-study page Build your own agent in R builds a small one.

title: Block 1: AI-assisted R programming
section: What is a large language model?
text:
What is a large language model?
A large language model predicts the next fragment of text from what came before, having learnt from a large share of the public internet, code included. Every tool today is built on one. Models differ in code quality and in how often they invent functions that do not exist, so if a model gives you consistently poor suggestions and your plan lets you switch, switching is a cheap experiment.

title: Block 1: AI-assisted R programming
text:
Why the context window matters
An LLM has no memory between calls: each one starts with only what you supply, up to the limit of its context windowThe maximum amount of text a language model can consider in one call. The model has no memory between calls, so it sees only what is in the context window.. That one fact explains the day. Instruction files and skills give the model context it would not otherwise have; because they are only requests, Block 6 adds controls that hold either way, and tests check the result.
Remember: the AI sees only what you give it, and everything it sees has left your machine.

title: Block 1: AI-assisted R programming
text:
Going further (not covered live)
This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you.






TipWhich tool does what







Claude Code runs in the Terminal tab of RStudio or Positron, which starts in your project’s root folder: the folder it acts on. Every block’s main text uses it, and checks its work from the R console and Git pane.

Posit Assistant is the in-IDE chat and agent in RStudio and Positron. It can also see your live R session. See What’s new in Posit AI.

GitHub Copilot gives inline completions in all three IDEs. Its cloud agent, used only in some Going further sections, needs a paid plan; see the Copilot plans page.










TipModels





Claude Code uses Anthropic’s Claude models; Posit Assistant runs on Posit AI or a provider key you configure; GitHub Copilot offers Claude, GPT and Gemini models. You do not need strong opinions about which model is best, only to know that the choice exists and changes the output.









TipTwo modes of execution





The tools you use today are synchronous and local: they work on your machine, respond in seconds, and can be interrupted. Their reach differs: the current file for inline completion, the project folder and the output of its own commands for Claude Code, and your live R session too for Posit Assistant. An asynchronous, remote agent, such as the Copilot cloud agent, works on its own branch on someone else’s servers and returns a pull request minutes later; you meet it in the Going further sections of Blocks 4, 6 and 9. The first invites you to watch and interrupt; the second, to write a precise specification and review what comes back. Block 4 turns this into a ladder of autonomy.









TipThe thread, in more detail





Day 1 introduced renv; Day 4 checks that an agent has kept to it. On Day 2 you saw what a reviewable project needs (TADA! and the README, and the SORTEE checklist); Day 4 shows how AI can help produce that record without inventing any of it. Many journals, funders and institutions now ask authors to declare AI use, and a log written at the time is easier and more accurate than one reconstructed later.

text:
Glossary




term
definition



agent
An assistant that can read across a project's files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises.


AI-use log
A record written at the time of each piece of AI-assisted work, in the form: date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed. It becomes the AI declaration in a README.


assistant
Any AI tool that helps you write or understand code, from inline completion to a chat window. In this course "assistant" is the general word; "agent" is used when the tool acts on your files.


characterisation test
A test that checks new code reproduces the saved output of the original code exactly. It shows the output is unchanged, not that it is correct.


context window
The maximum amount of text a language model can consider in one call. The model has no memory between calls, so it sees only what is in the context window.


fresh R session
An R session with nothing loaded from earlier work: Session > Restart R in RStudio or Positron (with "never save .RData" set, as on Day 1), callr::rscript() from the console, or Rscript in the terminal. Code that only works in your current session depends on something you did not record.


lockfile
The renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment.

title: Setting up Claude Code
text:
Before you install: three questions
Claude Code is an AI agentAn assistant that can read across a project’s files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises. that runs in the Terminal tab of RStudio or Positron. It reads, edits and runs the files in your project, asking your permission as it goes. You need very little terminal: one command to start it, and the R console and Git pane for everything else.
⏱ ~30 minutes, before the workshop day. If a command here fails, check the Claude Code setup page first.

title: Setting up Claude Code
text:
Are you permitted to use it on this work? Claude Code sends what it reads, and the output of commands it runs, to Anthropic. Check your institution’s policy and, near research data, your ethics approval and data agreements (Block 4).

Which account? A Claude Pro or Max subscription, a Claude Team or Enterprise seat, a Claude Console account (billed per request), or access your institution has set up through a cloud provider.

Is your computer supported? macOS 13 or later, Windows 10 (1809) or later, or a recent Linux.

title: Setting up Claude Code
section: Step 1: Open the Terminal tab in your IDE
text:
Step 1: Open the Terminal tab in your IDE


RStudio: the Terminal tab next to the Console.

Positron: Terminal → New Terminal.

With a project open, the Terminal tab starts in the project’s root folder, which is where Claude Code needs to run. You never need to cd.
Which shell is it? A prompt starting PS is PowerShell (Windows); one ending $ is Git Bash (Windows) or bash/zsh (macOS, Linux).

title: Setting up Claude Code
section: Step 2: Check git and R are reachable
text:
Step 2: Check git and R are reachable
In the terminal:
git --version
Rscript --version
Both should print a version number.


git not found: install git (on Windows, Git for Windows).

Rscript not found (common on Windows): run R.home("bin") in the R console and add that folder to your PATH (Windows: Start menu → “Edit environment variables for your account” → Path). Then quit and reopen RStudio or Positron: its terminals keep the PATH they started with.

title: Setting up Claude Code
text:
Step 3: Install Claude Code
macOS or Linux, in the terminal:
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
Windows, in PowerShell (a prompt starting PS; if your Terminal tab is Git Bash, open the PowerShell app for this one step):
irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex
Then quit and reopen RStudio or Positron, and check the version in the Terminal tab:
claude --version
You are done when it prints 2.1.281 or later. This minimum is about your instruction file: from this version, Claude Code reads your AGENTS.md directly.

text:
Step 4: Prepare your workshop repository
Do this before you sign in, so that Claude Code starts in the right folder.


Fork, clone and open the template in one step, in the R console: usethis::create_from_github("<template-owner>/<template-repo>", fork = TRUE). Your instructor gives you the exact name.

Restore the packages: renv::restore() in the R console, once. It installs the versions in the template’s lockfileThe renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment. and can take several minutes.

Your workshop repository

Your workshop repository starts Claude Code in Manual mode (default), a permission modeThe setting that decides how much Claude Code may do without asking: plan (read only), default (asks before edits and commands), acceptEdits (edits without asking) and bypassPermissions (never asks). in which it asks before every edit and command. Where am I typing?






Where
What runs there



The Claude Code prompt, inside the Terminal tab
Your requests to Claude Code. A line starting ! runs a shell command, and its output is added to the conversation, so it reaches the model too.

R code. Claude Code cannot see it, or anything you load there.

title: Setting up Claude Code
text:
Step 8: Check everything works


Pre-workshop check (15 minutes)


Start state: your workshop repository is open, and the Git pane shows no uncommitted changes.
1. Manual mode, and a plan. Type claude in the Terminal tab. It should say it is in Manual mode (default), not auto. Then:
/plan Describe the structure of this repository and what each top-level folder
contains. Do not change anything.
Read the plan. When it asks whether to proceed, choose “No, keep planning”, then press Esc to leave it. Check that the mode shown is Manual again (Shift+Tab cycles the modes) before step 2.
2. R is reachable.
Run Rscript -e "sessionInfo()" and show me the output.
Approve the command when asked: you should see your R version.
3. Settings and instructions load. /permissions should list the deny rules, and /memory should list AGENTS.md. On a Pro or Max account, also open /privacy-settings and decide whether your conversations may be used for model training. Type /exit.
4. The project is ready. In the R console:

renv::status()
callr::r(\(d) testthat::test_dir(d), list(here::here("tests")))

renv::status() should report no problems, and the tests should run with no failures: most skip for now, waiting for the block that creates their files.
5. Inline completion works. In a new R script, type # Calculate the mean of 1 to 100: grey suggested text should appear (Block 2 uses it first).
6. The checkpoint branches are there. The Git pane’s branch menu should show block5-done, block7-done and block9-done. Stay on main.
You are done when the Git pane shows no changes, Claude Code starts in Manual mode, /permissions lists the deny rules, and the tests run with no failures. Copy the output of steps 2 and 4 into a text file to bring on the day, and note there how many deny rules /permissions showed in step 3.
If it goes wrong: Rscript not found, return to Step 2; no ghost text, return to Step 7; empty /permissions list, start claude from the workshop repository’s Terminal tab; a changed file, Revert in the Git pane; package problems, run renv::restore() again and send the error to your instructor before the day.

title: Block 2: Inline completions
text:
Setup
Inline completion is the simplest kind of assistantAny AI tool that helps you write or understand code, from inline completion to a chat window. In this course “assistant” is the general word; “agent” is used when the tool acts on your files.: grey “ghost text” appears as you type, and you accept it with Tab, reject it with Esc, or carry on typing. By the end of this block you will know how to get useful suggestions every time: write a specific comment just before the cursor.
Claude Code has no inline completion, so this is the one block where GitHub Copilot is the main tool.
⏱ ~25 minutes
You signed in to GitHub Copilot in the pre-work (Setting up Claude Code, Step 7). Check it still works: in a blank R script, type # Calculate the mean of 1 to 100. Within a few seconds you should see ghost text such as mean(1:100); if not, press Enter and wait.
If no ghost text appears, follow the instructor’s screen for this block and fix the set-up at the break.

title: Block 2: Inline completions
text:
NoteSet-up routes, plans and data







RStudio: enable GitHub Copilot in RStudio’s options and sign in to GitHub.

Positron: choose GitHub Copilot as the completions provider (see Positron’s completions documentation).

VS Code: select Use AI Features from the Copilot icon in the Status Bar and sign in with GitHub.

Copilot Free allows a limited number of completions per month (2,000 at the time of writing); paid plans do not meter them. Completions send the code around your cursor to the provider, so the disclosure points in Block 4 apply here too. Use one completion provider at a time, so you know which tool made each suggestion.









TipUsing Posit Assistant





In RStudio and Positron you can use Posit AI Next Edit Suggestions instead: in RStudio, turn it on from the Posit Assistant toolbar button (it needs a Posit AI account); in Positron, choose it as the completions provider. Posit AI does not meter completions.

title: Block 2: Inline completions
text:
The context principle
A suggestion can only use what is in the model’s context windowThe maximum amount of text a language model can consider in one call. The model has no memory between calls, so it sees only what is in the context window. when it is made. Copilot fills that window mainly from the current file, and above all from the comment just before the cursor. In Positron and VS Code it may also use other open tabs. It does not see your R session.






TipUsing Posit Assistant





Posit AI Next Edit Suggestions also sees your live R session: the columns of loaded data frames, the functions you have defined and the packages you have loaded. What you have loaded becomes one more lever.

title: Block 2: Inline completions
text:
Activity: The context demonstration


The context demonstration (10 minutes)


Start state: your workshop repository is open, and the set-up check produced ghost text.
The data are voles_metabolism.csv: a synthetic trial in 72 voles, with columns subject_id, sex, treatment_arm, mass_pre_g, mass_post_g and metabolic_rate_post. The names were chosen so that no model has seen them before.
1. No context. Restart R, so you are in a fresh R sessionAn R session with nothing loaded from earlier work: Session > Restart R in RStudio or Positron (with “never save .RData” set, as on Day 1), callr::rscript() from the console, or Rscript in the terminal. Code that only works in your current session depends on something you did not record., and open a blank R script. Type only this comment, and wait.
In the R script:

# calculate the mean change in mass by treatment

Note the suggestion. With no data and no column names in view, the model has to guess.
2. Context in the file. In a new blank script, type the lines below down to glimpse(voles), and run them, so that voles is loaded. Then type the same comment on a new line, and wait.
In the R script:

# Voles metabolism trial: effect of treatment on body mass
# 72 voles, three treatment arms (Control, Low_dose, High_dose), two sexes
# Native pipe |>, tidyverse

library(tidyverse)

voles <- read_csv(here::here("data", "raw", "voles_metabolism.csv"))
glimpse(voles)

# calculate the mean change in mass by treatment



A typical good result


voles |>
  mutate(mass_change_g = mass_post_g - mass_pre_g) |>
  summarise(
    mean_change = mean(mass_change_g, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = treatment_arm
  )

The exact form varies between people and sessions.

Compare the two suggestions. Did the second use real column names? Did it compute post minus pre?
You are done when you can say what the second suggestion had that the first did not.
If it goes wrong: if no suggestion appears, type the comment again on a new line; if the script stops running, Session → Restart R and run it from the top.








TipUsing Posit Assistant: context in the session





With Posit AI Next Edit Suggestions, keep voles loaded from step 2, then type only the comment from step 1 in a new blank script. If the suggestion now uses the real column names, it came from your session, not from the file.

title: Block 2: Inline completions
text:
Activity: Build a small analysis


Build a small analysis (10 minutes)


Start state: the script from step 2, with voles loaded.
For each step, write the comment first, then accept, modify or reject the suggestion, and note which you did. The note is what makes you notice an unchecked acceptance.
1. Summary table. The mean and standard deviation of mass_change_g by treatment_arm and sex, with the number of observations per cell. (Create mass_change_g first if your script does not have it.)
2. Plot. mass_change_g against metabolic_rate_post, coloured by treatment_arm.
You are done when a fresh R session (Session → Restart R, then run the script from the top) produces the table and the plot without error.
If it goes wrong: delete the last suggestion you accepted, and write a more specific comment naming the data frame and its columns.


An example


# Voles metabolism trial: effect of treatment on body mass
library(tidyverse)
library(here)

voles <- read_csv(
  here("data", "raw", "voles_metabolism.csv"),
  col_types = cols(
    subject_id = col_character(),
    sex = col_character(),
    treatment_arm = col_character(),
    mass_pre_g = col_double(),
    mass_post_g = col_double(),
    metabolic_rate_post = col_double()
  )
) |>
  mutate(mass_change_g = mass_post_g - mass_pre_g)

# mean and SD of mass_change_g by treatment_arm and sex, with n per cell
voles |>
  summarise(
    mean_change_g = mean(mass_change_g),
    sd_change_g = sd(mass_change_g),
    n = n(),
    .by = c(treatment_arm, sex)
  ) |>
  arrange(treatment_arm, sex)

# mass_change_g against metabolic_rate_post, coloured by treatment_arm
ggplot(voles, aes(metabolic_rate_post, mass_change_g, colour = treatment_arm)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Metabolic rate (post-treatment)", y = "Change in mass (g)")

The plot drops the one animal with no metabolic rate and says so in a warning: read it rather than ignore it.









NoteCheck · Reproduce · Record





You can now: steer inline completion with a specific comment and the right code above the cursor, trusted because you decided on every suggestion and the script runs from a fresh R session.

Check: accept, modify or reject every suggestion deliberately.

Reproduce: good suggestions come from context in the file or session, so keep that context in the script, where it reruns.

Record: nothing to log yet; your AI-use logA record written at the time of each piece of AI-assisted work, in the form: date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed. It becomes the AI declaration in a README. starts in Block 4, once an agentAn assistant that can read across a project’s files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises. starts doing work.

The single most reliable way to improve inline suggestions in a new script is to:

Switch to a different underlying modelOpen more files in the editor as additional contextWrite a specific comment immediately before the code you want, naming the data frame and its columnsRestart the IDE so the assistant has a fresh context

You get correct column names in a blank script using Posit AI Next Edit Suggestions, but not with Copilot. The most likely reason is:

Posit AI uses a larger modelNext Edit Suggestions can see the data frame loaded in your R session; Copilot sees only the filesCopilot cannot read R codeThe column names were in Posit AI's training data
