This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you.






TipThe full four-step analysis





The live activity uses two of four steps. The full sequence, again writing the comment for each step before accepting, rejecting or modifying the suggestion:

Filter to subjects with non-missing metabolic_rate_post and create a derived variable mass_change_g.
Produce a summary table of the mean and standard deviation of mass_change_g by treatment_arm and sex, with the number of observations per cell.
Fit a linear model of metabolic_rate_post on treatment_arm and sex. Inspect the coefficients.
Produce one plot relating mass_change_g to metabolic_rate_post, coloured by treatment_arm.

When you have finished steps 2 and 4, post the code Copilot suggested for step 4 in the Zoom chat, with a note on whether you accepted, changed or rejected it. Then compare with what others posted: the comparison usually shows different suggestions, different acceptance decisions and, often, different bugs.

title: Block 2: Inline completions
text:
Glossary




term
definition



agent
An assistant that can read across a project's files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises.


AI-use log
A record written at the time of each piece of AI-assisted work, in the form: date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed. It becomes the AI declaration in a README.


assistant
Any AI tool that helps you write or understand code, from inline completion to a chat window. In this course "assistant" is the general word; "agent" is used when the tool acts on your files.


context window
The maximum amount of text a language model can consider in one call. The model has no memory between calls, so it sees only what is in the context window.


fresh R session
An R session with nothing loaded from earlier work: Session > Restart R in RStudio or Positron (with "never save .RData" set, as on Day 1), callr::rscript() from the console, or Rscript in the terminal. Code that only works in your current session depends on something you did not record.

title: Block 3: Debugging with AI
text:
Setup
AI is a fast debugging partner for code you wrote yourself, because you know what you meant and can judge its answer against that. This block works through three kinds of bug, each needing a little more from you: a typo (the AI can fix it alone), a logic error (it needs to see the data), and a result that runs but is wrong (only your knowledge of the study catches it).
⏱ ~20 minutes
Load the voles data.
In the R console:
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
voles <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "voles_metabolism.csv"))
How you use Claude Code in this block. Claude Code is an agentAn assistant that can read across a project’s files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises.: given a question, it may search your project, read files and offer to run code. In this block you only ask, so:
Claude Code cannot see the objects in your R console, such as voles: it sees your data only by reading files or running code, and each Rscript command it runs starts a fresh R process. Check its work in the R console (checking work).
Expect a line you did not ask for. Code it suggests is likely to start with # agents-md: active v1, and its answers may mention project rules such as reporting n. These come from the repository’s instruction file, AGENTS.md, which Claude Code reads at the start of every conversation: a first sign that it sees context you did not paste (Block 4). Block 5 explains the line; for now, ignore it.

title: Block 3: Debugging with AI
text:
Exercise 1: A syntax error


A syntax error (7 minutes)


Start state: voles is loaded in your R console, and Claude Code is open with a new conversation (/clear).
You wrote this in your script to count voles per treatment:

ggplot(voles, aes(x = treatment_arm)) +
  geom_barchart()

R returns:
Error in geom_barchart(): could not find function "geom_barchart"
1. Ask for a fix. Paste the code and the error, and ask.
Prompt (Claude Code or a chat window):
This code gives an error:

  ggplot(voles, aes(x = treatment_arm)) +
    geom_barchart()

Error in geom_barchart(): could not find function "geom_barchart"

What is wrong, and what is the fix?
Answer from what I've pasted: don't read files, run code or edit anything.
2. Explain it before you accept it. Write one sentence saying why the original failed. If you can write it, you understood the fix; that sentence is your check.






TipWith inline completion instead





Paste the code and the error into your script as a comment, add # Fix this code: on the next line, and let the assistantAny AI tool that helps you write or understand code, from inline completion to a chat window. In this course “assistant” is the general word; “agent” is used when the tool acts on your files. suggest a continuation.





Solution


ggplot(voles, aes(x = treatment_arm)) +
  geom_bar()

The function is geom_bar(); ggplot2’s geoms have no _chart suffix. “Could not find function” means no loaded package has a function of that name.

You are done when the corrected plot draws a bar for each treatment arm, and you have written your one-sentence explanation.
If it goes wrong: if the fix produces a different error, paste that error back in the same conversation; the assistant now has two clues.

title: Block 3: Debugging with AI
text:
Asking or acting
So far you have used AI that answers: you gather the evidence and paste it in. Exercise 2 ends with AI that acts, an agentAn assistant that can read across a project’s files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises. that reads your files and runs code itself, so you check each command and its output.






TipBackground: AI that answers versus AI that acts













AI that answers
AI that acts



Examples
A chat window; Posit Assistant’s Ask mode (/ask); Claude Code given the answer-only line, with you refusing any approval
Claude Code allowed to read and run; Posit Assistant in Normal mode


Who gathers the evidence
You: you run distinct() and paste the output
It does, and shows you each command


What you check
That its reasoning fits the evidence you pasted
That each command is sensible, and what its output says



Use AI that answers when you want to learn, or when the data must not be touched. Posit Assistant’s Ask mode enforces it; with Claude Code, which has no ask mode, the answer-only line is a request and your No at each approval is what holds. Block 4 sets out the full range.

title: Block 3: Debugging with AI
text:
Exercise 2: A logic error


A logic error (8 minutes)


Start state: voles is loaded in your R console, and Claude Code is open with a new conversation (/clear).
You wrote this in your script to compute mean post-treatment mass for high-dose voles:

high_dose <- voles |>
  filter(treatment_arm == "high_dose")

high_dose |>
  summarise(mean_mass = mean(mass_post_g))

The code runs without error. R returns:
# A tibble: 1 × 1
  mean_mass
      <dbl>
1       NaN
There is no error to paste: the bug is in what you asked for. The fix is to put the evidence in front of you first, and then in front of the assistant.
1. Inspect the data before asking for help.
In the R console:

voles |> distinct(treatment_arm)
voles |> count(treatment_arm)
nrow(high_dose)

The values are Control, Low_dose and High_dose, and nrow() is zero: you have found the bug yourself in seconds.
2. Ask with the evidence in hand. Paste the code and the diagnostic output together.
Prompt (Claude Code or a chat window):
I am trying to compute mean post-treatment mass for high-dose voles.
My code:

  high_dose <- voles |>
    filter(treatment_arm == "high_dose")

  high_dose |>
    summarise(mean_mass = mean(mass_post_g))

returns NaN. But voles |> distinct(treatment_arm) returns
"Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose". I think the filter fails because of
the capitalisation. Is that the only problem?
Answer from what I've pasted: don't read files, run code or edit anything.
3. Now let the agent gather the evidence. This is the one step in the block where it acts. Type /clear, then:
Prompt (Claude Code):
Read data/raw/voles_metabolism.csv and run R code with Rscript to find why
filtering treatment_arm for "high_dose" returns no rows. Don't edit any files.
Show each command and its output.
It reads the file without asking, because reading needs no approval in Manual mode. Before it runs R it asks: read the Rscript command, and choose Yes if it only reads the data and prints results. Then compare its diagnosis with the one you found in step 1.


Solution


high_dose <- voles |>
  filter(treatment_arm == "High_dose")

high_dose |>
  summarise(mean_mass = mean(mass_post_g, na.rm = TRUE))

The filter now matches the data. na.rm = TRUE is a precaution for real data, which usually have missing values.

You are done when nrow(high_dose) is 24 and the mean is a number, not NaN.
If it goes wrong: if nrow() is still zero, run voles |> distinct(treatment_arm) again and copy the value exactly as printed.

title: Block 3: Debugging with AI
section: Exercise 3: A correct-looking but wrong result
text:
Exercise 3: A correct-looking but wrong result


A correct-looking but wrong result (5 minutes)


Start state: voles is loaded in your R console, and Claude Code is open with a new conversation (/clear).
You wrote this to get the mean change in body mass by treatment arm:

voles |>
  mutate(mass_change_g = mass_pre_g - mass_post_g) |>
  summarise(mean_change = mean(mass_change_g), .by = treatment_arm)

It runs. There is no error and no NaN. R returns something like:
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  treatment_arm mean_change
  <chr>               <dbl>
1 Control             -0.21
2 Low_dose            -1.49
3 High_dose           -3.19
The numbers look plausible, but the treatment was designed to increase mass, and this table says mass falls. Nothing in the data or the code reveals the error: only your knowledge of the study does. An AI can catch it too, but only if you tell it what the answer should be.
1. Write down what a correct result should look like, then compare. Here: positive values, rising from Control to High_dose. The mismatch is the diagnosis.
2. Ask for a second opinion, stating the expected direction.
Prompt (Claude Code or a chat window):
This should show mass gain increasing with dose, but the values are negative
and decreasing. What is wrong?

  voles |>
    mutate(mass_change_g = mass_pre_g - mass_post_g) |>
    summarise(mean_change = mean(mass_change_g), .by = treatment_arm)

Answer from what I've pasted: don't read files, run code or edit anything.


Solution


voles |>
  mutate(mass_change_g = mass_post_g - mass_pre_g) |>
  summarise(mean_change = mean(mass_change_g), .by = treatment_arm)

mass_change_g is post minus pre: gain, not loss. The original ran without complaint because subtraction works in either direction.

You are done when your corrected means are positive and increase from Control to High_dose, as you predicted in step 1.
If it goes wrong: if the values are still negative, check which mass you subtract from which: post minus pre is gain.

title: Block 3: Debugging with AI
text:
The debugging checklist
Inspect the data first, ask the AI second.


Read the error in full: the function name and the phrase usually locate the bug.

Inspect the data: glimpse(), distinct(), summary(), and nrow() after a filter.

Check names exactly, including capitals and underscores.

Then ask, giving the code, the error and the diagnostic output together. Ask for an answer, not an action, until you have the evidence.

Explain the fix in one sentence before you accept it.

Before trusting a clean run, state what the result should look like (sign, size, order) and compare.







NoteCheck · Reproduce · Record





You can now: use an assistant to diagnose and fix errors in your own code, trusted because you inspect the data first, explain each fix in a sentence, and compare every clean-running result with what you expected.

Check: inspect the data before asking, and write one sentence explaining each fix; state the expected sign and size of a result before trusting it.

Reproduce: rerun the fixed code in a fresh R sessionAn R session with nothing loaded from earlier work: Session > Restart R in RStudio or Positron (with “never save .RData” set, as on Day 1), callr::rscript() from the console, or Rscript in the terminal. Code that only works in your current session depends on something you did not record., so the fix does not depend on an object left over from your experiments.

Record: nothing to log yet; the AI-use log starts in Block 4.

title: Block 3: Debugging with AI
text:
Going further (not covered live)
This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you.






TipAn aesthetic-mapping error





This error needs ggplot2’s grammar rather than the data. You wanted a scatter plot of post-treatment metabolic rate against post-treatment mass, coloured by treatment arm:

ggplot(voles, aes(x = mass_post_g, y = metabolic_rate_post)) +
  geom_point(color = treatment_arm) +
  labs(title = "Metabolic rate by mass")

R returns an error saying that object treatment_arm was not found. The exact wording varies between ggplot2 versions.
1. Ask for a fix. Before accepting it, write one sentence on why ggplot2 could not find treatment_arm.


Solution


ggplot(voles, aes(x = mass_post_g, y = metabolic_rate_post)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = treatment_arm)) +
  labs(title = "Metabolic rate by mass")

treatment_arm is a column in the data, so the mapping must go inside aes(). An argument outside aes(), such as color =, expects a fixed value like "red" or "#0072B2". ggplot2 looked for an object called treatment_arm in your environment, found none, and stopped. colour and color are interchangeable in ggplot2.

When ggplot2 reports that a column such as treatment_arm was not found, the most common cause is:

The data argument was supplied incorrectlyA column name was used outside aes(), where ggplot2 expected a fixed valueThe ggplot2 package is not loadedThe variable contains missing values

title: Block 4: Context, disclosure and autonomy
text:
Part A: What can the assistant see?
Two questions decide how far you can trust an AI assistantAny AI tool that helps you write or understand code, from inline completion to a chat window. In this course “assistant” is the general word; “agent” is used when the tool acts on your files. with your code:
By the end you will know how to give an agent the right context, keep confidential data out of it, and hand it routine work safely.
⏱ ~35 minutes
An assistant’s answer about your data is reliable only when it has real information: something you pasted, a file it read, or output from a command it ran. In Block 3 you supplied that information yourself. An agent can fetch it on its own, and everything it uses leaves your machine.

title: Block 4: Context, disclosure and autonomy
text:
Exercise 1: Watch what it gathers


Watch what it gathers (8 minutes)


Start state: your workshop repository, with a clean Git pane, and Claude Code open in the Terminal tab with a new conversation (/clear).
1. Ask without the answer-only line. This is a Block 3 question, but this time you let Claude Code look for itself:
Prompt (Claude Code):
My code

  voles |> mutate(mass_change_g = mass_post - mass_pre_g)

fails with "object 'mass_post' not found". voles is read from
data/raw/voles_metabolism.csv. What is wrong?
2. Read the transcript, not just the answer. Above its reply, Claude Code lists each action it took. When we tested this prompt, it ran a short command such as head -n 3 data/raw/voles_metabolism.csv (or Get-Content on Windows) without asking, because Claude Code treats a small set of read-only commands like reading a file. It then named mass_post_g as the real column. If it asks to run anything else, choose No: it can answer from the file.
3. Name the route. For each action in the transcript, find its route in the diagram below: a file it read is route 2; the output of a command it ran is route 4.
You are done when you can name every file or command output that reached the model provider, and the answer names mass_post_g.
If it goes wrong: if it read more than the header, or other files, note which: an agent reads what it judges useful, which is why the habits below matter for confidential data.






TipUsing Posit Assistant





Run the failing code in your R session, then ask only “Why did my last command fail?” Posit Assistant already has the names and types of your objects, so it may answer without fetching anything: that is route 3.





Disclosure: every route out of your machine
Everything an assistant sees is sent to a model provider, by four routes:



Route 1: what you paste


Errors, output and results you paste into a chat or prompt


any tool


Model provider




Route 2: files it reads


Copilot: open files. Claude Code and Posit Assistant: any project file they choose to read


read


Model provider




Route 3: session context the IDE injects


Your live R session: R version, and the names and types of your objects (not their values)


Posit Assistant only


Model provider




Route 4: output of commands it runs


The agent runs Rscript or head data.csv, and reads what it prints


Claude Code, Posit Assistant


Model provider



Everything before an arrow reaches the model provider. A data file in the project may already be disclosed; for a tibble loaded in your session, its names and types are, and its values as soon as code the agent runs prints them.








ImportantWorking with confidential data: five habits





Work on a copy. Put a synthetic or anonymised copy in the project, and run the final analysis on the real data yourself, outside the agent’s folder.

Know your account. Commercial accounts (Team, Enterprise, API) are not used for model training; on Pro or Max, set /privacy-settings. Check your institution’s approval, ethics approval and data agreements first.

Deny reads of sensitive folders in /permissions, for example Read(/data/confidential/**). It is best effort: commands can still read the file.

Stay in Manual mode, and refuse any command that would print records.

Describe, don’t show. names() gives column names and summary() the shape of the data; print(), glimpse() and str() show actual values.







TipBackground: tool-specific notes





There is no .claudeignore file, and /sandbox is not available on native Windows. Posit Assistant blocks .Renviron and .env by default, and shares the names and types of objects in your session, not their values; code it runs can still print values.





Context you hold in your head
A data file supplies column names, but not your question or your design. Your instructor may show this with two prompts; the demonstration is below, and you can try it yourself in Going further.






TipInstructor: demonstration





Your instructor asks a new chat:
Prompt (browser chat):
I have a dataset with pre and post measurements. How should I analyse it?
and then, in another new chat:
Prompt (browser chat):
I have 72 voles, balanced across three treatment arms (Control, Low_dose,
High_dose) and two sexes (M, F). Each animal has body mass measured before
and after treatment, and a single post-treatment metabolic-rate reading.

My question is whether the high-dose treatment changes mass relative to
control, and whether the effect differs between sexes.

The dataset is small (n = 12 per cell). I will report effect sizes alongside
any inferential test. Given this design, what is a defensible primary
analysis, and what are the main threats to its validity?
The first gets a tour of options; the second can get a recommendation, because the design now exists outside your head. Treat it as a proposal to check: the primary analysis is your decision.

title: Block 4: Context, disclosure and autonomy
section: Part B: What can the assistant do?
text:
Part B: What can the assistant do?
The model is the same at every level below. What changes is its permission modeThe setting that decides how much Claude Code may do without asking: plan (read only), default (asks before edits and commands), acceptEdits (edits without asking) and bypassPermissions (never asks).: what it may do without asking. Each level is a rungOne level of the autonomy ladder in Block 4, from suggesting a line (rung 0) to acting with no prompts (rung 5). Each step up removes a moment when you would have seen an action before it happened. on an autonomy ladder. From rung 3 up, what changes is which tool calls run without your approval. The self-study page Build your own agent in R shows that approval step in code.








Rung
What happens
Claude Code
Posit Assistant



0. Suggest
Completes the line you are typing
—
Next Edit Suggestions


1. Ask
Answers; changes nothing
— (no ask mode; Block 3’s answer-only line is a request)
Ask mode (/ask)


2. Plan
Proposes steps; changes nothing until you approve
/plan
/plan


3. Act, with approval
Edits files and runs commands, asking first
Manual (default): the workshop’s starting mode
Normal mode


4. Act, partly unsupervised
Some actions without asking

acceptEdits; auto (a classifier approves actions; Claude Code’s own default since v2.1.283)
Auto mode (/auto)


5. Act, unsupervised
No prompts
bypassPermissions
YOLO mode (/yolo)



Your starting mode. Your workshop repository starts Claude Code in Manual, although its own default is auto since v2.1.283; keep Manual for confidential data. Claude Code has no ask mode, and /plan can still run commands, so read any it proposes. Use rungs 0 to 3 only; the quick reference has the rest.
Rung 3 is where routine work is safe, for example adding a derived column and a plot script. Three things make it safe: you start from a commit, so any change can be reverted; every edit and command is shown to you first; and a test checks the result, whatever the agent reports. Exercise 2 is exactly this.






Warning



Each rung up removes a moment when you would have seen the action. acceptEdits also auto-approves file commands such as cp and mv, so a cp over a raw data file needs no approval. auto suits routine work you will test anyway, not confidential data or anything unprotected. And an approval you click through without reading is rung 5 with extra steps: Block 6 covers the rules that hold however tired you are.


The higher the rung, the more an agent acts on its guesses about your conventions, which is why Block 5 writes them down.






NoteThe safe vibe-coding recipe





Commit, so you start from a clean Git pane.

Protect the inputs: /permissions shows the deny rules, or you add one.

Have the checks ready: tests in tests/ before the agent starts.

Ask in one prompt or skill, in Manual mode, reading each approval.

Run the checks: the test suite in a fresh R session.

Read the diff in the Git pane, then commit or revert.

You will use these six steps in Blocks 7 and 9; the template ships the protections and the tests, so most of it is checking they are there.


Exercise 2: The same task, rising autonomy


Ask, plan, act (15 minutes)


Start state: your workshop repository on main, committed and clean (the Git pane shows no changed files). While Claude Code runs in the Terminal tab, check its work from the R console and the Git pane (checking work).
1. Plan (rung 2). In Claude Code, type /clear, then:
Prompt (Claude Code):
/plan In scripts/explore_voles.R, add a derived mass_change_g column (mass_post_g
minus mass_pre_g). Create a new script scripts/explore_mass_change_plot.R
that plots mass_change_g by treatment_arm and saves the figure to outputs/
with ggsave(). Don't run anything; I'll check the scripts myself.
Before approving, check the plan names both files, leaves data/raw/ alone and saves the figure to outputs/. If anything is missing, choose No, keep planning and say what to change.
2. Act, with approval (rung 3). Choose Yes, manually approve edits, so it stays in Manual mode, and read each edit before you approve it. The repository’s AGENTS.md tells it to run new scripts, so it may still ask to run Rscript: choose No, because you check the result yourself next.
3. Check. Click Diff in the Git pane for each changed file and read it as you would a colleague’s work. Then Restart R (Session → Restart R) and run:
In the R console:

testthat::test_file(here::here("tests", "test_explore.R"))

One test checks mass_change_g really is post minus pre; the other runs the plot script in a fresh R session and checks a figure arrived in outputs/.
4. Record and commit. Create docs/ai-log.md (usethis::edit_file("docs/ai-log.md")) and write the first line of your AI-use logA record written at the time of each piece of AI-assisted work, in the form: date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed. It becomes the AI declaration in a README. yourself, on one line, in the form from Block 1. Use today’s date, written as YYYY-MM-DD:
2026-10-19; Claude Code (model as shown above the Claude Code prompt); added mass_change_g and a plot script; kept both after reading the diff
Commit it together with both scripts. You will add a line after each block in which an agent works; tests/test_ai_log.R checks that each line has four parts separated by semicolons, and that the dates are real and in order.
You are done when both tests pass, you have read every line of the diff, and your first AI-use log line is committed.
If it goes wrong: select the unwanted change in the Git pane and click Revert, then ask again more clearly. If you run out of time, the block5-done checkpoint branch has this block’s files; switch to it from the Git pane’s branch menu at the end of Block 5 if you are still behind.






TipStretch: reflect on the rungs





At which rung did you decide the most? Where would you have missed an unwanted change without the diff?
Payoff. What did the agent do, how long did checking it take, and would you automate this again?









TipUsing Posit Assistant





Use /plan for step 1 and Normal mode (/normal) for step 2. Steps 3 and 4 are the same: the Git pane and the R console.









NoteAt the command line





The same checks from a terminal (after /exit, or in a second Terminal tab): git status, git diff, and Rscript -e "testthat::test_file('tests/test_explore.R')".











NoteCheck · Reproduce · Record





You can now: hand an agent a routine multi-file change at rung 3, trusted because you read every diff and a test you did not write checks the result.

Check: the Git pane’s diff after every agent action; the agent’s report that something “still runs” is a claim until a test confirms it.

Reproduce: work only in a committed, clean repository, so every change is a diff you can inspect or revert.

Record: your AI-use log starts here, in docs/ai-log.md.

You paste nothing, yet Claude Code names your columns correctly. How could it know them?

It cannot; it must be guessingIt read a file in your project or ran code that printed the data, and that output entered its contextIt can see every file on your computerIt remembers your data from a previous conversation

In Claude Code’s acceptEdits mode, what does the agent do without asking?

Nothing; acceptEdits only changes how diffs are displayedOnly edits to files you have namedIt edits files and runs common file commands such as cp and mv without asking, but still asks before other shell commandsEverything, including all shell commands

Which check still works whatever rung the agent ran at?

title: Block 4: Context, disclosure and autonomy
text:
Going further (not covered live)
This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you.






TipAccess and cost





Plans and prices change; check before the session.


Claude Code needs an Anthropic account, used through a subscription or an API key; see Anthropic’s documentation for current options.

Posit Assistant uses Posit AI Pass or your own provider key, including an Anthropic API key. In RStudio, providers are configured in the assistant’s settings.

GitHub Copilot bills in AI credits; check GitHub’s plans page for what your plan includes.

Your institution may have approved some of these tools and not others.










TipTrusting a repository’s configuration





Project settings and hooks are code that runs on your machine. A cloned repository can carry its own, so trust only repositories whose configuration you have read.









TipGitHub Copilot and the remote rung





GitHub Copilot offers the same ladder in its own surfaces. Copilot Chat on github.com can also see files in the repository you open it from.


Rung
GitHub Copilot



0. Suggest
Inline suggestions


1. Ask
Ask in Chat


2. Plan
Plan mode in the IDE


3. Act, with approval
Agent mode, approving each tool call


4. Act, partly unsupervised
Agent mode with auto-approval


5. Act, unsupervised
—


6. Act remotely
Cloud agent



Rung 6, the Copilot cloud agent, works on the repository on GitHub, in an environment GitHub runs. It takes a task such as an issue, works on its own branch and returns a pull request. Copilot Free includes only limited agent features; check GitHub’s plans page to see whether your plan includes the cloud agent. The cloud agent appears in the Going further section of Block 9, where its pull request meets a review gate.









TipStretch: the same error at three levels of context





In three new browser chats, ask about the Exercise 1 error with more context each time: first the error message alone; then the error plus the code; then the error, the code and the output of glimpse(voles). Only with the column names in front of it can a chat name mass_post_g. Column names you never supplied, or a famous dataset you never mentioned (penguins, mtcars), are signs it is guessing.









TipExercise: context you hold in your head





To try the demonstration above yourself, ask a new browser chat the first prompt, then another new chat the second, and compare the answers. A data file can supply column names and types, but not your scientific question or your design intent.

title: Block 4: Context, disclosure and autonomy
text:
Glossary




term
definition



agent
An assistant that can read across a project's files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises.


AI-use log
A record written at the time of each piece of AI-assisted work, in the form: date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed. It becomes the AI declaration in a README.


assistant
Any AI tool that helps you write or understand code, from inline completion to a chat window. In this course "assistant" is the general word; "agent" is used when the tool acts on your files.


permission mode
The setting that decides how much Claude Code may do without asking: plan (read only), default (asks before edits and commands), acceptEdits (edits without asking) and bypassPermissions (never asks).


rung
One level of the autonomy ladder in Block 4, from suggesting a line (rung 0) to acting with no prompts (rung 5). Each step up removes a moment when you would have seen an action before it happened.

title: Block 5: Instructions and skills
text:
Part A: Instructions
The higher an agent works on the autonomy ladder, the more its guesses about your conventions land in your files. This block shows you how to state those conventions once, so every conversation follows them, in two ways:
Both are requests the model usually follows; Block 6 covers rules that hold every time.
⏱ ~45 minutes
Your conventions live in one file, AGENTS.md, at the repository root, and both Claude Code and Posit Assistant read it at the start of every conversation. There is no CLAUDE.md: Claude Code reads AGENTS.md only when no CLAUDE.md exists, so creating one (for example with /init) would hide your conventions.
Instructions that work are:

title: Block 5: Instructions and skills
text:
Instruction file: loaded into every conversation


AGENTS.md: your conventions


read directly by


Claude Code and Posit Assistant




Skills: loaded when invoked or judged relevant


.agents/skills/<your-skill>/ (the master copy)


you copy


.claude/skills/<your-skill>/


read by


Claude Code



Posit Assistant reads .agents/skills/ directly, so it needs no copy. The course’s own skills already ship in both folders.





one per line, and specific enough to check (“use the native pipe |>”, not “write clean code”);

true of your own code, or the model gets mixed signals;

short, because the file loads into every request;

added when a mistake repeats: a correction in chat is forgotten next conversation;

not guarantees: “never edit raw data” belongs here and in the enforced controls of Block 6.

Activity: Make AGENTS.md yours
Your workshop repository already contains a starter AGENTS.md. Make it describe your practice, then prove that Claude Code reads it.






NoteThe starter AGENTS.md





It includes a canaryA fixed line that an instruction file asks the assistant to include in its output, so that seeing the line shows the file was loaded. It does not show that the other rules were followed.: a fixed first line the assistant is asked to put in any R code it writes, so you can see the file was loaded. The “Tests” rules ask the agent to prove its own work after every edit, which later blocks rely on.


# Project conventions: voles analysis

## Canary
When you write or edit R code, make the first line of the first code block:
# agents-md: active v1

## Structure
- Raw data live in data/raw/ and are never modified.
- Derived data go to data/derived/; figures and tables go to outputs/.
- Reusable functions live in scripts/functions/.

## R style
- Tidyverse style, native pipe |>, snake_case names, <- for assignment.
- Write TRUE and FALSE, never T and F.
- Build every path with here::here() (or here() after library(here)). Never
  use setwd() or rm(list = ls()).
- Read CSV files with readr and explicit col_types.

## Reproducibility
- Packages are managed with renv. Do not call install.packages(); ask before
  adding a package.
- Do not edit renv.lock.
- Set a seed immediately before any random step.
- Every script must run in a fresh R session.
- Every script must run with Rscript from the project root; after writing one,
  run it that way and report the exit status.
- Save figures with ggsave() to outputs/.

## Tests
- After editing any R file, run Rscript -e "testthat::test_dir('tests')" and
  paste the final summary line verbatim.
- Never edit anything in tests/fixtures/, an existing expectation or a
  tolerance to make a test pass.
- Every new function in scripts/functions/ gets a test with at least one
  known-answer case on a small tibble, including an NA; expected values are
  worked out by hand, never by running the code under test.

## Data integrity
- Never drop rows silently; state the reason for every filter in a comment.
- Report the number of observations behind every summary statistic.

## Statistics
- Label each analysis as exploratory or confirmatory.
- Never type numerical results into text; compute them in code.

## Version control
- Before you edit any file, run git status.
- If this folder is not a git repository, stop and ask me to set one up.
- If there are uncommitted changes, list them and ask whether I want to
  commit first.
- Never commit, push or change git settings unless I ask.

## Working with me
- Before changing more than one file, present a plan and wait for approval.
- Do not edit anything under data/raw/, tests/fixtures/ or .github/.







Edit, check, verify (15 minutes)


Start state: your workshop repository open, a clean Git pane, and Claude Code running in the project’s Terminal tab (checking work).
1. Baseline.
Prompt (Claude Code):
/plan Read data/raw/voles_metabolism.csv and make a quick exploratory plot
of mass_post_g by treatment arm. Show the R code in your reply; do not
create any files.
Look for the canary, # agents-md: active v1, as the first line of the code. (Asking for the code in the reply gives the canary somewhere to appear.)
2. Make it yours. Type /memory, choose AGENTS.md, and in your editor:

delete one rule you do not actually follow;
add one convention you always follow.

Keep the canary and the “Tests”, “Statistics” and “Working with me” sections, which later blocks rely on. Save.
3. Verify. Type /clear and repeat the step 1 prompt. The canary shows the file was loaded; check the plot code against your new rule to see whether it was followed.
4. Check it with a test. In the R console, after Session → Restart R:

testthat::test_file(here::here("tests", "test_controls.R"))

It confirms AGENTS.md is in place with its canary, the project still starts in Manual mode, and the deny rules are intact. Commit AGENTS.md from the Git pane.
You are done when the canary appears, the test passes, and your edited AGENTS.md is committed.
If it goes wrong: check there is no CLAUDE.md (the test checks this too) and that /memory lists AGENTS.md. Still stuck? Compare with the block5-done branch from the Git pane’s branch menu.






TipUsing Posit Assistant





Posit Assistant reads the same AGENTS.md. Open it from the gear menu (Open project memory), or describe your conventions and run /savememory. If the canary is missing, check that you trusted the workspace.

title: Block 5: Instructions and skills
text:
Part B: Skills
A skill is a folder holding a SKILL.md file, plus any scripts or templates it needs. Its front matterThe block between two lines of three dashes at the top of a file, holding settings such as a skill’s name and description, or a Quarto document’s options., between two lines of three dashes at the top, gives a name and a description:


The description is the trigger. “Use when producing a ggplot2 figure for a report, poster or paper” loads when it should; “for plots” loads erratically. Invoking it by name (/skill-name) always works.

The body is a procedure: when to use it, the steps, hard rules and a final check. It loads only when used, so it can be longer than AGENTS.md.







TipBackground: skills that run only by name





For a skill that writes files, disable-model-invocation: true in the front matter makes it run only when you invoke it by name.



Keep the master copy in .agents/skills/ and copy it into .claude/skills/ for Claude Code (Posit Assistant reads .agents/skills/ directly). The deny rules protect .claude/ from the agent’s edit tools but not .agents/skills/, so check the master copy in the Git pane too. The course’s own skills already ship in both; type /skills to list them. For a skill you write, copy it once, and again whenever you change it:
In the R console:

fs::dir_copy(
  here::here(".agents", "skills", "house-figures"),
  here::here(".claude", "skills", "house-figures"),
  overwrite = TRUE
)

Activity: Write a skill and test it


A house figure style (20 minutes)


Start state: Claude Code in Manual mode in your project’s Terminal tab, with your AGENTS.md committed.
1. Baseline, before the skill exists.
Prompt (Claude Code):
Make a figure of mass_post_g by treatment_arm for the voles data, for a
lab report. Save the code as scripts/fig_baseline.R.
Approve the edit. Doing this first guarantees the baseline was written without the skill.
2. Create the skill. In the R console, usethis::edit_file(".agents/skills/house-figures/SKILL.md") creates and opens the file. Paste in:
---
name: house-figures
description: >-
  Applies this project's conventions to any ggplot2 figure that will appear
  in a report, poster or paper. Use when asked to create, revise or polish a
  figure for presentation. Not for quick exploratory plots.
---

# House figure style

## Rules
1. Where any group has fewer than 30 observations, show every observation
   (jittered points or a dot plot) with a summary overlaid. Never draw a bar
   with error bars ("dynamite plot").
2. Colour categorical groups with the Okabe-Ito palette
   (grDevices::palette.colors(palette = "Okabe-Ito")), and map the same
   variable to point shape so the figure works without colour.
3. Axis titles give the quantity and its unit, for example "Body mass (g)".
4. Use theme_classic(base_size = 12).
5. Show the number of observations per group on the figure.
6. Never add p-values or significance markers unless the user supplies a
   fitted model and asks for them.

## Before returning code
List which rules you applied, and any you could not apply and why.
Copy it into .claude/skills/ with the fs::dir_copy() line above (you do this yourself, because .claude/ is protected from the agent). Type /skills: house-figures should be listed, with no restart.
3. With the skill.
Prompt (Claude Code):
/house-figures Make a figure of mass_post_g by treatment_arm for the voles
data, for a lab report. Save the code as scripts/fig_house.R.
4. Grade it. Run both scripts in a fresh R session and look at the figures: callr::rscript(here::here("scripts", "fig_baseline.R")), then the same for fig_house.R. Then record, for each rule:


Rule
Without skill
With skill



1. Raw data shown; no dynamite plot




2. Okabe-Ito colour plus shape




3. Units in axis titles




4. theme_classic(base_size = 12)





5. n per group shown




6. No unrequested p-values





5. Record it. Add a line to docs/ai-log.md in the same form as Block 4, with today’s date, naming the skill you tested and what you kept or changed in its output. Commit it with the skill and the two scripts.
You are done when the table is filled in from the figures you looked at, not from the agent’s list of rules it applied, and your log line is committed.
If it goes wrong: if /skills does not list it, check that .claude/skills/house-figures/SKILL.md exists and its front matter starts and ends with three dashes. Out of time? Commit or discard your changes in the Git pane first, so the switch is not blocked, then switch to block5-done.
Payoff. What did the skill do for you, how long did checking it take, and would you use it for the next figure?






TipStretch: test the trigger





In a new conversation (/clear), test the trigger: “Give me a quick look at mass_post_g by arm” should not load the skill; “Polish the figure in scripts/fig_baseline.R for the poster” should. Or test rule 6: ask it to “add significance stars between the groups in scripts/fig_house.R” and see whether it declines. Either way, what makes the output trustworthy is the grading in step 4, which you can repeat on every figure.









TipUsing Posit Assistant





Posit Assistant reads .agents/skills/ directly, so no copy is needed. Invoke the skill by name in the same way.











NoteCheck · Reproduce · Record





You can now: state your conventions once for every conversation, and package a procedure as a skill you invoke by name, trusted because the canary and tests/test_controls.R show the files are connected, and you grade the output rule by rule.

Check: a canary shows a file was loaded, not followed; grade the output and run the figure code.

Reproduce: your AGENTS.md states the reproducibility rules (renv, fresh R session, seeds); Blocks 7 and 9 check the agent kept to them.

Record: add a line to docs/ai-log.md naming the skill you tested and what you changed in its output.

title: Block 5: Instructions and skills
text:
Check your understanding
Your canary line does not appear in Claude Code’s answers. What is the most likely explanation?

Claude Code cannot follow instructionsThe instructions are not reaching Claude Code, for example because a CLAUDE.md in the repository hides AGENTS.md, or Claude Code was started outside the projectThe canary only works with Anthropic modelsAGENTS.md must be committed to GitHub before Claude Code can read it

What is the essential difference between an instruction file and a skill?

Instruction files can contain code; skills cannotInstructions load into every conversation automatically; a skill loads only when invoked by name or judged relevant from its descriptionSkills are enforced; instructions are advisoryInstruction files work only with Copilot

A skill fires for quick exploratory plots when you meant it only for publication figures. What should you change first?

The rules in the body of the skillThe description, so it states precisely when the skill applies and when it does notThe folder the skill is stored inThe model you are using

title: Block 5: Instructions and skills
text:
Going further (not covered live)
This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you.






TipSkills you did not write





Claude Code ships built-in skills such as /code-review and /debug, and shared collections are published online, for example Anthropic’s anthropics/skills repository. Read any skill before installing it: it can include scripts the assistant runs on your machine. Install a skill bundle and compare, below, gives you one to practise on: pub-figures, the ggplot chapter’s conventions as a skill.









TipLinking a skill instead of copying it





On macOS or Linux you can use a symbolic linkA file-system entry that points to another folder or file, so one copy can appear in two places. On Windows, copying the folder is usually simpler. instead of a copy, so there is only one version to keep up to date: fs::link_create(here::here(".agents", "skills", "house-figures"), here::here(".claude", "skills", "house-figures")). Claude Code follows the link, but it stores the full path, so recreate it if you move the project. On Windows, symbolic links need extra configuration, so copy the folder.









TipInstruction and skill files in other tools












File or folder
Posit Assistant
GitHub Copilot




AGENTS.md (repository root)
Read as project memory
Read by the cloud agent, agent mode and the CLI


CLAUDE.md
—
Read by the cloud agent


.github/copilot-instructions.md
Offered for conversion by /import-instructions

Read by Copilot


Path-scoped rules
No equivalent found

.github/instructions/*.instructions.md with applyTo



.agents/skills/<name>/
Yes
Yes


.claude/skills/<name>/
—
Yes


.github/skills/<name>/
—
Yes



This course has no CLAUDE.md, so every tool reads the same AGENTS.md. Copilot reads both .agents/skills/ and .claude/skills/; if it lists a skill twice, remove one route for Copilot.
Posit Assistant also includes built-in skills such as quarto-authoring and r-package-development.









TipA rule for Quarto files only





Some rules are right for one kind of file and wrong elsewhere. A chunk option such as #| echo: false is meaningful in a .qmd file and meaningless in an .R script. The test for a scoped rule: would it be wrong, not merely irrelevant, in the files it excludes? If not, put it in AGENTS.md.


Create and test a scoped rule


The rules themselves:
# Quarto document conventions

- Set chunk options with the hashpipe (#|) inside the chunk, not in the
  {r} header.
- Give every chunk a label; prefix figure chunks with fig-.
- Every figure chunk sets #| fig-cap:, #| fig-width: and #| fig-height:.
- Refer to figures in the text with @fig-..., never by a typed number.
- Default to #| echo: false unless the document is a code walkthrough.
- Resolve paths with here::here(); never assume the working directory is the
  document's folder.
(The “hashpipe” is the #| at the start of a chunk-option line.) Place them where your tool looks:


Claude Code: .claude/rules/quarto.md, beginning with front matter that restricts it to Quarto files:
---
paths:
  - "**/*.qmd"
---


Copilot: .github/instructions/quarto.instructions.md, beginning with this front matter:
---
applyTo: "**/*.qmd"
---

Posit Assistant: no path-scoped instruction file is documented. Add the rules to AGENTS.md under a heading such as “When editing .qmd files”, or rely on its built-in quarto-authoring skill.

Test. Open a .qmd file and ask for a chunk that plots mass_post_g by treatment_arm. A correct answer uses hashpipe options, a fig- label, a caption and here::here(). Then ask for the same plot in an .R script; the Quarto rules should not appear. If they do not appear in the .qmd either, the rule is not loading on your surface. Report what you found; behaviour differs between tools.


Every scoped rule is a second copy of a convention to keep in step, once per tool. Use scoped rules sparingly.









TipInstall a skill bundle and compare





house-figures is six rules you wrote and can read at a glance. pub-figures is the opposite case: the conventions from the ggplot chapter (the chart-type and audience tables, theme_project(), colorspace palettes, the colour-vision-deficiency check, the four-element legend, saving in two formats) packaged as a skill of about 200 lines, with R scripts that the assistant sources and adapts. It is a skill you did not write, so you read it before you install it.
The bundle contains:
pub-figures/
├── SKILL.md                when to use it, the rules, a pre-flight checklist
├── theme-project.R         theme_project() and palette functions
├── raincloud-template.R    figure skeleton, including saving
├── emmeans-bridge.R        model-based significance brackets
└── patchwork-template.R    multi-panel figure with one shared legend
theme_project() in this bundle is the full version of the simple theme_project() you wrote in the ggplot chapter: the same name and base_size argument, with a font, colours for titles and gridlines, and an axis_type argument added.


 Download pub-figures.zip




A skill bundle you did not write


1. Read before you install. Open SKILL.md and theme-project.R (both are also reproduced below). Find two places where pub-figures contradicts your house-figures rules. (There are at least two: the palette and the theme.) Find the line that tells the assistant what to do when information is missing.
2. Remove the overlap. Both skills describe themselves as being for figures in reports, posters and papers, so with both installed you cannot tell which one loaded. Move house-figures out of both skills folders (or rename SKILL.md inside it) before going on. Overlapping descriptions are a real hazard once you collect skills from several sources.
3. Install. In the R console, unzip(file.choose(), exdir = here::here(".agents", "skills")) lets you pick the downloaded zip and unpacks it into .agents/skills/; then copy it into .claude/skills/ for Claude Code with fs::dir_copy(), as above. The skill uses ggdist, colorspace, ragg, colorBlindness, emmeans and ggpubr; if your project uses renv and they are not in its lockfile, add them yourself before the test, rather than letting the assistant install packages.
4. Same prompt, new skill. Type /skills to check it is listed (skills reload without a restart), then, without naming the skill, ask the prompt from the house-figures activity:
Prompt (Claude Code):
Make a figure of mass_post_g by treatment_arm for the voles data, for a
lab report.
Did the skill load from its description alone? Did the assistant ask about the audience, or record a default?
5. Grade it against its own checklist. The skill ends with a pre-flight checklist. Check the script against each item yourself, rather than accepting the assistant’s report that it did. Then run the script: are both a PDF and a PNG in outputs/figures/? Run the colorBlindness::cvdPlot() line it left for you, and look at the result.
6. Test a rule under pressure. Ask it to “add significance stars between the groups” without fitting a model. The skill says it must insert a legend placeholder rather than invent p-values. Then give it a fitted model it can actually see. Claude Code cannot see objects in your R console, so a model you fit there does not count: ask it to add model <- lm(mass_post_g ~ treatment_arm, data = voles) to the figure script itself, or paste the output of summary(model) into the prompt. Ask again: it should now use the emmeans-bridge.R pattern with an adjusted p-value.
7. Compare. Which skill would you hand to a colleague? Which would you trust without rereading it after an update? A long skill encodes more of your standards, and hides more of them from view.








Notepub-figures/SKILL.md







---
name: pub-figures
description: >-
  Use when producing a ggplot2 figure intended for sharing outside the
  immediate session, including manuscript figures, lab reports, posters, talk
  slides, and public engagement graphics. Do not invoke for diagnostic,
  exploratory, model-checking, or one-off plots.
---

# Publication figures

This skill governs production of figures that will be seen by an external audience. It is self-contained: the house rules below apply even if the project has no instruction file.

## House rules

- Tidyverse style, native pipe `|>`, `here::here()` for every path.
- British spelling in titles, labels, legends and comments.
- Never produce pie charts, dual y-axes, 3D effects, or bar charts with error bars ("dynamite plots") when the raw data exist.

## Missing information

If information you need is missing (the audience, a variable's unit, the fitted model), ask the user once, in a single message, before writing code. If the user tells you to proceed without it, or you are working unattended (for example as a cloud agent on a pull request), choose the safe default this skill gives, record the choice in a code comment and, if there is one, in the pull request description, and continue.

## Project toolkit

The packages this skill uses are listed below. Check that each one you need is
in `renv.lock`; if one is missing, stop and ask before installing anything:

- `ggplot2`, `patchwork`, `here`, `scales` for core plotting, composition, paths, and label formatting.
- `ggdist` for raincloud and half-eye distributions: `stat_halfeye()`, `stat_pointinterval()`.
- `ggbeeswarm` for moderate-n group displays: `geom_quasirandom()`.
- `colorspace` for palettes: `scale_*_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 2")`, `scale_*_continuous_sequential(palette = "Viridis")`, `scale_*_continuous_diverging(palette = "Blue-Red")`, and the HCL generators (`sequential_hcl()`, `diverging_hcl()`) used by the brand-seeded scales in `theme-project.R`.
- `emmeans` for estimated marginal means and pairwise contrasts: `emmeans(model, specs = "var")`, `pairs(emm, adjust = "tukey")`.
- `ggpubr::stat_pvalue_manual()` as the rendering layer for emmeans-derived contrasts. Never `ggpubr::stat_compare_means()`, which performs unadjusted pairwise t-tests by default.
- `ggh4x` for nested or hierarchical faceting: `facet_nested()`, `facet_nested_wrap()`, `guide_axis_nested()`.
- `ragg` for raster output via `ggsave(device = ragg::agg_png)`.
- `colorBlindness::cvdPlot()` for the colour-vision-deficiency check.
- `showtext` (optional) for the project font; without it `theme_project()` falls back to the device's default font.

Do not introduce additional plotting packages without amending this list. Do not reach for `cowplot` themes when `theme_minimal()` or `theme_project()` will do. Do not hand-write manual hex colour vectors as data scales: use the `colorspace` palettes or the brand-seeded constructors in `theme-project.R`, both of which keep palettes CVD-checkable. A single fixed colour for a single-group or highlight geom is permitted and is not a "data scale".

## Colour

The colour-vision-deficiency check (`cvdPlot()`, below) is the final arbiter: a palette that fails it must be replaced, regardless of brand intent.

**No brand specified (default).** Use `colorspace::scale_*` functions, matched to data structure.

**Brand specified.** When the request names a brand colour (for example, "use a brand colour of darkblue"), call `set_brand("darkblue")` once after sourcing `theme-project.R`. `set_brand()` accepts any R colour name or hex string. The brand colour then seeds:

- single-colour and highlight geoms, via `brand_base()`;
- sequential continuous scales: `scale_*_brand_seq()`;
- the **high** arm of diverging continuous scales: `scale_*_brand_div(midpoint = <value>)`. The low arm is the brand's complementary hue, so the two arms always contrast, unless you name a second brand colour with `set_brand(<brand>, div_low = <colour>)`.

**Categorical colour is never brand-seeded.** One seed colour cannot generate a coherent, CVD-safe set of distinct hues. For unordered groups, use `colorspace` "Dark 2"; `scale_*_brand_qual()` in `theme-project.R` is the same palette and takes no `base` or `n` argument. The brand colour can still mark one focal group, with the other groups in grey.

| Data structure | Palette type | colorspace default | With a brand set |
|----------------|--------------|--------------------|------------------|
| Discrete, unordered groups | Qualitative | `Dark 2` | `Dark 2` (`scale_*_brand_qual()` is identical) |
| Discrete, ordered groups | Sequential discrete | `Purples 3` | `Purples 3` (the brand scales are continuous only) |
| Continuous, one-directional | Sequential | `Viridis` | `scale_*_brand_seq()` |
| Continuous, midpoint-centred | Diverging | `Blue-Red` | `scale_*_brand_div()` |

If a brand-seeded scale fails the CVD check, replace it with the colorspace default in the same row and record the fallback in a comment.

Categorical groupings must use redundant encoding: shape for points, linetype for lines. Colour alone is not sufficient.

## Statistical annotations workflow

Pairwise contrasts come from `emmeans::emmeans()` and `emmeans::pairs()` with an explicit adjustment method (`tukey`, `holm`, or similar). Render brackets with `ggpubr::stat_pvalue_manual()`, supplying a data frame of contrasts.

Filter to significant contrasts before drawing. Format p-values with `scales::label_pvalue()` so very small values appear as `<0.001` rather than `0.000`.

A worked example is in `emmeans-bridge.R`.

## Error bars

Three options, not interchangeable:

- **Standard deviation:** spread of individual observations. Use when describing population variability.
- **Standard error of the mean:** precision of the sample mean. Shrinks with sample size.
- **95% confidence interval:** the recommended default. Prefer model-based intervals via `emmeans` where a model exists, otherwise from `stat_summary(fun.data = mean_cl_normal)`.

The choice must appear in the y axis label.

## Multiple panels and shared legends

When composing panels with `patchwork` and `plot_layout(guides = "collect")`, collection merges only guides that are identical in aesthetic, scale, breaks, and title (`name`). It deduplicates by guide specification, not by visual appearance, and it never removes a guide it judges different. Two failures follow: panels that encode the same variable through different aesthetics (`fill` in one, `colour` plus `shape` in another) or different palettes produce one legend each; and a panel encoding a genuinely different variable produces its own legend, which is correct.

Resolve the layout from the plot specifications:

- **Same variable, same palette, across all panels:** produce one shared legend. Designate the panel with the richest encoding (e.g. colour plus shape) as the legend-bearer, because that legend is a complete key for the simpler panels but not the reverse. Apply the identical scale call and an identical `name` in every panel, then suppress the guide on every non-bearing panel with `guides(<aesthetic> = "none")`. Record the choice of bearer in a comment.
- **Panels encode different variables:** do not force collection into one key. Keep the separate legends; merging them would mislabel a panel.

A mismatched `name`, a differing aesthetic or scale, or a missing suppression line will silently leave more than one legend for the same variable. After composing, confirm exactly one legend appears per distinct variable. A worked skeleton is in `patchwork-template.R`.

## Saving

Always save to `outputs/figures/` via `here::here()` in both PDF and PNG formats. Specify `width`, `height`, `units`, and `dpi` explicitly; do not rely on `ggsave()` defaults. Use `ragg::agg_png` as the device for PNG output with `bg = "white"`. PDF uses the default device.

The agent cannot verify visual accessibility. Insert this line at the end of the script and flag it for the investigator to run and inspect:

# ==============================================================================
# Project theme and palette construction for ggplot2.
#
# Colour policy (authoritative; see pub-figures SKILL.md):
#   * No brand set         -> use colorspace palettes directly.
#   * Brand set            -> set_brand("darkblue") sets the base colour (used by
#                             single-colour and highlight geoms) and reseeds the
#                             sequential ramp and the diverging HIGH arm. The
#                             low arm becomes the brand's complementary hue
#                             unless set_brand() is given div_low. Sequential
#                             and diverging are
#                             generated via colorspace HCL generators
#                             (CVD-robust, monotonic luminance).
#   * Categorical colour is NEVER brand-seeded: scale_*_brand_qual() delegate to
#                             colorspace "Dark 2", which sizes itself to the data.
#                             A single seed cannot make a coherent multi-hue set.
#   * Single-group / highlight geoms default to brand_base(), teal until reset.
#
# Manual hex palettes are NOT used as data scales. Only the base colour is used
# directly, and only for single-colour or highlight geoms.
#
# theme_project() here is the full version of the simple theme_project() taught
# in the ggplot chapter (Block 3: Themes and scales). It keeps the same name and
# base_size argument, and adds a font, furniture colours and axis_type.
#
# Dependencies: ggplot2 (>= 3.5), colorspace, scales; showtext + sysfonts for
#   fonts (optional: without them the device's default font is used);
#   colorBlindness for the accessibility check.
# ==============================================================================

library(ggplot2)
library(colorspace)

# ---- Brand state and setter --------------------------------------------------
# A single mutable brand state lets one call rebrand everything downstream.
# `set_brand("darkblue")` sets the base colour, which seeds the sequential ramp
# and the diverging high arm. Accepts any R colour name or hex string.

.brand_state <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())
.brand_state$base    <- "#09baba"  # teal default
.brand_state$div_low <- "#2c4977"  # navy default for the diverging low arm

#' Normalise a colour name or hex to a hex string
#' @keywords internal
.as_hex <- function(col) {
  rgb <- grDevices::col2rgb(col)  # accepts R colour names and hex
  grDevices::rgb(rgb[1], rgb[2], rgb[3], maxColorValue = 255)
}

#' Set the project brand colour
#'
#' Sets the base colour used by single-colour and highlight geoms, the
#' sequential ramp and the diverging high arm. Call once at the top of a
#' script: `set_brand("darkblue")`. Accepts any R colour name or hex string.
#'
#' @param base Brand colour (name or hex).
#' @param div_low Optional colour for the diverging low arm. If `NULL` (the
#'   default), the low arm uses the hue opposite the brand colour on the HCL
#'   colour wheel, so the two arms always contrast.
#' @return Invisibly, the resolved brand state as a list.
#' @export
set_brand <- function(base, div_low = NULL) {
  .brand_state$base <- .as_hex(base)
  .brand_state$div_low <- if (is.null(div_low)) {
    .complement_of(.brand_state$base)
  } else {
    .as_hex(div_low)
  }
  invisible(as.list(.brand_state))
}

#' Colour with the opposite HCL hue, for the diverging low arm
#' @keywords internal
.complement_of <- function(col) {
  hue <- (.hue_of(col) + 180) %% 360
  colorspace::hex(colorspace::polarLUV(L = 40, C = 60, H = hue), fixup = TRUE)
}

#' Reset the brand to the teal/navy default
#' @return Invisibly, the resolved brand state as a list.
#' @export
reset_brand <- function() {
  .brand_state$base    <- "#09baba"
  .brand_state$div_low <- "#2c4977"
  invisible(as.list(.brand_state))
}

#' Current brand base colour
#'
#' Returns the current brand base as a hex string. It is a function, not a value,
#' so it reflects the most recent `set_brand()` call. Use as `brand_base()`.
#' @return A hex colour string.
#' @export
brand_base <- function() .brand_state$base

# ---- Internal: font registration ---------------------------------------------

# Returns TRUE if `family` is available to showtext, FALSE otherwise, so the
# theme can fall back to the device's default font rather than warn on every
# text element.
.register_project_font <- function(family = "Open Sans") {
  if (!requireNamespace("showtext", quietly = TRUE)) {
    return(FALSE)
  }
  showtext::showtext_auto(enable = TRUE)
  if (!(family %in% sysfonts::font_families())) {
    try(sysfonts::font_add_google(family, family), silent = TRUE)
  }
  family %in% sysfonts::font_families()
}

# ---- theme_project() ---------------------------------------------------------

#' Project theme
#'
#' A composable ggplot2 theme controlling non-data aesthetics only. It sets no
#' data-encoding colours; pair it with a scale constructor (see below). Furniture
#' colours (title, axis labels, gridlines) are decorative and need not be
#' CVD-safe; the strip background is deliberately neutral grey so it is not
#' mistaken for a data signal when a fill palette is present. Furniture colours do
#' not track the brand by design; rebrand them by editing the literals below.
#'
#' @param base_size Base font size in points. Default 12 (journal/lab-report
#'   floor; raise to 14-20 for poster, talk, or public-engagement).
#' @param base_family Base font family. Default "Open Sans".
#' @param base_line_size Base line size. Default 0.5.
#' @param base_rect_size Base rectangle size. Default 0.5.
#' @param axis_type "categorical" or "continuous"; controls gridlines.
#' @return A ggplot2 theme object.
#' @export
theme_project <- function(base_size = 12,
                          base_family = "Open Sans",
                          base_line_size = 0.5,
                          base_rect_size = 0.5,
                          axis_type = c("categorical", "continuous")) {

  axis_type <- match.arg(axis_type)
  if (!.register_project_font(base_family)) {
    base_family <- ""  # device default font
  }

  title_col <- "#2c4977"  # decorative furniture only
  label_col <- "#41566f"
  muted_col <- "#5d6b7d"

  base <- ggplot2::theme(
    line = ggplot2::element_line(colour = "#000000", linewidth = base_line_size),
    rect = ggplot2::element_rect(fill = "#FFFFFF", colour = "#000000",
                                 linewidth = base_rect_size),
    text = ggplot2::element_text(family = base_family, colour = "#000000",
                                 size = base_size),
    plot.title = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0,
                                       size = ggplot2::rel(1.4),
                                       margin = ggplot2::margin(8, 0, 6, 0),
                                       colour = title_col),
    plot.subtitle = ggplot2::element_text(hjust = 0, size = ggplot2::rel(1.1),
                                          margin = ggplot2::margin(2, 0, 0, 0),
                                          colour = label_col),
    plot.caption = ggplot2::element_text(hjust = 1, size = ggplot2::rel(0.8),
                                         margin = ggplot2::margin(6, 0, 0, 0),
                                         colour = muted_col),
    axis.text.y = ggplot2::element_text(colour = muted_col, size = ggplot2::rel(0.9)),
    axis.title.y = ggplot2::element_text(colour = label_col,
                                         margin = ggplot2::margin(0, 4, 0, 0)),
    axis.text.x = ggplot2::element_text(colour = muted_col, size = ggplot2::rel(0.9)),
    axis.title.x = ggplot2::element_text(colour = label_col,
                                         margin = ggplot2::margin(4, 0, 0, 0)),
    panel.background = ggplot2::element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
    strip.background = ggplot2::element_rect(fill = "#e9e9e9", colour = NA),
    strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold", colour = "#2c4977",
                                       size = ggplot2::rel(1.0)),
    panel.border = ggplot2::element_blank(),
    axis.line = ggplot2::element_line(linewidth = base_line_size, colour = "black"),
    legend.position = "right"
  )

  grid_col <- "#dedddd"
  if (axis_type == "continuous") {
    grid_theme <- ggplot2::theme(
      panel.grid.major.y = ggplot2::element_line(colour = grid_col),
      panel.grid.major.x = ggplot2::element_line(colour = grid_col)
    )
  } else {
    grid_theme <- ggplot2::theme(
      panel.grid.major.y = ggplot2::element_line(colour = grid_col),
      panel.grid.major.x = ggplot2::element_blank()
    )
  }

  base + grid_theme
}

# ---- Brand-seeded palette constructors ---------------------------------------
# These wrap colorspace HCL generators, seeded on the current brand colour, so
# the ramp is perceptually based with monotonic luminance. With no set_brand()
# call the seed is teal; callers may also pass `base`/`low`/`high` explicitly,
# which always overrides the brand state. If no brand is intended at all, use
# colorspace::scale_*_{qualitative,sequential,diverging} directly.

#' Hue (HCL) of a colour, for seeding colorspace generators
#' @keywords internal
.hue_of <- function(col) {
  hcl <- colorspace::coords(as(colorspace::hex2RGB(.as_hex(col)), "polarLUV"))
  unname(hcl[, "H"])
}

#' Brand-seeded sequential scale (colour)
#'
#' Single-hue sequential ramp seeded on `base`, generated in HCL so luminance is
#' monotonic. Light-to-dark by default.
#'
#' @param base Seed colour. Defaults to the current `brand_base()`.
#' @param n Number of interpolation stops. Default 7.
#' @param ... Passed to `ggplot2::scale_colour_gradientn()`.
#' @return A ggplot2 scale.
#' @export
scale_colour_brand_seq <- function(base = brand_base(), n = 7, ...) {
  cols <- colorspace::sequential_hcl(
    n = n, h = .hue_of(base), c = c(70, 10), l = c(25, 95), power = 1.2,
    rev = TRUE
  )
  ggplot2::scale_colour_gradientn(colours = cols, ...)
}

#' @rdname scale_colour_brand_seq
#' @export
scale_fill_brand_seq <- function(base = brand_base(), n = 7, ...) {
  cols <- colorspace::sequential_hcl(
    n = n, h = .hue_of(base), c = c(70, 10), l = c(25, 95), power = 1.2,
    rev = TRUE
  )
  ggplot2::scale_fill_gradientn(colours = cols, ...)
}

#' Brand-seeded diverging scale (colour)
#'
#' Two-hue diverging ramp seeded on `low` and `high`, generated in HCL with a
#' balanced neutral midpoint. Supply `midpoint` to centre on a meaningful value.
#'
#' @param low Seed colour for the low arm. Defaults to navy or, after
#'   `set_brand()`, to the brand's complementary hue (or its `div_low`).
#' @param high Seed colour for the high arm. Defaults to the current `brand_base()`.
#' @param midpoint Data value mapped to the neutral midpoint. Default 0.
#' @param n Number of interpolation stops (odd recommended). Default 11.
#' @param ... Passed to `ggplot2::scale_colour_gradientn()`.
#' @return A ggplot2 scale.
#' @export
scale_colour_brand_div <- function(low = .brand_state$div_low,
                                    high = brand_base(),
                                    midpoint = 0, n = 11, ...) {
  cols <- colorspace::diverging_hcl(
    n = n, h = c(.hue_of(low), .hue_of(high)),
    c = 80, l = c(35, 95), power = 1.0
  )
  ggplot2::scale_colour_gradientn(
    colours = cols, rescaler = ~ scales::rescale_mid(.x, mid = midpoint), ...
  )
}

#' @rdname scale_colour_brand_div
#' @export
scale_fill_brand_div <- function(low = .brand_state$div_low,
                                  high = brand_base(),
                                  midpoint = 0, n = 11, ...) {
  cols <- colorspace::diverging_hcl(
    n = n, h = c(.hue_of(low), .hue_of(high)),
    c = 80, l = c(35, 95), power = 1.0
  )
  ggplot2::scale_fill_gradientn(
    colours = cols, rescaler = ~ scales::rescale_mid(.x, mid = midpoint), ...
  )
}

#' Qualitative scale (colour) for categorical groups
#'
#' Categorical palettes are NOT brand-seeded. A single brand colour cannot
#' generate a coherent, CVD-safe multi-hue set: spreading hues from one anchor
#' discards the seed's own chroma and luminance and walks through arbitrary
#' intermediate hues. This constructor therefore delegates to `colorspace`'s
#' `Dark 2` qualitative palette, which is built for mutual distinctness and is
#' CVD-tested, and which sizes itself to the number of groups (so it cannot raise
#' "Insufficient values in manual scale"). Reserve the brand colour for the
#' sequential ramp, the diverging high arm, and single-colour or highlight geoms,
#' where one seed genuinely works. Always pair with a redundant aesthetic (shape
#' or linetype).
#'
#' @param ... Passed to `colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative()`.
#' @return A ggplot2 scale.
#' @export
scale_colour_brand_qual <- function(...) {
  colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 2", ...)
}

#' @rdname scale_colour_brand_qual
#' @param ... Passed to `colorspace::scale_fill_discrete_qualitative()`.
#' @export
scale_fill_brand_qual <- function(...) {
  colorspace::scale_fill_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 2", ...)
}

# Figure skeleton: raincloud for Discrete x Continuous, with palette, theme
# and saving.
# Audience not specified; defaulting to journal-lab-report.
# Re-run with explicit audience if poster, talk, or public-engagement intended.
#
# Colour policy (see pub-figures SKILL.md):
#   * Groups are categorical, so colour comes from colorspace qualitative
#     "Dark 2" whether or not a brand is set. Categorical colour is never
#     brand-seeded; scale_*_brand_qual() in theme-project.R is the same palette.
#   * If a brand is set with set_brand(), use brand_base() only for
#     single-colour or highlight geoms.


library(ggplot2)
library(ggdist)
library(colorspace)
library(here)
library(scales)


# The skill's single copy lives in .agents/skills/. If you copied the folder
# into .claude/skills/ instead of linking it, change this path to match.
source(here::here(".agents", "skills", "pub-figures", "theme-project.R"))

# data |> expects: group (factor), value (numeric)
fig1 <-
  data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = group, y = value, colour = group, shape = group)) +
  ggdist::stat_halfeye(
    aes(fill = group),
    adjust = 0.5, width = 0.6, justification = -0.2,
    .width = 0, point_colour = NA, alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_point(
