  colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 2") +
  colorspace::scale_fill_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 2") +
  scale_shape_discrete() + # redundant encoding alongside colour
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Value (unit)") +
  theme_project()

# Save as PDF and PNG with explicit dimensions ----
fig_dir <- here::here("outputs", "figures")
dir.create(fig_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

ggsave(
  file.path(fig_dir, "fig1.pdf"), fig1,
  width = 160, height = 110, units = "mm"
)
ggsave(
  file.path(fig_dir, "fig1.png"), fig1,
  width = 160, height = 110, units = "mm", dpi = 300,
  device = ragg::agg_png, bg = "white"
)

# Accessibility check; investigator to run and inspect. Wrapped in
# interactive() so a run with Rscript does not write a stray Rplots.pdf.
if (interactive()) colorBlindness::cvdPlot(fig1)










Notepub-figures/emmeans-bridge.R






# emmeans-bridge.R
# Worked emmeans-to-ggpubr annotation pattern.
# Requires a fitted model object: fitted by code in this project that you have
# run or can read, or present in the user's live R session where your tool can
# see it. Never fabricate test statistics from descriptive data.

library(emmeans)
library(ggpubr)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

# model <- lm(value ~ group, data = data)  # supplied upstream

# fig1 <- ggplot(data, aes(group, value)) + geom_boxplot()   # supplied upstream
#
# ADAPT: `fig1` is your existing ggplot. `panel_yrange()` reads layer 1 by
# default, which must be the geom whose data the brackets sit above (e.g. the
# boxplot). If layer 1 is a reference line or similar, pass the correct index,
# e.g. panel_yrange(fig1, layer = 2L).

emm <- emmeans::emmeans(model, specs = "group")

# lowest and highest y values drawn by one layer ----
panel_yrange <- function(p, layer = 1L) {
  d <- ggplot2::ggplot_build(p)$data[[layer]]
  # positional y columns ggplot may compute
  cols <- intersect(
    c("ymin_final", "ymin", "lower", "ymax_final", "ymax", "upper", "y"),
    names(d)
  )
  if (length(cols) == 0L) {
    stop("No y-position column found in layer ", layer, ".")
  }
  range(unlist(d[cols]), na.rm = TRUE)
}

y_range <- panel_yrange(fig1)
# step between brackets as a fraction of the data range, so positions work for
# negative values and for data far from zero
y_step <- 0.07 * diff(y_range)

contrasts_df <-
  pairs(emm, adjust = "tukey") |>
  as_tibble() |>
  separate_wider_delim(
    contrast, delim = " - ", names = c("group1", "group2")
  ) |>
  # emmeans wraps level names containing spaces or operators in parentheses
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(
    c(group1, group2), \(x) stringr::str_remove_all(x, "^\\(|\\)$")
  )) |>
  dplyr::filter(p.value < 0.05) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    p.label = scales::label_pvalue()(p.value),
    y.position = y_range[2] + y_step * dplyr::row_number()
  )

# headroom so the top bracket isn't clipped: highest position + one more step
y_top <- y_range[2] + y_step * (nrow(contrasts_df) + 1)

fig1 +
  stat_pvalue_manual(
    contrasts_df, label = "p.label", tip.length = 0.01
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(NA, y_top))










Notepub-figures/patchwork-template.R






# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Composite figure: panels sharing ONE collected legend.
#
# Precondition: every panel maps the SAME grouping variable to the SAME palette.
# If a panel encodes a different variable, do not use this pattern for it; give it
# its own scale and accept a separate legend (forcing one key would mislabel it).
#
# Colour policy (see pub-figures SKILL.md):
#   * The shared grouping variable is categorical, so every panel uses
#     colorspace qualitative "Dark 2", with or without a brand. Categorical
#     colour is never brand-seeded. Keep an identical `name` across panels so
#     the legend collects to one.
#
# Legend-bearer: chosen here by richness of encoding. If unclear, use the panel
# with the most aesthetics mapped to the group and record the choice.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

# Legend-bearing panel: richest encoding (colour + shape), legend retained.
# Redundant encoding (shape) is required by the skill, and conveniently makes this
# panel a complete key for the simpler ones.
p_keep <- data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x1, y = y1, colour = group_var, shape = group_var)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 2", name = "Group") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 17, 15), name = "Group") +
  labs(x = "X1", y = "Y1") 

# Other panels: identical palette and identical name, guide suppressed.
# Suppression is what collection cannot do for you. Repeat per additional panel.
p_other <- data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x2, y = y2, colour = group_var)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 2", name = "Group") +
  labs(x = "X2", y = "Y2") +
  guides(colour = "none")

# Letters refer to plots in the order added (A = p_keep, B = p_other).
layout <- "
AB
"

fig1 <- p_keep + p_other +
  patchwork::plot_layout(design = layout, guides = "collect") +
  patchwork::plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        plot.tag = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12))

fig1

text:
Glossary




term
definition



canary
A fixed line that an instruction file asks the assistant to include in its output, so that seeing the line shows the file was loaded. It does not show that the other rules were followed.


front matter
The block between two lines of three dashes at the top of a file, holding settings such as a skill's name and description, or a Quarto document's options.


instruction file
A file the assistant loads into every conversation, such as AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, stating the project's standing conventions. Its contents are requests, not guarantees.


skill
A folder containing a SKILL.md file (and optionally scripts and templates) that an assistant loads only when it is invoked by name or judged relevant from its description.


symbolic link
A file-system entry that points to another folder or file, so one copy can appear in two places. On Windows, copying the folder is usually simpler.

title: Block 6: Enforced controls: permissions and detection
text:
Layers of control
Your instruction fileA file the assistant loads into every conversation, such as AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, stating the project’s standing conventions. Its contents are requests, not guarantees. and skills are requests: the model usually follows them, but nothing guarantees it. This block shows the controls that do hold (raw data untouched, references never regenerated, checks never quietly weakened) and where each one stops. By the end you can check in seconds what your repository prevents and what it detects, which is what lets you hand an agent real work. The same controls protect Block 7 and Block 9.
⏱ ~30 minutes
Git detects changes only from your last commit, so commit before an agent starts. Your repository’s AGENTS.md asks the agent to run git status before it edits anything, and to stop if there is no repository: a request that helps, but your commit is the control.

Exercise 1: What needs protecting?


Threat-model your repository (5 minutes)


As a group, fill in the last column: if this went wrong, how would you notice?







Asset

Overwritten or “tidied” in place

title: Block 6: Enforced controls: permissions and detection
text:
Exercise 2: Deny rules
Your workshop repository ships .claude/settings.json. It starts the project in Manual mode (default: asks before every edit and command) and holds 18 deny rulesA permission rule in the deny list of .claude/settings.json that stops Claude Code’s built-in tools from editing or reading the matching files. It checks shell output redirects such as > file, but not R code or most other commands that change the same files. protecting the raw data, the data provider’s note, the codebook, the checks, the references, the lockfile and the settings themselves. You never need to edit it: /permissions shows the rules and adds new ones.






NoteThe shipped .claude/settings.json







{
  "permissions": {
    "defaultMode": "default",
    "deny": [
      "Edit(/data/raw/**)",
      "Read(/docs/data_note.md)",
      "Edit(/docs/data_note.md)",
      "Edit(/docs/codebook.csv)",
      "Edit(/scripts/02_validate.R)",
      "Edit(/scripts/03_audit_cleaning.R)",
      "Edit(/scripts/functions/validate_voles.R)",
      "Edit(/tests/fixtures/**)",
      "Edit(/tests/make_reference.R)",
      "Edit(/tests/test_cleaning.R)",
      "Edit(/tests/test_audit.R)",
      "Edit(/renv.lock)",
      "Edit(/.github/**)",
      "Edit(/.claude/**)",
      "Edit(/.posit/**)",
      "Edit(/hooks/**)",
      "Read(/.Renviron)",
      "Read(/.env)"
    ]
  }
}


A leading / anchors a pattern to the project root. Edit rules cover Claude Code’s file-editing tools and shell output redirects (> file), not R code it runs, and the documentation does not say they cover rm, mv or cp. The rules protect named files rather than whole folders, so the agent can still write its scripts and tests in Blocks 7 and 9. Edit(/renv.lock) keeps renv::status() a real check.









TipUsing Posit Assistant





Posit Assistant sets permissions per tool in .posit/assistant/settings.json (for example "bash": {"rm *": "deny"}); deny rules hold in every mode, including auto and YOLO. It has no documented path rules for file edits, so rely on the Git pane in step 4. It blocks reading .env and .Renviron by default.





Read, test and add a rule, then find the gap (15 minutes)


Start state: your workshop repository open and the Git pane clean. Work on a scratch file, never on real data.
1. Make a scratch file and read the rules. In the R console:

writeLines("a", here::here("data", "raw", "scratch.csv"))

Commit it in the Git pane. Start claude in the Terminal tab and type /permissions: the 18 deny rules are listed.
2. See a rule refuse.
Prompt (Claude Code):
Add a second line, "test", to data/raw/scratch.csv.
Notice who refuses:






You see
What held



“denied by a permission rule”
The deny rule: enforced, whatever the model intends


The model declines, citing AGENTS.md

Your instruction file: a request that happened to work



If the model declined by itself, reply “This is a scratch file; please make the edit with your edit tool” to see the rule refuse.
3. Add a rule yourself. In /permissions, add Read(/data/confidential/**), one of the confidential-data habits in Block 4. It applies at once. Then, in the R console:

testthat::test_file(here::here("tests", "test_controls.R"))

The test confirms Manual mode and every shipped rule are still in place.
4. Find the gap.
Prompt (Claude Code):
Run this R code with Rscript: writeLines(c("a", "test"), "data/raw/scratch.csv")
Deny rules do not cover R code, so only the approval prompt stands in the way. Approve it (it is a scratch file). The Git pane now shows the file as modified, and Diff shows the new line: git caught what no rule prevented.
5. Tidy up. Revert the file in the Git pane, then delete it and commit the deletion:

file.remove(here::here("data", "raw", "scratch.csv"))

You are done when you have seen a rule refuse, added one of your own, seen the Git pane catch the R write, test_controls.R passes and scratch.csv is gone.
If it goes wrong: if the model keeps declining in step 4, write the line yourself in the console and carry on: the point is seeing git catch it. If /permissions asks where to save your rule, either project file works.






NoteAt the command line





git add/git commit for step 1, git diff data/raw for step 4, and git restore then git rm data/raw/scratch.csv for step 5. See checking work.





A hookA command the assistant runs automatically at a fixed point, for example before every tool call. A hook can block the call, but it matches text, so a differently written command can get past it. is a command the assistant runs before every tool callA single action an agent takes, such as reading a file, editing a file or running a shell command. Permission rules and hooks act on tool calls.. Your instructor may show one; the demonstration is below, and the full hook is in Going further.






TipInstructor: demonstration





Your instructor registers a guard hook, written in R, that blocks any call mentioning data/raw, and repeats step 4: the hook blocks it before any approval prompt. Then the same write using here::here("data", "raw", "scratch.csv"): the text data/raw never appears, so the hook lets it through. A text-matching hook is a tripwire, not a wall; the Git pane still shows the change. The full hook is in Going further, and the GitHub review gate (CODEOWNERSA GitHub file listing who must review changes to which paths. With branch protection, a pull request that touches those paths cannot merge without their review., branch protectionGitHub repository settings that stop changes reaching a branch such as main unless conditions are met, for example a passing check and an approved review.) is shown in Block 9.



Your repository now prevents and detects. The deny rules stop the agent’s edit tools touching raw data, the codebook, the checks, the references, the lockfile and the settings. Anything that gets past them by another route is detected: the Git pane shows every changed file, Block 7’s checksumA short fingerprint computed from a file’s contents, for example with tools::md5sum(). Any change to the file changes the checksum, so it detects changes made by any route. test fails if the raw data change, and test_controls.R fails if a rule disappears or Manual mode is switched off. Protecting something new takes 30 seconds in /permissions. For confidential data, add the five habits in Block 4; and since settings and hooks are code, trust only repositories whose configuration you have read.






NoteSet up controls in your own project



Your workshop repository came with its controls. A new project of your own starts with none, so set them up before the agent’s first task:


Git first. In the R console, usethis::use_git(), and make a first commit.

Add a starter settings.json. Download the one below, save it as .claude/settings.json, and edit the paths to match your project. It starts in Manual mode and protects raw data, test references, the lockfile, credentials and itself. Add project-specific rules with /permissions.

Ask for git checks. Copy the Version control section of your workshop AGENTS.md into your project’s instruction file.

Test it. Ask the agent to edit a protected file and watch the rule refuse; copy tests/test_controls.R and change its list of rules to yours. Then commit.



 Download the starter settings.json








TipReference: the starter settings.json







{
  "permissions": {
    "defaultMode": "default",
    "deny": [
      "Edit(/data/raw/**)",
      "Edit(/tests/fixtures/**)",
      "Edit(/renv.lock)",
      "Edit(/.claude/**)",
      "Read(/.Renviron)",
      "Read(/.env)"
    ]
  }
}





Let Claude draft rules, never decide them. You can ask it to propose deny rules for a project, but read each one: a rule with a wrong path, such as a missing leading /, protects nothing and fails silently. Claude Code asks before every write to .claude/, and the starter file’s Edit(/.claude/**) refuses such writes outright, so you install the rules yourself.








NoteCheck · Reproduce · Record





You can now: let an agent work in Manual mode in a repository where raw data, references and checks are protected, trusted because you have seen a deny rule refuse, seen git catch the route it misses, and have a test that fails if the rules are weakened.

Check: watch every control refuse something, and find the route it does not cover.

Reproduce: the rules live in .claude/settings.json, committed with the project, so everyone who clones it gets the same protection.

Record: the Git pane catches a change by any route, counted from your last commit, so commit before the agent starts. Add a line to docs/ai-log.md noting which requests were refused.

title: Block 6: Enforced controls: permissions and detection
text:
Going further (not covered live)
This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you.






TipA guard hook





A PreToolUse hook receives the pending tool call as JSON on standard input (stdin). If it exits with status 2, the call is denied and its message is passed to the model. Claude Code and Posit Assistant use the same shape for this, so one script can serve both.
The guard below is written in R. It denies any edit, shell command or R code that mentions a protected path.

#!/usr/bin/env Rscript
# hooks/guard_protected_paths.R ----
# PreToolUse guard for Claude Code and Posit Assistant.
# Reads the pending tool call from stdin and exits 2 (deny) if the call
# mentions a protected path. A tripwire, not a wall: see "Break your own
# guard".

protected <- c(
  "data/raw",
  "tests/fixtures",
  "make_reference.R",
  ".github/workflows"
)

payload <- jsonlite::fromJSON(
  paste(readLines(file("stdin"), warn = FALSE), collapse = "\n"),
  simplifyVector = FALSE
)

# search the whole tool input as text, so the same rule covers file edits,
# shell commands and R code whatever the tool calls its fields
call_text <- as.character(jsonlite::toJSON(payload$tool_input, auto_unbox = TRUE))
hits <- protected[vapply(protected, \(p) grepl(p, call_text, fixed = TRUE), logical(1))]

if (length(hits) > 0) {
  message(
    "Blocked by project guard: this ", payload$tool_name,
    " call refers to a protected path (", paste(hits, collapse = ", "), "). ",
    "Do not modify protected files; ask the user to do it."
  )
  quit(save = "no", status = 2)
}

quit(save = "no", status = 0)

The script runs with Rscript --vanilla, so it does not start renv, and jsonlite must be installed in your user library.
Register it with Claude Code by adding a hooks key to .claude/settings.json, alongside the existing permissions key. The deny rules protect .claude/, so make this edit yourself, not through the agent.
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Edit|Write|Bash",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "Rscript --vanilla \"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR\"/hooks/guard_protected_paths.R"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
The matcher lists the tool names the hook runs for.
Register it with Posit Assistant in .posit/assistant/settings.json. The tool names differ: edit, bash, and executeR for R code run in your session.
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "edit|bash|executeR",
        "hooks": [
          { "type": "command", "command": "Rscript --vanilla hooks/guard_protected_paths.R" }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
Posit Assistant runs project hooks only in a workspace you have trusted.


Test the hook before you trust it


Hooks fail open. If the script crashes, for example because jsonlite is not installed, both tools continue as if the hook had allowed the call. So test the script directly, without the agent. The R below runs the hook exactly as Claude Code does, a fresh Rscript --vanilla process given the tool call on standard input, and works the same on Windows, macOS and Linux.
In the R console:

rscript <- file.path(R.home("bin"), "Rscript")
hook <- shQuote(here::here("hooks", "guard_protected_paths.R"))

run_hook <- function(json) {
  system2(rscript, c("--vanilla", hook), input = json,
          stdout = FALSE, stderr = FALSE)
}

# can the hook's own R session load jsonlite? 0 means yes
system2(rscript, c("--vanilla", "-e", shQuote("library(jsonlite)")),
        stdout = FALSE, stderr = FALSE)

# a call naming a protected path: expect 2
run_hook('{"tool_name":"Bash","tool_input":{"command":"Rscript tests/make_reference.R"}}')

# a harmless call: expect 0
run_hook('{"tool_name":"Bash","tool_input":{"command":"Rscript scripts/05_analysis.R"}}')

Any result other than 2 for the first call and 0 for the second means the hook is broken and is silently allowing everything.
Now repeat the request from step 4 of Exercise 2. The R code mentions data/raw, so the guard should deny it before you see an approval prompt.
To see exactly what each tool sends to hooks, temporarily add a PostToolUse hook with no matcher that appends its input to a log file (Posit Assistant’s hooks documentation gives an example), and read the log.











TipBreak your own guard







Red-team the tripwire


The live block removed the scratch file at the end. Recreate it first, in the R console, and commit it from the Git pane:

writeLines("a", here::here("data", "raw", "scratch.csv"))

Prompt (Claude Code):
Run this R code:
writeLines(c("a", "test"), here::here("data", "raw", "scratch.csv"))
The guard searches for the text data/raw. This call never contains it, because here::here() assembles the path from separate pieces, so the guard allows the call. A Windows path written with backslashes would also slip past.
This is the general limit of hooks that match text: they catch the obvious form of a dangerous action, not every way of expressing it. Claude Code’s documentation makes the same point about command patterns. A guard hook is a tripwire that stops accidents and makes intent visible; it is not a wall. The Git pane still shows the change. Revert the file there before moving on.


Your guard hook depends on jsonlite, which is not installed. What happens when the agent tries to edit a protected file?

The edit is blocked, because the hook could not approve itThe edit goes ahead: hooks fail open, so a crashing hook is treated as allowing the callThe agent stops and waits until jsonlite is installedThe edit is blocked only in plan mode










TipThe review gate on GitHub





Local controls do not exist for an agent that works remotely, such as the Copilot cloud agent. There, the controls are on the repository itself. Neither file below is in the workshop template; you create them.
1. CODEOWNERS. Create .github/CODEOWNERS on your default branch:
/data/raw/            @your-github-username
/tests/               @your-github-username
/.github/             @your-github-username
/hooks/               @your-github-username
/.claude/             @your-github-username
/.posit/              @your-github-username
Code owners are requested for review automatically when a pull request changes the files they own. CODEOWNERS works in public repositories on free plans; for private repositories it requires a paid plan.
2. Branch protection. In the repository settings, add a rule for main that requires a pull request before merging, requires review from code owners, and requires the r-checks status check to pass. The r-checks workflow is set up in the Going further section of Block 9.
3. Test it. Open a pull request that changes a file under tests/, for example by asking the Copilot cloud agent to “update the test to use a tolerance of 1e-6”. Confirm that the pull request cannot merge until you have reviewed it.
GitHub does not let you approve your own pull request. In a repository where you are the only person, a pull request you open yourself may need an administrator override, which is a reason to test this gate with an agent’s pull request.









TipFeedback hooks: useful, with a warning





Hooks can do more than block. A PostToolUse hook can run lintr on each R file the agent edits and pass the result back to it. A Stop hook can run the test suite and refuse to let the agent finish while tests fail. The second is powerful and dangerous: an agent told it cannot stop until tests pass may try to change the tests. Use it only when the deny rules and guard hook protect tests/.

title: Block 6: Enforced controls: permissions and detection
text:
Glossary




term
definition



branch protection
GitHub repository settings that stop changes reaching a branch such as main unless conditions are met, for example a passing check and an approved review.


checksum
A short fingerprint computed from a file's contents, for example with tools::md5sum(). Any change to the file changes the checksum, so it detects changes made by any route.


CODEOWNERS
A GitHub file listing who must review changes to which paths. With branch protection, a pull request that touches those paths cannot merge without their review.


deny rule
A permission rule in the deny list of .claude/settings.json that stops Claude Code's built-in tools from editing or reading the matching files. It checks shell output redirects such as > file, but not R code or most other commands that change the same files.


hook
A command the assistant runs automatically at a fixed point, for example before every tool call. A hook can block the call, but it matches text, so a differently written command can get past it.


instruction file
A file the assistant loads into every conversation, such as AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, stating the project's standing conventions. Its contents are requests, not guarantees.


tool call
A single action an agent takes, such as reading a file, editing a file or running a shell command. Permission rules and hooks act on tool calls.

title: Block 6: Enforced controls: permissions and detection

title: Block 7: Data cleaning and validation with AI
text:
Step 0: Check the safeguards are in place
Cleaning mistakes are silent: a missing-value code treated as a measurement, the same animal kept twice, a row quietly dropped. In this block an agent writes and runs the whole cleaning script from one command, and one test run tells you whether to trust it. You own the facts (the codebookA table describing each variable: its type, valid range, missing-value codes, unit and label mappings. It is the data dictionary from Day 2 with machine-readable rules, and you own it, not the AI.); everything else ships with the template:
⏱ ~50 minutes
The cleaning and the checks both read the codebook but never each other, so a misunderstanding in one is caught by the other:
The ranges in validate_voles.R are the agreed codebook’s (shown in Step 2), while the audit test reads your own docs/codebook.csv, so if your ranges differ the validation and the audit can disagree.
The voles data have errors planted in them; your instructor holds the answer key, so at the end you measure what your pipeline caught. The steps follow the safe vibe-coding recipe from Block 4.

title: Block 7: Data cleaning and validation with AI
text:
Recipe check (3 minutes)


Start state: your workshop repository on main, Git pane clean (behind on Block 5? switch to block5-done in the Git pane’s branch menu; Block 6 adds no files, so block5-done is the right checkpoint).
1. The protections. Start claude and type /permissions. Look for these deny rulesA permission rule in the deny list of .claude/settings.json that stops Claude Code’s built-in tools from editing or reading the matching files. It checks shell output redirects such as > file, but not R code or most other commands that change the same files.: Edit(/data/raw/**), Read(/docs/data_note.md), Edit(/docs/codebook.csv), Edit(/tests/test_cleaning.R) and Edit(/tests/test_audit.R).
2. The checks. In the Files pane, tests/ holds test_cleaning.R, test_audit.R and fixtures/raw_checksum.txt (a checksumA short fingerprint computed from a file’s contents, for example with tools::md5sum(). Any change to the file changes the checksum, so it detects changes made by any route. of the raw file). The tests skip until clean data exist.
You are done when you have seen the five rules and the three files.
If it goes wrong: if /permissions lists no rules, check you started claude from the workshop repository’s Terminal tab; if the files are missing, switch to block5-done.

Step 1: Profile the raw data
Profiling is counting, so R does it, not the model.


Profile (5 minutes)


In the R console:

source(here::here("scripts", "00_profile.R"))
View(readr::read_csv(here::here("docs", "profile.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE))

Every column is read as text, so 9999 and -1 appear exactly as entered. Look for numbers far outside the rest and labels that differ only in spelling or case.
You are done when docs/profile.csv exists and you have noted anything that looks odd.
If it goes wrong: restart R (Session → Restart R) and run the line again.

section: Step 2: Draft the codebook with the agent, then audit it
text:
Step 2: Draft the codebook with the agent, then audit it
The codebook is Day 2’s data dictionary (README chapter) with machine-readable rules. The agent drafts it from the data alone, because it cannot read the data provider’s note: just like an analyst who never asked for the note.


Draft and audit the codebook (12 minutes)


1. Ask for a draft.
Prompt (Claude Code):
/plan Draft docs/codebook.csv with the columns column, type, rule, min, max,
missing_codes, unit, source, from docs/profile.csv only. In the source
column, say for every entry whether it comes from the profile or is your
assumption. Show the CSV in your reply; do not write any file.
Read rules are best effort: if it proposes a command that would open the note, refuse it.
2. Save it yourself. usethis::edit_file("docs/codebook.csv") in the R console, paste, save. The agent is denied this file: the codebook is yours. (Avoid Excel, which can silently change quoted fields.)
3. Audit the draft. Before you open docs/data_note.md, answer:

Did the draft list 9999 as a missing-value code, or treat it as a large measurement?
Did it notice that -1 is a code?
Where did its min and max come from? A range read off the data includes its errors, so valid ranges must come from the biology or the protocol.

4. Correct it against the note. Open docs/data_note.md and make every line trace to the note or to a decision you can defend. Where the note gives no unit (metabolic rate), write <unit>, not a guess: Block 10 relies on it. Commit in the Git pane.
You are done when docs/codebook.csv is committed, with every rule traceable to the note or to your own decision.
If it goes wrong: if you are short of time, copy the codebook below into docs/codebook.csv and commit it; it is what most groups converge on.




A codebook you could converge on

column,type,rule,min,max,missing_codes,unit,source
subject_id,character,"pattern ^V[0-9]{3}$; unique; pad digits to three",,,,,data note
sex,character,"allowed M, F; recode male to M, female to F",,,,,data note
treatment_arm,character,"allowed Control, Low_dose, High_dose; match case-insensitively",,,,,data note
mass_pre_g,double,,15,60,9999,g,data note (range from colony records)
mass_post_g,double,,15,60,9999,g,data note (range from colony records)
metabolic_rate_post,double,,5,30,-1,<unit>,data note (range from equipment)

title: Block 7: Data cleaning and validation with AI
text:
Step 3: Clean with one command
The skill holds the procedure; your codebook holds the facts. It ships with the template and runs only when you invoke it by name.






NoteWhat the skill tells the agent (clean-with-codebook/SKILL.md)







---
name: clean-with-codebook
description: >-
  Writes or revises a reproducible R cleaning script that applies a
  human-authored codebook (docs/codebook.csv) to raw tabular data. Use when
  asked to clean, recode or prepare raw data in a project that has a codebook.
  Not for exploratory analysis or modelling.
disable-model-invocation: true
---

# Clean data against a codebook

## Hard constraints
1. Never modify anything under data/raw/. Read raw files with explicit
   column types.
2. The codebook is the only source of rules. Do not infer units, ranges,
   missing-value codes or label mappings that the codebook does not state.
3. Do not edit docs/, scripts/functions/, scripts/02_validate.R,
   scripts/03_audit_cleaning.R or anything under tests/. If a check fails,
   report it; never change a check to make it pass.
4. Never drop a row silently. Every excluded row goes in the exclusion log
   with a reason.
5. Every changed cell goes in the cleaning log.
6. A value outside a codebook range that no codebook rule explains is set to
   NA, logged with rule "out_of_range_query", and listed in the final report.
   Never correct it by guessing a unit or decimal error.
7. No imputation.
8. Tidyverse style, native pipe, here::here() for all paths.

## Procedure
1. Present a plan before writing anything: every rule you will apply, the
   codebook row it comes from, and the order. Wait for the user to confirm.
2. If the data contain a value the codebook does not cover, stop and ask.
3. Write scripts/01_clean.R. It reads docs/codebook.csv when it runs; do not
   copy rules into the script by hand. Run it in a fresh R session
   (Rscript scripts/01_clean.R), then run it a second time and confirm the
   outputs are identical.
4. Run scripts/02_validate.R (raw data should fail, clean data should pass)
   and every test: Rscript -e "testthat::test_dir('tests')". Report both
   outputs verbatim, including skips.

## Outputs (exact columns)
- data/derived/voles_clean.csv: raw_row, then the codebook columns. raw_row
  is the 1-based row number in the raw file, not counting the header.
- data/derived/exclusion_log.csv: raw_row, subject_id (as it appears in the
  raw file), reason.
- data/derived/cleaning_log.csv: raw_row, subject_id, column, old_value,
  new_value, rule.
- rule is one of: missing_code, label_recode, id_format, out_of_range_query.

## Final report
Row counts in, out and excluded; every value set to NA for query; any gaps
in the codebook you found.







Plan, review, then execute (15 minutes)


Start state: the codebook committed and the Git pane showing no changed files.
1. Invoke the skill.
Prompt (Claude Code):
/clean-with-codebook Clean data/raw/voles_raw.csv using docs/codebook.csv.
2. Review its plan before approving. Check that:

every rule cites a codebook row;
out-of-range values are set to NA and queried, not “corrected”;
no file outside scripts/01_clean.R and data/derived/ will be written;
duplicates are handled by a stated rule, with each exclusion logged.

3. Approve, then read each request. Choose Yes, manually approve edits, an option that appears once the plan is shown. Watch the Git pane: new files should appear only in scripts/ and data/derived/. The skill runs the script twice, then the validation and the tests, and reports the output.






TipUsing Posit Assistant





Invoke the skill with the same prompt in Normal mode, so it asks before each change; use /plan first if you want the plan without any edits.



You are done when data/derived/ contains voles_clean.csv, cleaning_log.csv and exclusion_log.csv, and the agent has reported the validation and test output.
If it goes wrong: if it stalls, loops or writes elsewhere, press Ctrl+C, Revert in the Git pane, and switch to block7-done (a working 01_clean.R and its outputs).

section: Step 4: One check, in a fresh R session
text:
Step 4: One check, in a fresh R session
The agent says its tests pass: that is a claim. One command, in a fresh R sessionAn R session with nothing loaded from earlier work: Session > Restart R in RStudio or Positron (with “never save .RData” set, as on Day 1), callr::rscript() from the console, or Rscript in the terminal. Code that only works in your current session depends on something you did not record., turns it into evidence.


Run the checks (6 minutes)


1. Run every test. Restart R (Session → Restart R), then:
In the R console:

callr::r(\(d) testthat::test_dir(d), list(here::here("tests")))

What a pass proves:






Tests
A pass proves



raw data are unchanged
The raw file still matches its checksum: nothing changed it, by any route


every raw row is in the clean data or the exclusion log
No row was dropped silently


the four log tests (old values, new values, every changed cell, agreed rule names)
Every change is recorded, truthfully


each excluded subject_id is the one in the raw file
Exclusions refer to real rows


no more values set to NA than the codebook explains; clean data pass every codebook rule
Nothing was over-cleaned, and the result obeys your codebook


cleaning is reproducible
A fresh run writes byte-identical files



2. Read the change. In the Git pane, Diff scripts/01_clean.R for anything the plan did not mention, then commit the script and its outputs.
You are done when every cleaning test passes (other blocks’ tests may skip) and the work is committed.
If it goes wrong: a failing test names the problem. Ask the agent to fix 01_clean.R, quoting the test; never the test itself (it is deny-protected). Short of time? Switch to block7-done.




The shipped tests/test_cleaning.R


# tests/test_cleaning.R ----
# Block 7: the raw data are untouched, every row is accounted for, and the
# clean data pass every codebook rule.
library(testthat)
testthat::local_edition(3)
source(here::here("scripts", "functions", "validate_voles.R"))

read_chr <- function(...) {
  readr::read_csv(
    here::here(...),
    col_types = readr::cols(.default = readr::col_character())
  )
}

clean_path <- here::here("data", "derived", "voles_clean.csv")

test_that("raw data are unchanged", {
  checksum_path <- here::here("tests", "fixtures", "raw_checksum.txt")
  skip_if_not(file.exists(checksum_path), "Block 7 Step 0 not done yet")
  recorded <- readLines(checksum_path)
  current <- unname(tools::md5sum(here::here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv")))
  expect_identical(current, recorded)
})

test_that("every raw row is either in the clean data or in the exclusion log", {
  skip_if_not(file.exists(clean_path), "Block 7 not done yet: no clean data")
  raw_df <- read_chr("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv")
  clean_df <- read_chr("data", "derived", "voles_clean.csv")
  excluded_df <- read_chr("data", "derived", "exclusion_log.csv")

  expect_equal(nrow(raw_df), nrow(clean_df) + nrow(excluded_df))
  expect_setequal(
    c(clean_df$raw_row, excluded_df$raw_row),
    as.character(seq_len(nrow(raw_df)))
  )
  expect_false(any(is.na(excluded_df$reason) | excluded_df$reason == ""))
})

test_that("cleaning is reproducible: a fresh run writes identical files", {
  skip_if_not(file.exists(clean_path), "Block 7 not done yet: no clean data")
  derived <- here::here("data", "derived",
                        c("voles_clean.csv", "cleaning_log.csv", "exclusion_log.csv"))
  before <- unname(tools::md5sum(derived))
  callr::rscript(here::here("scripts", "01_clean.R"), wd = here::here(),
                 show = FALSE)
  expect_identical(unname(tools::md5sum(derived)), before)
})

test_that("clean data pass every codebook rule", {
  skip_if_not(file.exists(clean_path), "Block 7 not done yet: no clean data")
  clean_df <- readr::read_csv(clean_path, col_types = voles_col_types())
  expect_equal(nrow(readr::problems(clean_df)), 0)
  validation <- validate_voles(clean_df, "Clean data")
  expect_true(pointblank::all_passed(validation))
})




The shipped tests/test_audit.R


# tests/test_audit.R ----
# Block 7: the cleaning log is truthful and complete, and the cleaning did no
# more than the codebook allows. Raw values are read as text, exactly as
# entered, so a logged old value can be compared character for character.
library(testthat)
testthat::local_edition(3)

log_path <- here::here("data", "derived", "cleaning_log.csv")

allowed_rules <- c("missing_code", "label_recode", "id_format", "out_of_range_query")

read_chr <- function(...) {
  readr::read_csv(
    here::here(...),
    col_types = readr::cols(.default = readr::col_character())
  )
}

to_long <- function(data, value_name) {
  data |>
    tidyr::pivot_longer(-raw_row, names_to = "column", values_to = value_name)
}

same <- function(x, y) (is.na(x) & is.na(y)) | (!is.na(x) & !is.na(y) & x == y)

audit_inputs <- function() {
  raw_df <- read_chr("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv") |>
    dplyr::mutate(raw_row = as.character(dplyr::row_number()))
  clean_df <- read_chr("data", "derived", "voles_clean.csv")
  log_df <- read_chr("data", "derived", "cleaning_log.csv")
  list(
    raw = raw_df,
    clean = clean_df,
    log = log_df,
    raw_long = to_long(raw_df, "raw_value"),
    clean_long = to_long(clean_df, "clean_value")
  )
}

test_that("every logged old value matches the raw file", {
  skip_if_not(file.exists(log_path), "Block 7 not done yet: no cleaning log")
  x <- audit_inputs()
  untruthful <- x$log |>
    dplyr::left_join(x$raw_long, by = c("raw_row", "column")) |>
    dplyr::filter(!same(old_value, raw_value))
  expect_equal(nrow(untruthful), 0)
})

test_that("every logged new value is the value in the clean file", {
  skip_if_not(file.exists(log_path), "Block 7 not done yet: no cleaning log")
  x <- audit_inputs()
  mismatched <- x$log |>
    dplyr::inner_join(x$clean_long, by = c("raw_row", "column")) |>
    dplyr::filter(!same(new_value, clean_value))
  expect_equal(nrow(mismatched), 0)
})

test_that("every changed cell appears in the log", {
  skip_if_not(file.exists(log_path), "Block 7 not done yet: no cleaning log")
  x <- audit_inputs()
  numeric_cols <- c("mass_pre_g", "mass_post_g", "metabolic_rate_post")
  changed <- x$clean_long |>
    dplyr::left_join(x$raw_long, by = c("raw_row", "column")) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      # numbers are compared as numbers, so 28.30 and 28.3 count as unchanged
      differs = dplyr::if_else(
        column %in% numeric_cols,
        !same(suppressWarnings(as.numeric(clean_value)),
              suppressWarnings(as.numeric(raw_value))),
        !same(clean_value, raw_value)
      )
    ) |>
    dplyr::filter(differs)
  unlogged <- dplyr::anti_join(changed, x$log, by = c("raw_row", "column"))
  expect_equal(nrow(unlogged), 0)
})

test_that("every cleaning-log rule comes from the agreed list", {
  skip_if_not(file.exists(log_path), "Block 7 not done yet: no cleaning log")
  rules <- unique(audit_inputs()$log$rule)
  expect_true(all(rules %in% allowed_rules),
              label = paste("unexpected rule(s):",
                            paste(setdiff(rules, allowed_rules), collapse = ", ")))
})

test_that("each excluded row's subject_id is the one in the raw file", {
  skip_if_not(file.exists(log_path), "Block 7 not done yet: no cleaning log")
  x <- audit_inputs()
  excluded <- read_chr("data", "derived", "exclusion_log.csv") |>
    dplyr::left_join(dplyr::select(x$raw, raw_row, raw_id = subject_id),
                     by = "raw_row")
  expect_true(all(same(excluded$subject_id, excluded$raw_id)))
})

test_that("no more values were set to NA than the codebook explains", {
  skip_if_not(file.exists(log_path), "Block 7 not done yet: no cleaning log")
  x <- audit_inputs()
  codebook <- read_chr("docs", "codebook.csv")
  numeric_rules <- dplyr::filter(codebook, !is.na(min) | !is.na(max) | !is.na(missing_codes))

  for (i in seq_len(nrow(numeric_rules))) {
    col <- numeric_rules$column[[i]]
    codes <- trimws(strsplit(dplyr::coalesce(numeric_rules$missing_codes[[i]], ""), ";")[[1]])
    lo <- as.numeric(numeric_rules$min[[i]])
    hi <- as.numeric(numeric_rules$max[[i]])

    kept_raw <- x$raw[[col]][match(x$clean$raw_row, x$raw$raw_row)]
    value <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(kept_raw))
    explained <- !is.na(kept_raw) & (
      kept_raw %in% codes |
        (!is.na(lo) & !is.na(value) & value < lo) |
        (!is.na(hi) & !is.na(value) & value > hi)
    )
    newly_na <- !is.na(kept_raw) & is.na(x$clean[[col]])

    expect_equal(sum(newly_na), sum(explained),
                 label = paste("values newly set to NA in", col))
  }
})

text:
Step 5: Grade against the answer key
Instructor-led, about 6 minutes. Your instructor releases the answer key. For each planted error, record:








Planted error
Failed validation on raw?
Handled as intended?
In the log?



9999 in mass_post_g (two animals)






-1 in metabolic_rate_post







treatment_arm label in lower case






treatment_arm label in upper case






sex spelled out






mass_pre_g recorded in kilograms






mass_pre_g ten times too large





Exact duplicate row





Near duplicate with a malformed ID






The columns measure your rules, the cleaning and the record. A planted error that passed validation on raw data is a hole in your codebook.






TipInstructor: debrief (3 minutes)






Which planted errors did the agent’s first draft of the codebook miss before you corrected it against the note? What does that say about who should own the codebook?
What did the agent do with the mass recorded in kilograms and the value ten times too large? If it “corrected” them, on whose authority?

Payoff. What did the agent do, how long did checking it take, and would you automate this again?









NoteCheck · Reproduce · Record





You can now: hand an agent the cleaning of a raw file against a codebook you own, with one command, trusted because one test run proves the raw data are untouched, every row is accounted for, every change is logged truthfully, and a second run gives the same files.

Check: tests written from the codebook, not the cleaning code; the Git pane diff; the answer key.

Reproduce: the reproducibility test reruns the cleaning in a fresh R session; Block 9 shows how to freeze a result as a reference.

Record: the codebook, both logs, and a line in docs/ai-log.md.

title: Block 7: Data cleaning and validation with AI
text:
Check your understanding
Why must the codebook be written or confirmed by the analyst rather than inferred by the AI from the data?

Because AI tools cannot read CSV filesBecause missing-value codes, units and valid ranges are facts about how the data were collected; ranges read off the data include the very errors they are meant to detectBecause codebooks must be written in a specific file formatBecause the AI would take too long to profile the data

The agent reports “all tests pass”. What should you do next?

Nothing; the agent ran the testsRun the tests yourself in a fresh R session and read the diff; the agent's report is a claimAsk the agent to run them againDelete the tests, since they have done their job

How does the checksum test differ from the deny rule?

They are equivalent; one is redundantThe deny rule blocks one route (the agent's editing tools) before a change happens; the checksum detects a change by any route, after it happensThe checksum prevents edits; the deny rule only reports themThe deny rule works on GitHub; the checksum works only locally

title: Block 7: Data cleaning and validation with AI
text:
Going further (not covered live)
This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you.






TipThe validation rules





scripts/functions/validate_voles.R was transcribed from the codebook by a person, not by the agent that writes the cleaning script. It uses the pointblank package: each line is one rule, and interrogate() reports how many rows break it. (pointblank calls the object that holds the rules an “agent”; it has nothing to do with AI agents.)

# scripts/functions/validate_voles.R ----
# Rules transcribed from docs/codebook.csv by a human, not by the agent
# that writes the cleaning script.

voles_col_types <- function() {
  readr::cols(
    subject_id = readr::col_character(),
    sex = readr::col_character(),
    treatment_arm = readr::col_character(),
    mass_pre_g = readr::col_double(),
    mass_post_g = readr::col_double(),
    metabolic_rate_post = readr::col_double(),
    .default = readr::col_character()
  )
}

validate_voles <- function(data, label) {
  data |>
    pointblank::create_agent(label = label) |>
    pointblank::col_vals_not_null(columns = c(subject_id, sex, treatment_arm)) |>
    pointblank::col_vals_regex(columns = subject_id, regex = "^V[0-9]{3}$") |>
    pointblank::rows_distinct(columns = subject_id) |>
    pointblank::col_vals_in_set(columns = sex, set = c("M", "F")) |>
    pointblank::col_vals_in_set(
      columns = treatment_arm,
      set = c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose")
    ) |>
    pointblank::col_vals_between(
      columns = c(mass_pre_g, mass_post_g),
      left = 15, right = 60, na_pass = TRUE
    ) |>
    pointblank::col_vals_between(
      columns = metabolic_rate_post,
      left = 5, right = 30, na_pass = TRUE
    ) |>
    pointblank::interrogate()
}

scripts/02_validate.R runs the rules on the raw data, which should fail (for example Raw data (expected to FAIL): 7 of 10 rules fail), and, once the cleaning has run, on the clean data, which should pass. It also lists any value that could not be read as a number: such a value would become NA and slip past the range rules. In an interactive session it opens the full report in the Viewer.
In the R console:

source(here::here("scripts", "02_validate.R"))


# scripts/02_validate.R ----
# Runs the codebook rules on the raw data (expected to FAIL) and, once
# 01_clean.R has run, on the clean data (expected to PASS). In an interactive
# session the full pointblank report also opens in the Viewer.
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
source(here("scripts", "functions", "validate_voles.R"))

report_validation <- function(validation) {
  steps <- validation$validation_set
  n_failed <- sum(!steps$all_passed)
  cat(
    validation$label, ": ",
    if (n_failed == 0) "all rules pass" else paste(n_failed, "of", nrow(steps), "rules fail"),
    "\n",
    sep = ""
  )
  if (interactive()) print(validation)
  invisible(validation)
}

raw_df <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv"), col_types = voles_col_types())
# values that could not be read as numbers become NA and would pass the
# range rules, so list them
print(problems(raw_df), width = Inf)
report_validation(validate_voles(raw_df, "Raw data (expected to FAIL)"))

clean_path <- here("data", "derived", "voles_clean.csv")
if (file.exists(clean_path)) {
  clean_df <- read_csv(clean_path, col_types = voles_col_types())
  report_validation(validate_voles(clean_df, "Clean data (expected to PASS)"))
}







Warning



na_pass = TRUE lets genuine missing values through. It would also let through a cleaning script that replaced every mass with NA. Validation alone cannot catch over-cleaning; tests/test_audit.R can.











TipWrite the validation rules independently





Instead of using the shipped validate_voles.R, you can have the rules written by an AI that has never seen the cleaning code, for example a browser chat window given only the codebook:
Prompt (browser chat):
Using only the codebook below, write an R file containing a function
validate_voles(data, label) that builds a pointblank agent with one
validation step per codebook rule, and interrogates it. Also write
voles_col_types(), returning readr column types for the codebook columns,
with character as the default for anything else.

[paste docs/codebook.csv]
Compare what it writes with the shipped version. A rule it missed, or a range it took from the data rather than the codebook, is the kind of error the separate conversation is meant to expose.









TipRead the log yourself





Tests check consistency; they cannot tell you whether a change was the right decision. The shipped audit script shows what kinds of change were made and samples ten logged changes for you to check by eye against the raw file (View(), or Positron’s Data Explorer).

source(here::here("scripts", "03_audit_cleaning.R"))


# scripts/03_audit_cleaning.R ----
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
source(here("scripts", "functions", "validate_voles.R"))

to_long <- function(data, value_name) {
  data |>
    pivot_longer(
      -raw_row,
      names_to = "column",
      values_to = value_name,
      values_transform = as.character
    )
}

# raw values are read as text, exactly as entered, so a logged old value can be
# compared character for character
raw_long_df <- read_csv(
  here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv"),
  col_types = cols(.default = col_character())
) |>
  mutate(raw_row = as.character(row_number())) |>
  to_long("raw_value")

clean_long_df <- read_csv(here("data", "derived", "voles_clean.csv"), col_types = voles_col_types()) |>
  to_long("clean_value")

cleaning_log_df <- read_csv(
  here("data", "derived", "cleaning_log.csv"),
  col_types = cols(.default = col_character())
)

# 1. Truthful: every logged old value matches the raw file ----
untruthful_df <- cleaning_log_df |>
  left_join(raw_long_df, by = c("raw_row", "column")) |>
  filter(!map2_lgl(old_value, raw_value, identical))

# 2. Complete: every changed cell appears in the log ----
unlogged_df <- clean_long_df |>
  left_join(raw_long_df, by = c("raw_row", "column")) |>
  filter(!map2_lgl(clean_value, raw_value, identical)) |>
  anti_join(cleaning_log_df, by = c("raw_row", "column"))

# both tables should have no rows; tests/test_audit.R checks the same things
# and fails if they do not
print(untruthful_df, width = Inf)
print(unlogged_df, width = Inf)

# 3. What kinds of change were made ----
cleaning_log_df |> count(column, rule, sort = TRUE)

# 4. Ten logged changes to check by hand against the raw file ----
set.seed(2026)
cleaning_log_df |> slice_sample(n = 10) |> print(width = Inf)










TipThe fresh-run checks, one by one





The test suite already reruns the cleaning in a fresh R session. To do the same checks by hand, commit the outputs, then in the R console:

renv::status()
callr::rscript(here::here("scripts", "01_clean.R"))

renv::status() should report a consistent state; if the agent used a package that is not in the lockfileThe renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment., decide whether you want it and record it yourself with renv::snapshot(), as on Day 1 (the agent is denied renv.lock). After the callr::rscript() run the Git pane should show no changes.






NoteAt the command line





Rscript -e "testthat::test_dir('tests')", Rscript -e "renv::status()", Rscript scripts/01_clean.R and git status --short data/derived, run after /exit or in a second Terminal tab. See checking work.












TipHow the template’s safeguards were made





The checksum. The template’s tests/fixtures/raw_checksum.txt was written once, from the shipped raw file, like this:

fs::dir_create(here::here("tests", "fixtures"))
writeLines(
  unname(tools::md5sum(here::here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv"))),
  here::here("tests", "fixtures", "raw_checksum.txt")
)

Do the same for your own raw data, then commit it. The template’s .gitattributes contains data/raw/** -text, so git does not convert line endings, which would change the checksum on Windows.
The deny rules. This is the .claude/settings.json in your workshop repository, the same file you read in Block 6:


{
  "permissions": {
    "defaultMode": "default",
    "deny": [
      "Edit(/data/raw/**)",
      "Read(/docs/data_note.md)",
      "Edit(/docs/data_note.md)",
      "Edit(/docs/codebook.csv)",
      "Edit(/scripts/02_validate.R)",
      "Edit(/scripts/03_audit_cleaning.R)",
      "Edit(/scripts/functions/validate_voles.R)",
      "Edit(/tests/fixtures/**)",
      "Edit(/tests/make_reference.R)",
      "Edit(/tests/test_cleaning.R)",
      "Edit(/tests/test_audit.R)",
      "Edit(/renv.lock)",
      "Edit(/.github/**)",
      "Edit(/.claude/**)",
      "Edit(/.posit/**)",
      "Edit(/hooks/**)",
      "Read(/.Renviron)",
      "Read(/.env)"
    ]
  }
}


A leading / anchors each pattern to the project root. The rules protect specific files rather than whole folders, so the agent can still write scripts/01_clean.R and data/derived/. To protect files of your own, add rules with /permissions. Posit Assistant has no documented path rules for file edits; use the guard hook from the Going further section of Block 6 instead.






Warning



What each control covers. The deny rule blocks the agent’s file-editing tools, and shell output redirects such as > file. It does not cover R code the agent runs: an R script that writes to data/raw/ is a different route. The checksum test catches a change made by any route, but only after the fact. Use both: one prevents, the other detects. A deny rule on reading does not stop data reaching the model provider by other routes; see Block 4.


The skill. The skill ships in .agents/skills/ and .claude/skills/. To use it in another project, download it and unzip it into that project’s .agents/skills/ (unzip(file.choose(), exdir = here::here(".agents", "skills"))), then copy the folder into .claude/skills/ with fs::dir_copy().


 Download clean-with-codebook.zip

title: Block 7: Data cleaning and validation with AI
text:
Glossary




term
definition



checksum
A short fingerprint computed from a file's contents, for example with tools::md5sum(). Any change to the file changes the checksum, so it detects changes made by any route.


codebook
A table describing each variable: its type, valid range, missing-value codes, unit and label mappings. It is the data dictionary from Day 2 with machine-readable rules, and you own it, not the AI.


deny rule
A permission rule in the deny list of .claude/settings.json that stops Claude Code's built-in tools from editing or reading the matching files. It checks shell output redirects such as > file, but not R code or most other commands that change the same files.


fresh R session
An R session with nothing loaded from earlier work: Session > Restart R in RStudio or Positron (with "never save .RData" set, as on Day 1), callr::rscript() from the console, or Rscript in the terminal. Code that only works in your current session depends on something you did not record.


lockfile
The renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment.


sentinel value
A number with a special meaning, such as 9999 for "not recorded" or -1 for "run failed". It must be documented in a codebook and recoded before analysis.

title: Block 8: AI-assisted code review
text:
Part 1: What AI is, and is not, good for in code review
You will hand a script to an AI reviewer and grade what it finds. Because you already know this script’s twelve problems, you can measure the machine rather than trust it.
⏱ ~40 minutes
⏱ ~5 minutes
An AI reviewer reads every line and never tires, but it sounds equally sure whether it is right or wrong. Here is where to expect help, on the four Rs of code review (Ivimey-Cook et al., 2023):
AI capability mapped onto the four Rs

R
AI is likely to be...
Why



Reported
Useful for drafting
It can summarise what the script appears to do and flag missing documentation or undocumented exclusions. It cannot know the intended analysis unless you state it.


Run
Strong, if it can execute
An agent that runs the script in a fresh R session can show whether it runs. A chat window can only predict, and its prediction can read as though it ran the code.


Reliable
Weak
Silent semantic errors (P4 precedence, P8 sentinel, P9 incomparable models, P10 wrong family) depend on context. Expect some caught, some missed and some invented, all in the same confident tone.


Reproducible
Mixed
It can flag a missing lockfile or session record. It can confirm that results reproduce only by running the code and comparing outputs.
The rule: treat every AI finding as a claim to check, and the absence of a finding as no evidence that the problem is absent.
Run your saved review prompt on a script before you share it, and spend your own attention on the Reliable questions.

title: Block 8: AI-assisted code review
text:
TipBackground: what the evidence says





Used that way, AI review is reliably good for:

summarising what an unfamiliar script does;
flagging missing documentation, unexplained filters and hard-coded paths;
finding run errors, when it can actually execute the code;
a second pair of eyes that never tires on line 300.

In software engineering, developers acted on about three-quarters of an AI reviewer’s comments but saw only minor gains in quality, and the reviewer did worse when it was not told what the code was meant to do (Cihan et al., 2025; Cihan, 2025). Nobody has measured it on analysis scripts like this one, which is what you will do.









Note



Opening poll (type in chat)
“If an AI code reviewer told you your analysis was clean, would you trust it enough to submit?”
A: Yes, it read every line B: Only if I had also read it myself C: No, I would trust my own review over the AI’s D: I would trust it for Run, not for Reliable
Keep the result visible; we return to it at the end.

title: Block 8: AI-assisted code review
section: Part 2: Telling the AI how to behave
text:
Part 2: Telling the AI how to behave
⏱ ~10 minutes
“Review my code” gets a vague, generous review. A good review prompt has four parts:






Part
Why




A role and a standard: “a critical reviewer applying the four Rs”
Gives the output a structure you can check



The intended analysis: the model from the OSF page, with TO a count and block B a random effect
Without it, the AI cannot see that a Gaussian lmer() is the wrong family (P10)



No flattery: line number, which R, severity, a fix
Keeps it to findings you can act on



Honest uncertainty: “NEEDS HUMAN CHECK” instead of guessing
Shows you where to look yourself





Write the review prompt (7 minutes)


1. Start from the draft below and check it has all four parts.
2. Split the room. Surnames A–M are Group A and keep the line about the 9999 sentinel valueA number with a special meaning, such as 9999 for “not recorded” or -1 for “run failed”. It must be documented in a codebook and recoded before analysis.; N–Z are Group B and delete it. Everything else stays the same.
3. Keep it. In your workshop project, run usethis::edit_file("docs/review-prompt.md") in the R console, paste your prompt and save. You will reuse it after the course.
You are done when your prompt has all four elements and is saved in docs/review-prompt.md.


Working draft

Prompt (Claude Code, or a chat window):
You are a critical code reviewer for an evolutionary-biology journal.
Review ANALYSIS.R using the four Rs: Reported, Run, Reliable, Reproducible.

The intended analysis (from the pre-registration) is:
  total offspring (TO, a count: non-negative integer, often overdispersed)
  modelled as TO ~ strain * diet + (1 | B), with block B as a random effect.

Rules:
- Do NOT praise the code. Report only problems.
- For each issue: line number(s), which R it violates, severity
  (critical / high / medium), and a concrete one-line fix.
- The raw data use 9999 as a "not recorded" code. Check whether this is
  handled.                                      <- Group B: delete this line
- Flag anything you CANNOT determine by reading alone as "NEEDS HUMAN
  CHECK" rather than guessing.
- If you are uncertain about a finding, say so explicitly.
Organise your output by the four Rs.

title: Block 8: AI-assisted code review
text:
Part 3: Running the review
⏱ ~25 minutes
Path A: Claude Code, read-only
For the A/B comparison to work, the agentAn assistant that can read across a project’s files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises. must see the script and nothing else; with the data it would find the 9999 code by itself.


Run the review (10 minutes)


Start state: the OSF project open in RStudio or Positron, and your Part 2 prompt saved in docs/review-prompt.md in your workshop repository.
1. Copy the script into an empty project. With the OSF project open, in the R console:

usethis::create_project("~/ai-review", open = FALSE)
fs::file_copy(here::here("ANALYSIS.R"), "~/ai-review/ANALYSIS.R")

Then open ~/ai-review in a new window: in RStudio, File → Open Project in New Session; in Positron, File → New Window and open the folder there.
2. Start Claude Code there. In the new window’s Terminal tab:
claude
This folder has none of your workshop settings, so Claude Code starts in its own default, auto. Starting your request with /plan keeps it to reading (rungOne level of the autonomy ladder in Block 4, from suggesting a line (rung 0) to acting with no prompts (rung 5). Each step up removes a moment when you would have seen an action before it happened. 2 in Block 4).
3. Ask for the review. Type /plan, a space, then paste your prompt.
4. Save the review. plan mode writes no files, so copy the review into a text file yourself.
You are done when you have the review saved in a file.
If it goes wrong: if Claude Code lists data files, you started it in the OSF project window, not the ai-review one: /exit, switch windows and start again. If you have no agent, use Path B.








TipUsing Posit Assistant





Open the folder holding only ANALYSIS.R in RStudio or Positron, and switch Posit Assistant to Ask mode, so it can read but not change anything. Give it your Part 2 prompt and copy the review into a file yourself. For the stretch step below, open the full OSF project folder and use Normal mode, so it asks before running anything.









TipStretch: let it run the script





An agent that can run R turns the Run question from a prediction into evidence. The script needs its data, so /exit, switch to the OSF project’s window and start claude in its Terminal tab. This folder starts in auto too: press Shift+Tab until it shows Manual (default), so it asks before running anything.
Prompt (Claude Code):
Run ANALYSIS.R from a fresh R session with Rscript and report the exact
output and any errors. Do not install packages; if a package is missing,
report which one. Do not edit any file.
Read the approval prompt, then the output. “The script runs” counts only if you can see the command and its output in the conversation; without them it is a claimed executionA statement that code runs or reproduces, made without the command that was run and the output it produced. Treat it as a prediction, not evidence.. A missing package is a finding about your machine, not about the code.



Path B: chat window
If you have no agent, paste the whole of ANALYSIS.R into any chat window, followed by your Part 2 prompt. Paste the script only, not the data.






Warning



A chat window cannot run anything, but its answer to “does this run?” can read as though it did. Ask “what would prevent this running?” instead.




Grade the machine (10 minutes)


1. Score the review. Open your P1–P12 catalogue beside the AI’s review:


Hits: which of P1–P12 did it identify correctly?

Misses: which did it miss? Look especially at P4 (precedence) and P8 (sentinel), the silent, consequential ones.

False positives: what did it flag that is not a real problem, or describe wrongly? Each one is a false positiveIn a code review, a problem the AI reports confidently that is not real, or describes wrongly..

Execution claims: did it claim the script runs or reproduces? On what evidence?

2. Post your result. In the chat, post your group (A or B), your hit count, your most consequential miss and your most confident false positive, with line numbers.
3. Decide. Which one finding would you act on first, and what would you check before acting on it?
You are done when every P1–P12 problem is marked hit or miss, and you have listed the false positives.
If it goes wrong: if your review never arrived, grade a neighbour’s review posted in the chat; the comparison works the same way.








NoteDebrief (5 minutes)




Compare P8 hit rates between Groups A and B. Only the data and your knowledge reveal that 9999 is a code: what does that say about reviewing code without the data?
Whose AI produced the most confident false positive?
Did any agent claim the script runs without having run it?
Back to the opening poll: would you change your answer?









NoteCheck · Reproduce · Record





You can now: hand a script to an AI reviewer with a prompt that makes its output checkable, trusted because you grade it against problems you already know, and treat every finding as a claim.

Check: grade every AI finding against the P1–P12 answer key; the absence of a finding is no evidence that the problem is absent.

Reproduce: a claim that the script runs counts only with the command and the output from a fresh R session; to run one yourself, see checking work.

Record: add a line to docs/ai-log.md in your workshop repository: the tool, its hit count and its most confident false positive. An AI-assisted README for the OSF project is in Going further.

title: Block 8: AI-assisted code review
text:
Check your understanding
An AI reviewer reports that ANALYSIS.R “runs without errors”. What do you need before treating that as evidence?

Nothing; the model has read every lineA second AI reviewer's agreementThe command it ran and the output it saw, from a fresh R session; without them the statement is a predictionA statement of confidence from the model

Why did Group A catch P8 more often than Group B?

Group A used a better modelNothing in the script reveals that 9999 is a code; the AI could only check for it when the prompt said soGroup B's prompt was longerP8 is a syntax error that only some models detect

title: Block 8: AI-assisted code review
text:
Going further (not covered live)
This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you.






TipCopilot code review on a pull request





If your repository is on GitHub, open a pull request containing ANALYSIS.R and request Copilot as a reviewer. Its comments appear on the changed lines, like a colleague’s. It reads the repository’s instruction files (.github/copilot-instructions.md, or AGENTS.md as in Block 5), but none of those exist in the OSF folder yet. To have Copilot apply the standard from Part 2, add your review rules (the four Rs, the intended analysis, no praise, NEEDS HUMAN CHECK) to .github/copilot-instructions.md in that repository before you request the review.









TipGenerating the README with AI





Self-study: about 20 minutes.
The second deliverable is the documentation that makes Reported and Run answerable: a README. You are provided with the research-readme skill: a SKILL.md, two helper scripts and a template.
Install the skill before you start. Download the bundle and unzip it into the OSF project folder at .agents/skills/, so that the folder .agents/skills/research-readme/ contains SKILL.md, scripts/ and references/.


 Download research-readme.zip




Posit Assistant and GitHub Copilot read .agents/skills/ directly.

Claude Code reads .claude/skills/. Link or copy the folder there, as described in Block 5.

Chat window: you do not need to install anything. You will run the two scripts yourself and paste the template into the chat.

Check that the skill is visible before going on. In Claude Code, type / and look for research-readme. In any tool, the test is behaviour: when you invoke /research-readme in Pass 2, its first reply should be the numbered plan that the skill’s “Before executing” section requires. If it is not, the skill did not load.
Put the folder under version control first. A folder downloaded from OSF is not a git repository, so there would be nothing to compare the README against. With the OSF project open in RStudio or Positron, run usethis::use_git() in the R console and let it make the first commit.
You run this in two passes. The first shows the failure; the second shows the fix.
Pass 1: README from the AI alone (self-study: about 4 minutes)
Give the AI only ANALYSIS.R and the data, and ask for a README with no constraints. The result reads as complete. It will assign plausible units, describe variables it cannot have verified, and may state package versions it has no way to know. Note what it asserts about the variables and dependencies; Pass 2 replaces each guess with a fact you generate.
Pass 2: README from verifiable inputs
The skill’s rules are that the AI must not fabricate metadata, and that automatic summaries describe; they do not interpret. So you generate the facts mechanically, and the AI only assembles and phrases them.
Step 1: Generate the inputs yourself (R, not AI)
In the R console, with the OSF project open in RStudio or Positron (so that here::here() points at it, not at your workshop repository):

skill_dir <- here::here(".agents", "skills", "research-readme", "scripts")

source(file.path(skill_dir, "describe_csv.R"))
# type, missing count and range per column, printed in full for pasting
describe_project_csvs(here::here()) |> print(n = Inf, width = Inf)

source(file.path(skill_dir, "scan_packages.R"))
print_lockfile(here::here("renv.lock"))  # R and package versions, or a finding

This project has no renv.lock. scan_packages.R reports that as an explicit finding rather than an error, and the README must say so. You cannot pin versions you never recorded.
Look at the offspring column in the summary: its range will read something like 2 to 9999. The 9999 code (P8) is a real number in the file, and the summary reports it without judgement. Judging plausibility is your job. That honest, uninterpreted range is the visible trace of the sentinel.
Step 2: Hand the AI the specification and the inputs
Agent path: invoke /research-readme and let its five stages run. It will ask you for what it cannot find.
Chat path: paste the structure from references/readme_template.md and the output you just generated, with this prompt:
Prompt (chat window):
Draft a research README.md for this analysis repository, using exactly the
sections in the template I paste below, in order.

Use ONLY the facts I provide. Do not invent DOIs, ORCIDs, units or package
versions. Where a value is missing, insert a visible placeholder:
  **TODO: supply [field]: not provided**

Per-column summaries: [paste describe_project_csvs() output]
Dependencies: [paste print_lockfile() output]
Run order: ANALYSIS.R (the only analysis script in the folder).

Add an AI declaration stating that an AI assisted in drafting this README,
naming the model and today's date. Make no claims about AI use elsewhere.


Audit the README (10 minutes)


Audit the draft against three of the skill’s rules:


No fabrication. Pick three facts. Can you trace each to an input you gave? If not, it is invented.

Describe, do not interpret. Did the AI assign units or meanings you did not supply? Did the 2 to 9999 range survive, or was it “tidied” into something plausible and wrong?

README only. The Git pane should show that nothing except README.md changed since the commit you made before Pass 1.

Note the worst fabrication or interpretation you caught, and whether the README’s offspring range alone would have led you back to P8. The AI declarationA statement, for example in a README, recording that an AI assisted, naming the tool, model and date, and making no claim about AI use beyond what was recorded. should say no more than you told it.


The skill bundle
The bundle you downloaded above is reproduced here for reference; you do not need to edit it. Read it before you use it, as you would any skill you did not write.
research-readme/
├── SKILL.md
├── scripts/
│   ├── describe_csv.R
│   └── scan_packages.R
└── references/
    └── readme_template.md






Notescripts/describe_csv.R






# describe_csv.R ----
# Purpose: one row per column of a CSV file: name, the type readr assigns,
# missing-value count, and a brief range (numeric) or distinct-value count
# (other). Describes; does not interpret.
# Used by: research-readme skill, Stage 2.

describe_range <- function(x) {
  if (all(is.na(x))) {
    return("all values missing")
  }
  if (is.numeric(x)) {
    return(paste(min(x, na.rm = TRUE), "to", max(x, na.rm = TRUE)))
  }
  paste(dplyr::n_distinct(x, na.rm = TRUE), "distinct values")
}

# one-row-per-column summary of a single CSV ----
describe_csv <- function(path) {
  stopifnot(is.character(path), length(path) == 1L, file.exists(path))
  data_df <- readr::read_csv(path, show_col_types = FALSE)
  tibble::tibble(
    file        = basename(path),
    column      = names(data_df),
    type        = purrr::map_chr(data_df, \(x) class(x)[1]),
    n_missing   = purrr::map_int(data_df, \(x) sum(is.na(x))),
    range       = purrr::map_chr(data_df, describe_range),
    # completed by the user during Stage 2:
    description = NA_character_,
    unit        = NA_character_
  )
}

# describe every CSV in a project, skipping renv and git folders ----
describe_project_csvs <- function(project_dir) {
  stopifnot(dir.exists(project_dir))
  csv_paths <- list.files(
    project_dir,
    pattern = "\\.csv$",
    recursive = TRUE,
    full.names = TRUE,
    ignore.case = TRUE
  )
  csv_paths <- csv_paths[!grepl("(^|/)(renv|\\.git)/", csv_paths)]
  if (length(csv_paths) == 0L) {
    message("No CSV files found under ", project_dir)
    return(tibble::tibble())
  }
  csv_paths |>
    purrr::map(describe_csv) |>
    purrr::list_rbind()
}










Notescripts/scan_packages.R






# scan_packages.R ----
# Purpose: read renv.lock and report the R version and pinned package
# versions. A missing lockfile is reported as a finding, not an error.
# Used by: research-readme skill, Stage 4.

read_lockfile <- function(lock_path = "renv.lock") {
  if (!file.exists(lock_path)) {
    return(list(found = FALSE, r_version = NA_character_, packages = tibble::tibble()))
  }
  lock <- jsonlite::read_json(lock_path)
  packages <- purrr::pluck(lock, "Packages", .default = list())

  packages_df <- tibble::tibble(
    package = unname(purrr::map_chr(packages, \(p) purrr::pluck(p, "Package", .default = NA_character_))),
    version = unname(purrr::map_chr(packages, \(p) purrr::pluck(p, "Version", .default = NA_character_)))
  ) |>
    dplyr::arrange(package)

  list(
    found = TRUE,
    r_version = purrr::pluck(lock, "R", "Version", .default = NA_character_),
    packages = packages_df
  )
}

print_lockfile <- function(lock_path = "renv.lock") {
  info <- read_lockfile(lock_path)
  if (!info$found) {
    cat(
      "No lockfile found at ", lock_path, ".\n",
      "FINDING: package versions were not recorded.\n",
      "README text: **TODO: supply R version and key package versions: ",
      "not recorded; resolve before submission**\n",
      sep = ""
    )
    return(invisible(info))
  }
  cat("R version: ", info$r_version, "\n\n", sep = "")
  print(info$packages, n = Inf)
  invisible(info)
}










NoteSKILL.md
