name: research-readme
description: >-
  Writes a README.md for a research repository whose code and data accompany
  a paper. Use when asked to write a README for an analysis project, document
  a repository for a paper, or prepare code for journal submission or
  archiving (Zenodo, Figshare, OSF). Not for general software READMEs and not
  for auditing code.
disable-model-invocation: true
---

# Research README generator

Produces one README.md for a repository of R code and data that accompanies a
manuscript, including the metadata that journals and archives expect:
persistent identifiers, ORCIDs, funding, per-variable descriptions with units,
an explicit script run order, and a dependency record.

## Operating constraints
These hold for the whole conversation unless the user explicitly withdraws
them.
1. The only file you create or overwrite is README.md. Do not edit, rename or
   delete any other file. If you notice an apparent error in code or data,
   record it under "Open questions" in the README or report it in chat, and
   leave the file untouched.
2. Do not fabricate metadata. DOIs, ORCIDs, grant numbers, collection dates,
   units and affiliations come from the user or from a file the user points to.
   If a value is unknown, insert a placeholder (see Placeholders).
3. Automatic summaries describe; they do not interpret. Report column type,
   missing count and range. Do not state what a variable means, its unit, or
   whether a value is plausible.
4. Work conversationally and write the file directly; do not build an app.

## Before executing
Present a short numbered plan: the folder to be scanned, that only README.md
will be written, and the five stages below. Wait for the user to confirm.

## Stage 1: Project information
Collect title, abstract, DOIs (paper; archived code and data), licences,
authors with ORCIDs and affiliations, and funders with grant numbers. Read
these from CITATION.cff, codemeta.json or DESCRIPTION if present, and ask only
for what is missing. Pair each author with their own ORCID and affiliation. If
no code licence is supplied, flag it prominently and use a placeholder; do not
choose a licence for the user.

## Stage 2: Files and variable summaries
List the data and code files. For CSV files, run
describe_project_csvs() from scripts/describe_csv.R and use its output as a
scaffold. Ask the user for each column's description and unit, and for
collection dates and locations per data file. List other tabular formats
(.xlsx, .tsv) and ask the user to describe their columns by hand. Never infer
units from column names.

## Stage 3: Script order
List executable files (.R, .Rmd, .qmd). Propose a run order using numeric
prefixes (01_, 02_) as the first signal, and ask the user to confirm or
reorder; the user's order is authoritative. Collect a one-line description of
each script. Do not run any script to determine the order.

## Stage 4: R packages and versions
Run print_lockfile() from scripts/scan_packages.R.
- If a lockfile exists, the Dependencies section states the R version, says
  that versions are pinned in renv.lock, gives the restore command
  renv::restore(), and includes the package table.
- If no lockfile exists, the Dependencies section states that package versions
  were not recorded, and contains the placeholder from print_lockfile(). Do not
  guess versions or scan the installed library.

## Stage 5: Assemble, preview and reader-test
Fill references/readme_template.md. Show the rendered Markdown in chat. Then
read it as a newcomer who has only the repository and the paper: could they
find the data, restore the environment, run the scripts in order and
understand every variable? List any section still holding a placeholder. On
confirmation, write README.md to the project root.

## Stage 6: Check the README against its sources
If the project has tests/test_readme.R, run it in a fresh R session
(Rscript -e "testthat::test_file('tests/test_readme.R')") and report the
output verbatim. Otherwise compare the README yourself: the R and package
versions against read_lockfile(), every numbered script against the scripts
folder, and every unit against the user's answers. Report the number of
placeholders left.

## AI declaration
State that an AI assisted in generating this README, naming the model if the
user wishes, with the date. Make no claims about AI use elsewhere in the
project unless the user states them, and then record exactly what they state.

## Placeholders
Write every unknown value as a visible placeholder, in exactly this form:
**TODO: supply [field]: not provided**
Flag a missing code licence and a missing code or data DOI as blocking for
submission, but still write the file so the user has a working draft.

## Scope
This skill does not audit code quality or reproducibility, and does not
produce figures. If asked to do either mid-run, say so and stop that part of
the request.

## References
- Ivimey-Cook, E.R. et al. (2023) Implementing code review in the scientific
  workflow. Journal of Evolutionary Biology 36(10), 1347–1356.
- Ivimey-Cook, E.R. et al. (2025) TADA! Simple guidelines to improve
  analytical code sharing for transparency and reproducibility. EcoEvoRxiv.

The Dependencies section is a single token, filled with one of the two versions defined in Stage 4 of SKILL.md, so the README is accurate whether or not a lockfile exists.

title: Block 8: AI-assisted code review
text:
Glossary




term
definition



agent
An assistant that can read across a project's files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises.


AI declaration
A statement, for example in a README, recording that an AI assisted, naming the tool, model and date, and making no claim about AI use beyond what was recorded.


claimed execution
A statement that code runs or reproduces, made without the command that was run and the output it produced. Treat it as a prediction, not evidence.


false positive
In a code review, a problem the AI reports confidently that is not real, or describes wrongly.


rung
One level of the autonomy ladder in Block 4, from suggesting a line (rung 0) to acting with no prompts (rung 5). Each step up removes a moment when you would have seen an action before it happened.


sentinel value
A number with a special meaning, such as 9999 for "not recorded" or -1 for "run failed". It must be documented in a codebook and recoded before analysis.

The code you will refactor
By the end of this block you can let an agent turn working code into a function and prove that nothing changed. The proof is a characterisation testA test that checks new code reproduces the saved output of the original code exactly. It shows the output is unchanged, not that it is correct., as in the tidy-evaluation chapter: you freeze the original output, and the new code must reproduce it exactly. The agent does the work through a shipped skill, and you hold the reference.
This block follows the safe vibe-coding recipe: the protections and checks are in place, so your part is one request, one test run and one read of the diff.

text:
Step 0: check the protections and capture the reference


Recipe check and capture (5 minutes)


Start state: your workshop project open in RStudio or Positron, the Git pane showing no changes, on the main branch.
1. Check the protections. Start claude in the Terminal tab and type /permissions. The deny rulesA permission rule in the deny list of .claude/settings.json that stops Claude Code’s built-in tools from editing or reading the matching files. It checks shell output redirects such as > file, but not R code or most other commands that change the same files. Edit(/tests/fixtures/**) and Edit(/tests/make_reference.R) keep the agent’s edit tools away from the reference; the Git pane shows a change by any other route.
2. Capture the reference yourself, in a fresh R session. In the R console:

callr::rscript(here::here("tests", "make_reference.R"))



What make_reference.R does


# tests/make_reference.R ----
# Run ONCE, by you, BEFORE any refactoring.
source(here::here("scripts", "05_analysis.R"))
dir.create(here::here("tests", "fixtures"), showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
saveRDS(
  metabolic_summary,
  here::here("tests", "fixtures", "metabolic_summary.rds")
)


3. Commit it. In the Git pane (RStudio) or Source Control view (Positron), commit tests/fixtures/metabolic_summary.rds with the message “Capture reference output before refactoring”. It must come first: after the refactor, the script runs through the function under test.
You are done when the Git pane shows the reference committed and no changed files.
If it goes wrong: if the .rds changes later, select it in the Git pane and choose Revert. If you are far behind, switch to the block9-done branch from the Git pane’s branch menu and read on.

Step 1: refactor with the skill
The shipped skillA folder containing a SKILL.md file (and optionally scripts and templates) that an assistant loads only when it is invoked by name or judged relevant from its description. characterisation-refactor (/skills lists it) carries every rule you would otherwise type: plan first, refactor only, stop for your diff review, then write a test that reads your reference.






Notecharacterisation-refactor/SKILL.md







---
name: characterisation-refactor
description: >-
  Refactors working R analysis code into documented functions under a
  characterisation test, so the output is proved unchanged. Use when asked to
  functionalise, refactor or tidy a script whose output must not change.
  Not for fixing bugs or changing results.
disable-model-invocation: true
---

# Refactor under a characterisation test

## The reference stays with the human
The frozen reference in tests/fixtures/ is captured by the user, once, before
any refactoring. A reference produced by the code under test proves nothing.
- Never create, regenerate or modify anything under tests/fixtures/.
- Never run tests/make_reference.R or any script that writes a fixture.
- If no reference exists, stop and ask the user to capture one.

## Procedure
1. Present a plan: the code to move, the function name and file, and the
   test file. Wait for the user to confirm.
2. Refactor only. Write the function in scripts/functions/ with a roxygen2
   block and an argument check, and make the original script call it. Do not
   write or edit tests in this step. Stop and let the user review the diff.
3. Test only. Write tests/test_<functions file>.R (for
   scripts/functions/summary_functions.R, that is
   tests/test_summary_functions.R). Start it with library(testthat) and
   testthat::local_edition(3), source the function files with
   here::here(), read the reference from tests/fixtures/ with readRDS(), and
   compare it with the function's output using expect_equal(). Never
   hard-code expected values, and never reimplement the computation inside
   the test. Include an expect_error() test showing that the argument check
   rejects data with a required column missing.
4. Run every test in a fresh R session,
   Rscript -e "testthat::test_dir('tests')", and report the output verbatim,
   including skips.

## Rules
- If the test fails, report the difference. Never change the test, the
  tolerance or the reference to make it pass.
- Sort the output rows explicitly with dplyr::arrange() on the grouping
  columns, so the order never depends on how the data happen to be stored.
- Do not change behaviour, including how missing values are handled. A
  passing test shows the output is unchanged, not that it is correct; list
  anything that looks wrong for the user to decide.







One request, one diff, one test run (18 minutes)


Start state: the reference committed, and Claude Code running in Manual mode in the Terminal tab (/clear if the conversation from Step 0 is still open).
1. Ask.
Prompt (Claude Code):
/characterisation-refactor Move the summary in scripts/05_analysis.R into
summarise_metabolic_rate() in scripts/functions/summary_functions.R.
Read its plan, choose “Yes, manually approve edits”, and read each edit before approving it.
2. Read the diff when it stops. Select each changed file in the Git pane and choose Diff, then tell it to carry on and write the test.
3. Protect the new test. Type /permissions and add the deny rule Edit(/tests/test_summary_functions.R). It takes effect at once, and from now on new tests go in new files.
4. Run the checks. Restart R (Session → Restart R), then in the R console:

callr::r(\(d) testthat::test_dir(d), list(here::here("tests")))







Test
Passing proves




test_summary_functions.R (the agent’s)
the function reproduces your reference exactly



test_reference_guard.R (shipped)
the agent’s test reads your reference rather than typing numbers, and the reference is unchanged since you committed it



test_controls.R (shipped)
every deny rule is in place, including the new one



You are done when the suite has no failures and the Git pane shows only the function, 05_analysis.R and the new test as changed. Commit them.
If it goes wrong: a failure on row order, not values, means the function used .by without sorting: ask the agent to add dplyr::arrange(treatment_arm, sex). If test_controls.R says the test is unprotected, check the rule’s spelling in /permissions. Otherwise Revert the agent’s files in the Git pane and ask again, or switch to block9-done.
Payoff. What did the agent do, how long did checking it take, and would you automate this again?








TipUsing Posit Assistant





Posit Assistant reads the same skill from .agents/skills/. Use it in Normal mode and run the same test suite; with no path rules for edits, the Git pane and test_reference_guard.R are what protect the reference.

title: Block 9: Functionalise a script step and prove the result is unchanged
text:
Step 2: unchanged is not correct
Your test passes, including the NA cell: the refactor faithfully kept a missing mean for one group. If you wanted the mean of the animals that were measured, the original code was wrong all along. A characterisation test cannot tell, because it compares against the past, not against the truth.


Decide, change, and test the change independently (12 minutes)


1. Decide. The mean and standard deviation should use measured animals only, and the count should not include the unmeasured animal (n() counts rows).
2. Ask for the change and a known-answer test.
Prompt (Claude Code):
Handle missing metabolic_rate_post values in summarise_metabolic_rate(): mean
and SD with na.rm = TRUE, and add n_used and n_missing instead of n. Put a
known-answer test on a small tibble in a new file,
tests/test_known_answers.R, and show me the expected values and how you
worked them out. Do not change tests/test_summary_functions.R.
A known-answer testA test that checks code against a result worked out independently, for example by hand. It can show code is correct, where a characterisation test only shows it is unchanged. checks the new behaviour against a result you can work out by hand. Check the arithmetic yourself: the mean of 10, 14 and a missing value is 12, from two measured animals and one missing.


A function and test you should converge on


# scripts/functions/summary_functions.R: missing values handled ----
summarise_metabolic_rate <- function(data) {
  stopifnot(is.data.frame(data))
  required <- c("treatment_arm", "sex", "metabolic_rate_post")
  missing_cols <- setdiff(required, names(data))
  if (length(missing_cols) > 0) {
    stop(
      "`data` is missing required column(s): ",
      paste(missing_cols, collapse = ", "),
      call. = FALSE
    )
  }

  data |>
    dplyr::summarise(
      mean_rate = mean(metabolic_rate_post, na.rm = TRUE),
      sd_rate   = stats::sd(metabolic_rate_post, na.rm = TRUE),
      n_used    = sum(!is.na(metabolic_rate_post)),
      n_missing = sum(is.na(metabolic_rate_post)),
      .by       = c(treatment_arm, sex)
    ) |>
    dplyr::arrange(treatment_arm, sex)
}


# tests/test_known_answers.R ----
library(testthat)
testthat::local_edition(3)
source(here::here("scripts", "functions", "summary_functions.R"))

test_that("means ignore missing values and n_used counts measured animals", {
  toy_df <- tibble::tibble(
    treatment_arm       = c("Control", "Control", "Control"),
    sex                 = c("F", "F", "F"),
    metabolic_rate_post = c(10, 14, NA)
  )
  result <- summarise_metabolic_rate(toy_df)

  expect_equal(result$mean_rate, 12)
  expect_equal(result$n_used, 2)
  expect_equal(result$n_missing, 1)
})


3. Watch the characterisation test fail, correctly. Run the suite as in Step 1: the output has changed, and the test tells you so. The known-answer test passes.
4. Re-capture the reference, as a recorded decision. In the R console:

callr::rscript(here::here("tests", "make_reference.R"))

5. Commit, then run the suite. Commit the reference, the function and the new test file with a message that says why, for example “Exclude missing metabolic rates from mean and SD; report n_used and n_missing”. Only then run the suite as in Step 1. The order matters: until the new reference is committed, test_reference_guard.R fails, because git reports uncommitted changes under tests/fixtures/.
Re-capturing is safe here for three reasons: you decided it, a known-answer test checks the new behaviour, and the commit records why.
You are done when the whole suite passes again and the re-captured reference is committed with its reason.
If it goes wrong: if the known-answer test fails, the arithmetic or the function is wrong; read both before changing either. If time is short, switch to the block9-done branch, which has Step 2 done.


The general rule: characterisation tests protect behaviour you have already judged correct. Judging it correct is a separate step, and it is yours.






NoteCheck · Reproduce · Record





You can now: let an agent refactor working analysis code into a tested function with one request, trusted because your reference proves the output is unchanged and a shipped guard test proves the agent’s test uses it.

Check: the whole test suite; the diff in the Git pane; the arithmetic of the known-answer test.

Reproduce: the suite passes in a fresh R session (callr), with nothing changed under tests/fixtures/.

Record: the re-captured reference is a decision with a commit message that says why. Add a line to docs/ai-log.md: the request, whether the test passed first time, and what you changed.

title: Block 9: Functionalise a script step and prove the result is unchanged
text:
Going further (not covered live)
This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you.






TipWhat the skill does, step by step





The skill turns two prompts into one request. Written out by hand, the two prompts are below. Splitting the work matters: a single prompt that writes both the refactor and the test lets one misunderstanding (about row order, say) shape both files at once, producing a passing test that proves nothing.
Prompt 1: the refactor only.
Move the computation in scripts/05_analysis.R into a documented function
summarise_metabolic_rate() in scripts/functions/summary_functions.R, with a
roxygen2 block and an argument check. Make 05_analysis.R call the new function
instead of the inline pipeline. Do not write any tests, and do not touch
anything under tests/.
Prompt 2: the test only.
Add tests/test_summary_functions.R. It must call local_edition(3), source
scripts/functions/load_voles.R and scripts/functions/summary_functions.R,
read tests/fixtures/metabolic_summary.rds, and compare it with
summarise_metabolic_rate(load_voles()) using expect_equal().

Do not create, regenerate or modify anything under tests/fixtures/, and do not
run tests/make_reference.R. I captured that reference myself; a reference you
generate proves nothing.
Before trusting a passing test you would check four things: the test reads the .rds rather than hard-coding numbers; it calls the function rather than reimplementing the pipeline; nothing changed under tests/fixtures/; and the agent’s commands (shown in the conversation) include no run of tests/make_reference.R. The shipped test_reference_guard.R now checks the first three automatically; the fourth is why you read approval requests in Manual mode.






Warning



What a deny rule does not cover. Claude Code’s deny rules apply to its built-in file tools, and to shell output redirects such as > file, but not to R code or most other commands it runs. An agent that ran Rscript tests/make_reference.R would overwrite your reference without touching an edit tool. That is why git, and test_reference_guard.R, are the final checks.


To use the skill in your own projects, download it and unzip it into your project’s .agents/skills/ (and copy it into .claude/skills/ for Claude Code):


 Download characterisation-refactor.zip











TipWithout an agent: write the function and the test yourself





A tidy refactor naturally reaches for the modern .by argument. Write this first attempt in scripts/functions/summary_functions.R:


First attempt (deliberately incomplete)


# scripts/functions/summary_functions.R: first attempt ----
summarise_metabolic_rate <- function(data) {
  data |>
    dplyr::summarise(
      mean_rate = mean(metabolic_rate_post),
      sd_rate   = stats::sd(metabolic_rate_post),
      n         = dplyr::n(),
      .by       = c(treatment_arm, sex)
    )
}


Now write the test and run it:

# tests/test_summary_functions.R ----
library(testthat)
local_edition(3)
source(here::here("scripts", "functions", "load_voles.R"))
source(here::here("scripts", "functions", "summary_functions.R"))

test_that("summarise_metabolic_rate() reproduces the original summary", {
  reference <- readRDS(here::here("tests", "fixtures", "metabolic_summary.rds"))
  expect_equal(summarise_metabolic_rate(load_voles()), reference, tolerance = 1e-8)
})

Run it with testthat::test_file(here::here("tests", "test_summary_functions.R")).


What happened

It fails, and not on the numbers. .by returns the groups in order of first appearance; the reference, made with group_by(), has them sorted. The values are right but the rows are in a different order, and expect_equal() reports a mismatch. Add dplyr::arrange(treatment_arm, sex) to the end of the pipeline and the test passes. That failure is the lesson in miniature: a change that improved the code altered the output, and the characterisation test caught it.
If your test passed first time, the data happen to be stored in sorted order. Check with load_voles() |> dplyr::distinct(treatment_arm, sex).

Do not type the expected numbers into the test as literals: a test that compares the function with numbers you transcribed proves nothing about whether the refactor preserved the original computation. The test must read the .rds.


Refactored function, and the script that calls it


# scripts/functions/summary_functions.R: refactored ----
#' Summarise post-treatment metabolic rate by treatment arm and sex
#'
#' @param data A data frame with columns treatment_arm, sex and
#'   metabolic_rate_post.
#' @return A tibble with one row per treatment_arm and sex, sorted by both,
#'   giving the mean, standard deviation and number of rows.
summarise_metabolic_rate <- function(data) {
  stopifnot(is.data.frame(data))
  required <- c("treatment_arm", "sex", "metabolic_rate_post")
  missing_cols <- setdiff(required, names(data))
  if (length(missing_cols) > 0) {
    stop(
      "`data` is missing required column(s): ",
      paste(missing_cols, collapse = ", "),
      call. = FALSE
    )
  }

  data |>
    dplyr::summarise(
      mean_rate = mean(metabolic_rate_post),
      sd_rate   = stats::sd(metabolic_rate_post),
      n         = dplyr::n(),
      .by       = c(treatment_arm, sex)
    ) |>
    dplyr::arrange(treatment_arm, sex)
}


# scripts/05_analysis.R: after refactoring ----
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
source(here("scripts", "04_load_data.R"))
source(here("scripts", "functions", "summary_functions.R"))

metabolic_summary <- summarise_metabolic_rate(voles)











TipProtecting the new test by editing the settings file





/permissions is the simple route. The same rule can be added by hand: open .claude/settings.json in the editor and add "Edit(/tests/test_summary_functions.R)" to the deny list, minding the comma after the line before. Claude Code reloads the file without a restart. test_controls.R checks the result either way.









TipThe review gate





Local controls do not exist for an agent that works remotely. On GitHub, a pull request that changes a file under tests/ can be held until the code owner reviews it. How to set up CODEOWNERS and branch protection is in the Going further section of Block 6.









TipReuse the skill on a second step





A skill earns its keep the second time you use it.


Reuse the skill (15 minutes)


1. Capture a reference yourself first. Pick a second step: the plotting code in scripts/explore_mass_change_plot.R from Block 4, or a step from your own project. Save its output to tests/fixtures/ yourself, as in Step 0.
2. Invoke the skill.
Prompt (Claude Code):
/characterisation-refactor Functionalise the step in
scripts/explore_mass_change_plot.R that I captured in tests/fixtures/.
Start with the plan.
3. Compare. Did the agent still stop between the refactor and the test? Run the whole suite, and check the Git pane for anything changed under tests/fixtures/.











TipAn asynchronous agent: the Copilot cloud agent





The same work can be handed to an agent that runs remotely while you do something else. It works on a branch in GitHub’s infrastructure and returns a pull request. Before you start, check that your Copilot plan includes the cloud agent, that copilot-setup-steps.yml is on your default branch (see The environment the test runs in below), and that the repository is protected.
Protect the reference on GitHub. Local deny rules do not exist for a remote agent. Add a .github/CODEOWNERS file naming yourself for the protected paths, and turn on branch protection for main so that merging requires your review and a passing r-checks run:
/tests/fixtures/      @your-github-username
/tests/make_reference.R @your-github-username
/.github/             @your-github-username
Keep the two-step discipline by writing two issues, and assign the second only after you have reviewed and merged the first.
Issue 1
Title: Move the metabolic-rate summary into a function

Move the summary computation in scripts/05_analysis.R into a documented
function summarise_metabolic_rate() in scripts/functions/summary_functions.R,
with a roxygen2 block and an argument check. Make 05_analysis.R call it.

Acceptance criteria:
- Do not add or change anything under tests/, data/ or .github/.
- The output must be identical to the current output, including row order
  and the existing NA value.
Issue 2 (after Issue 1 is merged)
Title: Add a characterisation test for summarise_metabolic_rate()

Add tests/test_summary_functions.R. It must call local_edition(3), source
scripts/functions/load_voles.R and scripts/functions/summary_functions.R, and
compare summarise_metabolic_rate(load_voles()) with
tests/fixtures/metabolic_summary.rds using expect_equal().

Acceptance criteria:
- Do not create, modify or regenerate anything under tests/fixtures/, and do
  not run tests/make_reference.R.
- Run the tests and report the result in the pull request description.
Assign each issue to Copilot. When a pull request arrives:

Open Files changed. Confirm that only the expected files changed. A change under tests/fixtures/ or .github/ should not merge, and CODEOWNERS will in any case require your review for it.
Read the test against the four checks in What the skill does, step by step above, or run test_reference_guard.R.
Check that the r-checks run on the pull request passed.
Pull the branch and run the test on your own machine. The agent’s report that “tests pass” is its claim; your run is the check.

If something is wrong, comment on the pull request to ask for a revision, or close it. Nothing reaches main until you merge.









TipThe environment the test runs in





A characterisation test is only as stable as the environment it runs in. The column types in load_voles() handle the finest-grained part. The R version and the package set are handled by two GitHub Actions workflows.
r-checks.yml is the independent check. It runs the tests from a clean checkout on every push to main and on every pull request:
name: r-checks
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  tests:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2
        with:
          r-version: "4.5.2"   # match the R version in renv.lock
          use-public-rspm: true
      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-renv@v2
      - name: Run tests
        run: Rscript -e 'testthat::test_dir("tests", stop_on_failure = TRUE)'
It is independent of your machine and of the agent’s environment, but it is not tamper-proof. A pull request can change the workflow file or the reference it checks against. CODEOWNERS and branch protection (above) are what make a passing run meaningful: you review every change to those paths before it merges.
copilot-setup-steps.yml builds the environment the Copilot cloud agent works in. Following GitHub’s documented pattern:
name: "Copilot Setup Steps"

# Runs when this file changes, so you can see whether setup succeeds,
# and can be run by hand from the Actions tab.
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
  push:
    paths:
      - .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml

jobs:
  # The job must be called copilot-setup-steps or Copilot will not use it.
  copilot-setup-steps:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
    steps:
      - name: Check out repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Set up R
        uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2
        with:
          r-version: "4.5.2"   # match the R version in renv.lock
          use-public-rspm: true
      - name: Restore packages from renv.lock
        uses: r-lib/actions/setup-renv@v2
Four requirements, each with a different failure mode:


The job name must be exactly copilot-setup-steps. If it is not, Copilot ignores the file and works without your packages. That failure is usually loud: the tests error on the first missing function.

The file must be on the default branch, or it is not used.

The runner must be Ubuntu x64 Linux or Windows 64-bit. The cloud agent does not support macOS runners; Ubuntu is the usual choice for R.

The lockfile must be restored. If it restores the wrong versions, the failure is quiet: tests run and pass against different package behaviour. The frozen reference then certifies sameness against the wrong baseline.

When the agent’s test run and the independent r-checks run disagree, suspect the environment before you suspect the code.

title: Block 9: Functionalise a script step and prove the result is unchanged
text:
Glossary




term
definition



characterisation test
A test that checks new code reproduces the saved output of the original code exactly. It shows the output is unchanged, not that it is correct.


deny rule
A permission rule in the deny list of .claude/settings.json that stops Claude Code's built-in tools from editing or reading the matching files. It checks shell output redirects such as > file, but not R code or most other commands that change the same files.


known-answer test
A test that checks code against a result worked out independently, for example by hand. It can show code is correct, where a characterisation test only shows it is unchanged.


skill
A folder containing a SKILL.md file (and optionally scripts and templates) that an assistant loads only when it is invoked by name or judged relevant from its description.

title: Block 10: Checking the statistics, and reporting the results
text:
Part A: Translation with an equivalence check
The day ends with two checks on the analysis and its report, then a README assembled from everything your repository now holds. Each part splits the work the same way:
You check the agent’s work from the R console and the Git pane, as in checking work. Two more statistical checks (robustness and simulation) are in Going further.
⏱ ~30 minutes
⏱ ~15 minutes
AI translates code quickly: base R to tidyverse, or SPSS, Stata or SAS to R. An equivalence checkA comparison showing that two versions of code, such as an original and an AI translation, give the same output once only presentation (types, row order) is normalised. runs both versions and compares the outputs, as in Block 9. The agent writes the translation; the shipped tests/test_translation.R, which it did not write, decides whether it is equivalent.
crumbs: Block 10: Checking the statistics, and reporting the results

title: Block 10: Checking the statistics, and reporting the results
text:
Translate and compare (15 minutes)


Start state: your workshop repository, committed and clean, with Claude Code in Manual mode (default) in the Terminal tab, which the repository sets.
1. Run the original. It reads voles_metabolism.csv, the clean trial data that load_voles() also reads, not Block 7’s dirty voles_raw.csv. In the R console:

library(tidyverse)
library(here)

voles <- read.csv(here("data", "raw", "voles_metabolism.csv"),
                  stringsAsFactors = TRUE)
rate_mean <- aggregate(metabolic_rate_post ~ treatment_arm + sex,
                       data = voles, FUN = mean)
rate_n <- aggregate(metabolic_rate_post ~ treatment_arm + sex,
                    data = voles, FUN = length)
names(rate_n)[3] <- "n"
legacy_summary <- merge(rate_mean, rate_n, by = c("treatment_arm", "sex"))
legacy_summary

2. Ask for a translation.
Prompt (Claude Code):
Translate this base R code into a tidyverse function summarise_rate_tidy(data)
in scripts/functions/summaries.R. It takes the tibble returned by load_voles()
and returns one row per treatment_arm and sex, with the columns treatment_arm,
sex, metabolic_rate_post (the mean) and n. Use the native pipe. Do not edit
any other file.

[paste the base R code from step 1]
Approve the edit when asked, after reading it.
3. Compare. Normalise only presentation (type and row order), never values; waldo::compare() shows what still differs. In the R console:

source(here("scripts", "functions", "load_voles.R"))
source(here("scripts", "functions", "summaries.R"))
tidy_summary <- summarise_rate_tidy(load_voles())

normalise <- function(data) {
  data |>
    as_tibble() |>
    mutate(across(where(is.factor), as.character)) |>
    arrange(treatment_arm, sex)
}

waldo::compare(normalise(tidy_summary), normalise(legacy_summary))

4. Find the difference. A different column name is presentation: ask for a rename. A different value is behaviour: find out why before reading on. No difference? Check how the translation handled the missing value anyway.


The difference

aggregate() with a formula silently drops rows with a missing value, so the animal with no metabolic_rate_post is left out of both the mean and the count. A direct translation with summarise(mean(metabolic_rate_post), n()) returns NA for that cell and counts the animal in n. Neither is “the translation”: they make different decisions about missing data. Decide which you want, write it explicitly (na.rm = TRUE and a count of non-missing values), and record the decision. It is Block 9’s “unchanged is not correct”, from a different direction.

5. Run the shipped test. Restart R (Session → Restart R), then in the R console:

testthat::test_file(here::here("tests", "test_translation.R"))

The test uses the original code as its reference. If you chose different missing-value handling, it fails, correctly: change the test’s reference and say why in your commit message.
6. Log it and commit. Add a line to docs/ai-log.md, for example:
2026-10-19; Claude Code (model as shown above the Claude Code prompt); translated summary script to tidyverse; kept the translation, matched the original's missing-value handling after the equivalence check
Then commit summaries.R and the log from the Git pane, with a message that records the missing-value decision.
You are done when test_translation.R passes in a fresh R session and your commit message records how missing values are handled.
If it goes wrong: if the agent edited anything other than summaries.R, select the file in the Git pane and choose Revert. If you run short of time, write summarise_rate_tidy() yourself from the hidden explanation above.








TipBackground: translating from SPSS, Stata or SAS





From other software, export the original’s results to a file and compare against those. Expect differences in defaults (missing values, quantiles, rounding); each needs a decision, not a looser tolerance.

title: Block 10: Checking the statistics, and reporting the results
section: Part B: Reporting without typed numbers
text:
Part B: Reporting without typed numbers
⏱ ~7 minutes
A typed number can be mistyped, or go stale when the data change, and an assistant drafting text may restate numbers it saw earlier. So every number in the prose comes from inline code: a code chunk computes the result, and the text calls it with `r round(primary$estimate, 2)`.






TipReference: how inline numbers look





In a code chunk of your report:

# fit the pre-registered primary analysis
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
source(here("scripts", "functions", "load_voles.R"))

voles_df <- load_voles() |>
  mutate(treatment_arm = factor(treatment_arm, levels = c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose")))

fit <- lm(mass_post_g ~ mass_pre_g + treatment_arm + sex, data = voles_df)
ci <- confint(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose", ]
primary <- tibble(
  estimate = unname(coef(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose"]),
  lower = unname(ci[1]),
  upper = unname(ci[2])
)

and in the text of the report:
High-dose voles were `r round(primary$estimate, 2)` g heavier than controls
after treatment (95% CI `r round(primary$lower, 2)` to
`r round(primary$upper, 2)` g).



Your AGENTS.md asks for this; the shipped find_typed_numbers() checks it, by listing prose lines that still contain numbers outside inline code.






Notescripts/functions/typed_numbers.R






# scripts/functions/typed_numbers.R ----
# List the prose lines of a .qmd file that still contain numbers outside
# inline code, for you to review by eye. Years, design sizes and YAML values
# are flagged too, so treat each hit as a question, not an error.
find_typed_numbers <- function(path) {
  lines <- readLines(path, warn = FALSE)
  is_fence <- grepl("^```", lines)
  in_chunk <- cumsum(is_fence) %% 2 == 1

  tibble::tibble(line = seq_along(lines), text = lines) |>
    dplyr::filter(!in_chunk, !is_fence) |>
    dplyr::mutate(prose = gsub("`\\{?r\\}? [^`]*`", "", text)) |>
    dplyr::filter(grepl("[0-9]+\\.[0-9]+|\\b[0-9]{2,}\\b", prose, perl = TRUE)) |>
    dplyr::select(line, text)
}






Scan a report (3 minutes)


Start state: the template’s reports/example_report.qmd, an interim summary of the voles trial with some numbers typed in.
1. Scan it. In the R console:

source(here::here("scripts", "functions", "typed_numbers.R"))
find_typed_numbers(here::here("reports", "example_report.qmd")) |>
  print(n = Inf, width = Inf)

2. Sort the hits. The scan flags five lines. Decide for each one whether it is a typed result that should be inline code, or a number that is fine as text.


Which are which

Lines 37 and 38 are typed results (the 1.53 g difference with its interval, and the mean of 29.4 g): both should be inline code. The other three can stay: the date in the YAML header (line 3), the design size of 12 per arm-by-sex combination (line 28), and “95%” in “95% CI” (line 34).

You are done when you can say which two lines are typed results and why the other three can stay.
If it goes wrong: if find_typed_numbers() is not found, check that the source() line ran without an error.


The same scan works on any .qmd you write, including your Quarto report from Day 3. Every hit is a question, not an error.

title: Block 10: Checking the statistics, and reporting the results
section: Part C: The repository you leave with
text:
Part C: The repository you leave with
⏱ ~8 minutes
Your repository now holds most of what a reader needs: a codebookA table describing each variable: its type, valid range, missing-value codes, unit and label mappings. It is the data dictionary from Day 2 with machine-readable rules, and you own it, not the AI., cleaning logs, numbered scripts, a lockfileThe renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment., tests and an AI-use logA record written at the time of each piece of AI-assisted work, in the form: date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed. It becomes the AI declaration in a README.. A README pulls them together. The rule: the AI may only phrase facts you can trace to a file; anything else becomes a visible placeholder for you to fill.



docs/codebook.csv


numbered scripts in scripts/


tests in tests/


renv.lock


docs/ai-log.md



the only sources


Drafts README.md, with placeholders for anything missing





You trace every statement to a file




Draft from the record, then test it (8 minutes)


Start state: your workshop repository, committed and clean. If Block 7 or 9 is unfinished, switch to the block9-done branch from the Git pane’s branch menu first, so the files the README draws on exist.
1. Draft. In Claude Code, in Manual mode (default):
Prompt (Claude Code):
Create or update README.md for this repository. Use ONLY these sources, and
name the source of each section:
- Data: docs/codebook.csv.
- Scripts and run order: the numeric prefixes of the files in scripts/.
- Dependencies: the R version and packages pinned in renv.lock, and the
  restore command renv::restore().
- How to verify: the command
  callr::r(\(d) testthat::test_dir(d), list(here::here("tests"))), and what
  the tests check.
- AI declaration: a summary of docs/ai-log.md, making no claim beyond it.
Where a value is not in these files (authors, ORCIDs, licence, DOI, funding,
units the codebook leaves blank), insert a visible placeholder in exactly
this form:
  **TODO: supply [field]: not provided**
Edit README.md only. Show me your plan first.
2. Let the test audit it. The shipped tests/test_readme.R checks the README against its sources: the R and package versions against renv.lock, every numbered script, no leftover {{ tokens, and no invented unit for metabolic_rate_post. In the R console:

testthat::test_file(here::here("tests", "test_readme.R"))

It also reports how many placeholders are left.
3. Confirm the scope and commit. The Git pane should show only README.md as changed. Commit it.
4. Payoff. What did the agent do, how long did checking it take, and would you automate this again?
You are done when test_readme.R passes and README.md is the only file the commit changed. You run the whole suite, which the README’s “How to verify” section points to, in the day’s wrap-up (15:55).
If it goes wrong: if the agent changed any file other than README.md, select it in the Git pane and choose Revert. If the README test fails, ask Claude Code to fix only the statements the test names, and run it again.








TipStretch: audit the README by hand





The test checks versions, scripts, tokens and units. Trace the statements it cannot check yourself: confirm that the AI declarationA statement, for example in a README, recording that an AI assisted, naming the tool, model and date, and making no claim about AI use beyond what was recorded. says no more than your log, and that each section names a source you gave it.
Before you share it, the placeholders are your to-do list. Work through licence, ORCIDs, DOI and archiving with the SORTEE checklist from Day 2. Then add the last line to docs/ai-log.md, and commit.



A fuller version, with a README skill, is in Going further in Block 8. Check your institution’s and target journal’s policy on declaring AI use.






NoteCheck · Reproduce · Record





You can now: have an agent translate analysis code and draft a README, trusted because shipped tests compare the translation with the original and the README with its sources, and the whole suite passes in a fresh R session.

Check: an equivalence test between the original and the translation; a scan for typed numbers; every README statement traced to a file.

Reproduce: numbers come from code, so the report updates when the data do; the README’s dependencies come from renv.lock, not from memory.

Record: the README and the AI-use log complete the record. Together with the codebook, logs, tests and lockfile, they are what a reviewer, a co-author or you in a year’s time will need.

title: Block 10: Checking the statistics, and reporting the results
text:
Check your understanding
A translated script and the original disagree only after you convert factors to characters and sort the rows. What should you do next?

Increase the tolerance until the test passesAccept the translation, since the AI wrote itFind the behavioural difference (for example, missing-value handling), decide which behaviour is correct, and record the decisionRevert to the original script

The README draft gives the unit of metabolic_rate_post, but your codebook leaves it blank. What should you do?

Keep it; the AI probably knows the usual unit for metabolic rateDelete the column from the READMEReplace it with a placeholder and get the unit from the data provider: the AI invented it, and the codebook is the source of truthAdd the unit to the codebook to match the README
crumbs: Block 10: Checking the statistics, and reporting the results

title: Block 10: Checking the statistics, and reporting the results
text:
Going further (not covered live)
This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you.






TipRobustness, not choice





AI should not choose your primary analysis. The BLADE benchmark compared language-model agents with expert analysts on open-ended research questions. It found that the models were often limited to basic analyses, and that agents able to explore the data made more varied but still sub-optimal analytical decisions (Gu et al., 2024). Its useful role is narrower: listing defensible alternatives to an analysis you have already fixed, so you can check whether your conclusion depends on the choice.
Run the steps yourself, and judge each answer before running it.


Enumerate, judge, run


1. Ask for alternatives, not a recommendation:
My pre-registered primary analysis is an ANCOVA:
mass_post_g ~ mass_pre_g + treatment_arm + sex, estimating the High_dose
versus Control difference. List alternative specifications a reasonable
analyst might use for the same question, and for each, say whether it
estimates the same quantity. Do not recommend one.
2. Judge each one yourself. Mark each alternative defensible or not, with a reason. Check especially whether it estimates the same quantity.
3. Run the defensible ones and report them beside the primary analysis.

library(tidyverse)
library(here)
source(here("scripts", "functions", "load_voles.R"))

voles_df <- load_voles() |>
  mutate(treatment_arm = factor(treatment_arm, levels = c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose")))

specs_df <- tribble(
  ~spec,                       ~formula,
  "Primary: ANCOVA",           "mass_post_g ~ mass_pre_g + treatment_arm + sex",
  "Change score",              "I(mass_post_g - mass_pre_g) ~ treatment_arm + sex",
  "ANCOVA with arm-by-sex",    "mass_post_g ~ mass_pre_g + treatment_arm * sex"
)

spec_results_df <- specs_df |>
  mutate(result = map(formula, \(f) {
    fit <- lm(as.formula(f), data = voles_df)
    ci <- confint(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose", ]
    tibble(
      estimate = unname(coef(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose"]),
      lower = unname(ci[1]),
      upper = unname(ci[2])
    )
  })) |>
  unnest(result)

spec_results_df



A trap in the table

In the third specification, the coefficient treatment_armHigh_dose is the High_dose effect in females only (the reference level of sex), because the model includes an interaction. It sits in the same column as the other estimates but answers a different question. It belongs in a separate analysis of whether the effect differs by sex, not in a table of estimates of the same quantity. An AI that lists it as an “alternative” without saying so has made exactly the error step 2 asks you to catch.









Warning



Running many specifications and reporting the one you like best is selective reporting. The primary analysis is fixed in advance; the others are reported as sensitivity analyses whatever they show.


Check your understanding: robustness
Why should the arm-by-sex interaction model not appear in the same robustness table as the primary ANCOVA?

Interaction models cannot be fitted with lm()Its High_dose coefficient estimates the effect in the reference sex only, a different quantity from the primary estimandIt always gives a larger estimateRobustness tables may contain only two models











TipSimulation and parameter recovery





If you simulate data from a mechanism whose parameters you chose, a correct analysis should recover those parameters on average, and its 95% confidence intervals should contain the true values about 95% of the time. This tests the analysis code against a known answer, which real data never provide.
Morris, White and Crowther (2019) give a structure for planning simulation studies: the aims, the data-generating mechanism, the estimand, the methods and the performance measures (ADEMP). Here:


Aim: check that the analysis code estimates the high-dose effect correctly.

Data-generating mechanism: 12 voles per arm-by-sex cell. Pre-treatment mass is normal with mean 28 g and SD 2 g. Post-treatment mass equals 2.8 g plus 0.9 times pre-treatment mass, plus 0.8 g for Low_dose, plus 1.5 g for High_dose, plus 1.0 g for males, plus normal error with SD 0.8 g.

Estimand: the difference in post-treatment mass between High_dose and Control, adjusted for pre-treatment mass and sex. True value: 1.5 g.

Method: linear model (ANCOVA), mass_post_g ~ mass_pre_g + treatment_arm + sex.

Performance measures: bias and confidence-interval coverage, each with its Monte Carlo standard error.

The written mechanism is yours. It is the equivalent of the codebook in Block 7: the AI turns it into code, and you check the code against it.


Write, check, recover


1. Simulation code. Give the AI the data-generating mechanism above, word for word, and ask for a function simulate_voles() returning a tibble with columns treatment_arm, sex, mass_pre_g and mass_post_g.
2. Check the simulated data against the specification. Before using the function, run it once and check that it matches what you wrote:

set.seed(1)
sim_df <- simulate_voles()
sim_df |> count(treatment_arm, sex)            # 12 per cell?
sim_df |> summarise(mean(mass_pre_g), sd(mass_pre_g))
sim_df |>
  summarise(mean_post = mean(mass_post_g), .by = c(treatment_arm, sex))

High_dose should be about 1.5 g above Control within each sex, and males about 1 g above females. If not, the simulation is wrong, and nothing built on it can be trusted.
3. Analysis code, in a separate session. Without showing it the simulation code, ask the AI for a function estimate_high_vs_control(data) that fits the model above and returns the High_dose estimate and its 95% confidence interval.
4. Run the recovery.


Reference code


simulate_voles <- function(n_per_cell = 12, effect_low = 0.8,
                           effect_high = 1.5, sex_effect = 1.0,
                           slope_pre = 0.9, sd_pre = 2, sd_resid = 0.8) {
  tidyr::expand_grid(
    treatment_arm = c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose"),
    sex = c("F", "M"),
    animal = seq_len(n_per_cell)
  ) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      mass_pre_g = stats::rnorm(dplyr::n(), mean = 28, sd = sd_pre),
      arm_effect = dplyr::case_when(
        treatment_arm == "Low_dose" ~ effect_low,
        treatment_arm == "High_dose" ~ effect_high,
        .default = 0
      ),
      mass_post_g = 28 * (1 - slope_pre) + slope_pre * mass_pre_g +
        arm_effect + sex_effect * (sex == "M") +
        stats::rnorm(dplyr::n(), sd = sd_resid)
    ) |>
    dplyr::select(treatment_arm, sex, mass_pre_g, mass_post_g)
}

estimate_high_vs_control <- function(data) {
  data <- dplyr::mutate(
    data,
    treatment_arm = factor(treatment_arm, levels = c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose"))
  )
  fit <- stats::lm(mass_post_g ~ mass_pre_g + treatment_arm + sex, data = data)
  ci <- stats::confint(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose", ]
  tibble::tibble(
    estimate = unname(stats::coef(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose"]),
    lower = unname(ci[1]),
    upper = unname(ci[2])
  )
}



set.seed(2026)
n_sim <- 1000
true_effect <- 1.5

results_df <- seq_len(n_sim) |>
  map(\(i) estimate_high_vs_control(simulate_voles(effect_high = true_effect))) |>
  list_rbind()

results_df |>
  summarise(
    bias          = mean(estimate) - true_effect,
    bias_mcse     = sd(estimate) / sqrt(n_sim),
    coverage      = mean(lower <= true_effect & upper >= true_effect),
    coverage_mcse = sqrt(coverage * (1 - coverage) / n_sim),
    empirical_se  = sd(estimate)
  )

Bias should be within about two Monte Carlo standard errors of zero. Coverage should be within about two Monte Carlo standard errors of 0.95, roughly 0.936 to 0.964 with 1,000 runs.
5. Prove the check can fail. Replace the analysis with a version that models the change the wrong way round, as in Block 3:

estimate_buggy <- function(data) {
  data <- dplyr::mutate(
    data,
    treatment_arm = factor(treatment_arm, levels = c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose")),
    mass_change_g = mass_pre_g - mass_post_g
  )
  fit <- stats::lm(mass_change_g ~ treatment_arm + sex, data = data)
  ci <- stats::confint(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose", ]
  tibble::tibble(
    estimate = unname(stats::coef(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose"]),
    lower = unname(ci[1]),
    upper = unname(ci[2])
  )
}

Rerun the recovery with estimate_buggy(). Bias should be about −3 g and coverage near zero. A check you have never seen fail is a check you are assuming works.








Warning



What recovery does not prove. It shows that the code estimates the right quantity under the mechanism you simulated. It says nothing about whether real voles behave like that. A change-score model fitted to these simulated data would also be nearly unbiased (randomisation makes both estimators valid), but less precise; compare empirical_se to see the cost. Recovery tests code, not scientific assumptions.


Check your understanding: simulation
A simulation recovers the true effect with negligible bias and 95% coverage. What has it shown?

That the real data follow the simulated mechanismThat the analysis code estimates the intended quantity correctly when the data follow the simulated mechanismThat the study has adequate powerThat the model's assumptions hold for the real data

Glossary




term
definition



AI-use log
A record written at the time of each piece of AI-assisted work, in the form: date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed. It becomes the AI declaration in a README.


AI declaration
A statement, for example in a README, recording that an AI assisted, naming the tool, model and date, and making no claim about AI use beyond what was recorded.


codebook
A table describing each variable: its type, valid range, missing-value codes, unit and label mappings. It is the data dictionary from Day 2 with machine-readable rules, and you own it, not the AI.


equivalence check
A comparison showing that two versions of code, such as an original and an AI translation, give the same output once only presentation (types, row order) is normalised.


lockfile
The renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment.

title: Build your own agent in R
text:
Before you start
Self-study: about 45 minutes, not part of the timed day.
All day you have worked with Claude Code. At its core it is a model, a harnessThe software around a model that keeps the conversation, sends it to the model, runs the tools the model asks for and sends back their results. Claude Code is a harness; so is a chat object made with ellmer. and a few toolsR functions (or other programs) that an agent may ask to have run, each described to the model by a name, a description and its arguments. The model only asks; the harness runs the tool on your computer and sends back the result. in a loop. On this page you build that loop yourself in R, in under 100 lines, with the ellmer package. Once you have built it, every control from Blocks 4 to 6 is something you can see in your own code: what Manual mode approves, what a deny rule blocks, and what leaves your machine.
The page follows the order of Hadley Wickham’s explainer What is an agent?: first a conversation, then a tool, then the loop. Joseph Barbier’s talk 50 lines of code to rebuild Claude Code in R builds the same kind of agent; the version here is our own.
You need:
Every request costs money. chat$get_cost() shows what a conversation has cost so far, so check it after each task. The code names its model explicitly, claude-opus-5-5, so your AI-use log can record it; you can swap in another Claude model ID.

title: Build your own agent in R
text:
ellmer, which talks to Claude and runs the loop: install.packages("ellmer"). The agent also uses callr and fs, which the course install script includes.

An Anthropic API key from a Console account. A Claude Pro or Max subscription does not include API use. ellmer reads it from the environment variable ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. Open your user-level .Renviron with usethis::edit_r_environ(), add the line ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=your-key-here, save, and restart R.

The key kept out of every repository. Your user-level .Renviron is outside your projects; never paste the key into a script. The workshop repository’s .gitignore lists .Renviron, and its deny rule Read(/.Renviron) stops Claude Code reading a project copy (Block 6).

title: Build your own agent in R
text:
A conversation is turns

library(ellmer)

chat <- chat_anthropic(model = "claude-opus-5-5")
chat$chat("Tell me a joke about R.")
chat$chat("Explain why it is funny, in one sentence.")
chat

Printing chat shows the conversation as a list of turnsOne message in a conversation with a model: either yours (the user turn) or the model’s reply (the assistant turn). Tool results go back to the model inside a user turn., in pairs: your user turn, then the model’s assistant turn. chat$get_turns() returns them as R objects.
The second question works because of the harness, not the model. The model keeps nothing between requests, so for each new question ellmer sends the whole conversation so far. That is why a long conversation costs more per question: you pay for every tokenThe unit a model reads and writes, roughly three-quarters of an English word. Providers charge per token, and because the whole conversation is re-sent with each request, a long conversation costs more per question. of it again. It is also the context window from Block 1, seen from the inside.

title: Build your own agent in R
section: A tool is an R function, run on your computer
text:
A tool is an R function, run on your computer
A model can only produce text. A tool lets it ask for something to be done:

today <- tool(
  function() format(Sys.Date()),
  name = "today",
  description = "Get today's date."
)

chat <- chat_anthropic(model = "claude-opus-5-5")
chat$register_tool(today)
chat$chat("How many days until 25 December?")

The model never sees your function, only its name and description, so the description is everything it knows about the tool. When it wants the date, its reply is not an answer but a request: “call today with no arguments”. ellmer runs today() on your computer and sends the result back in a new user turn. The model then answers, using the date it was given.
That is two roundsOne request to the model and its reply. A single question can take several rounds when the model asks for tools before it answers. for one question: one request that ended in a tool request, and one that ended in the answer. chat$get_rounds() shows them.

title: Build your own agent in R
text:
What an agent is
An agentAn assistant that can read across a project’s files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises. is a model in a harness, calling tools in a loop. Read tools let it look around: list files, read them. Write tools let it change things: edit a file, run code. With both, it can explore, make a change, check the result and try again, which is what Claude Code did for you all day.
The write tools are where the risk is. Wickham’s article warns with a tool that deletes files: give an agent one without confirmation and it may use it.
crumbs: Build your own agent in R

title: Build your own agent in R
text:
Build a mini coding agent
The agent below has four tools and three safeguards. Download it and save it outside your workshop repository, for example in your Downloads folder, so the agent cannot edit its own rules, just as Block 6 protects .claude/settings.json.


 Download mini_agent.R


The walkthrough below explains each part of the file.






TipReference: the full mini_agent.R






# mini_agent.R ----
# A small coding agent: Claude, four tools, and the loop ellmer runs for you.
# Source it from the root of your workshop repository, then talk to `chat`.
library(ellmer)

# the agent's own deny rule: stay inside the project, out of data/raw/,
# and away from credentials files
inside_project <- function(path) {
  root <- fs::path_abs(getwd())
  full <- fs::path_norm(fs::path_abs(path, start = root))
  inside <- full == root || fs::path_has_parent(full, root)
  if (!inside || fs::path_has_parent(full, fs::path(root, "data", "raw")) ||
      fs::path_file(full) %in% c(".Renviron", ".env")) {
    stop("Refused: ", path, " is outside the project, under data/raw/, ",
         "or a credentials file")
  }
  full
}

# read tools: they observe the project and change nothing
list_files <- tool(
  function(path = ".") list.files(inside_project(path), recursive = TRUE),
  name = "list_files",
  description = "List the files in a folder of the project.",
  arguments = list(path = type_string("A folder, relative to the project.")),
  annotations = tool_annotations(read_only_hint = TRUE)
)
read_file <- tool(
  function(path) {
    paste(readLines(inside_project(path), warn = FALSE), collapse = "\n")
  },
  name = "read_file",
  description = "Read a text file in the project.",
  arguments = list(path = type_string("A file, relative to the project root.")),
  annotations = tool_annotations(read_only_hint = TRUE)
)

# write tools: they change the project, so they need your approval
write_file <- tool(
  function(path, content) {
    writeLines(content, inside_project(path))
    paste("Wrote", path)
  },
  name = "write_file",
  description = "Replace the whole contents of a text file in the project.",
  arguments = list(
    path = type_string("A file, relative to the project root."),
    content = type_string("The complete new contents of the file.")
  )
)
run_r <- tool(
  function(code) {
    out <- callr::r(function(code) utils::capture.output(
      tryCatch(source(exprs = parse(text = code), print.eval = TRUE),
               error = function(e) cat("Error:", conditionMessage(e), "\n"))
    ), list(code = code))
    paste(utils::head(out, 60), collapse = "\n") # keep long output short
  },
  name = "run_r",
  description = "Run R code in a fresh R session; return its printed output.",
  arguments = list(code = type_string("The R code to run."))
)

# Manual mode: show every write or run request, and ask before it happens
ask_first <- function(request) {
  if (request@name %in% c("write_file", "run_r")) {
    cat("\nThe agent wants to call", request@name, "with:\n")
    for (arg in names(request@arguments)) {
      cat("--", arg, "--\n", request@arguments[[arg]], "\n")
    }
    # outside an interactive session there is no one to ask, so refuse
    if (!interactive() || utils::menu(c("Yes", "No"), title = "Allow it?") != 1) {
      tool_reject()
    }
  }
}

chat <- chat_anthropic(
  model = "claude-opus-5-5",
  system_prompt = paste(
    "You are a careful R assistant working in this project.",
    "Read files before you change them, and check your work by running it.",
    "Never touch data/raw/. Say what you changed,",
    "and stop when the task is done."
  )
)
chat$register_tools(list(list_files, read_file, write_file, run_r))
chat$on_tool_request(ask_first)




Each part matches something you met during the day:


Read and write tools. list_files() and read_file() only observe; tool_annotations(read_only_hint = TRUE) labels them, but a label is only a hint and enforces nothing. write_file() and run_r() change things.

inside_project() is the agent’s deny rule. Every file tool calls it, and it refuses paths outside the project, under data/raw/, or to a credentials file (.Renviron or .env, in any folder). An error in a tool does not stop the agent: ellmer sends the error message back to the model, which can try something else.

ask_first() is Manual mode. chat$on_tool_request() runs it before every tool call. Read calls go straight through; for a write or a run it prints the arguments, the file contents or the code, and calls tool_reject() unless you choose Yes.

run_r() uses a fresh R session. callr::r() runs the code in a new R process, so it cannot change the objects in yours, and only the first 60 lines of output go back to the model.

The system prompt is its AGENTS.md. The system promptStanding instructions sent with every request, before the conversation itself. It does the job an instruction file such as AGENTS.md does for Claude Code. is sent with every request, and like an instruction file it is only a request.

run_r() shows the limit Block 6 found in deny rules. inside_project() guards the file tools, but R code run by run_r() can write anywhere, data/raw/ included. Only your approval stands in the way, which is why you read the code before you choose Yes, and why the raw-data checksum test checks the result whatever route a change took.


Run your agent (20 minutes)


Start state: your workshop repository open in RStudio or Positron, committed and clean in the Git pane. If scripts/explore_voles.R already has a mass_change_g line from Block 4, delete that line and commit first. The working directory must be the repository’s root, as it is when you open the project.
1. Load the agent. In the R console, with the path to where you saved it:

source("~/Downloads/mini_agent.R")

2. Give it the task.

chat$chat(paste(
  "Add a mass_change_g column (mass_post_g minus mass_pre_g) to the voles",
  "data in scripts/explore_voles.R, then run",
  "testthat::test_file('tests/test_explore.R') to check it."
))

3. Watch and decide. The read calls run without asking. For each write_file or run_r request, read what it prints, then choose Yes only if you would have written it yourself. Try choosing No once and watch how the agent responds.
4. Look inside. In the console:

chat                # the turns, with tokens and cost
chat$get_rounds()   # one entry per request to the model
chat$get_cost()

5. Check its work. Open the Git pane and read the diff of explore_voles.R. Then run the test yourself in a fresh session, as in checking work:

callr::r(\(f) testthat::test_file(f), list(here::here("tests", "test_explore.R")))

6. Record it. Add a line to docs/ai-log.md, for example:
2026-10-22; mini agent (ellmer, claude-opus-5-5); added mass_change_g; kept after reading the diff and running the test
You are done when the test passes when you run it yourself, the Git pane shows only the change you approved, and you can say how many rounds the task took and what it cost.
If it goes wrong: if the agent changed something you did not want, revert the file in the Git pane. If chat_anthropic() reports a missing key, check Sys.getenv("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY") != "" and restart R after editing .Renviron. If the agent refuses a path you expected it to reach, check getwd() is the repository’s root.

What Claude Code adds






Your mini agent
Claude Code




ask_first() and tool_reject()

Manual mode (default) and the other permission modes


inside_project()
Deny rules in .claude/settings.json, such as Read(/.Renviron)



The system prompt

AGENTS.md, read at the start of each session



run_r() in a fresh R session with callr::r()

Commands it runs in the Terminal; you check results in a fresh R session



get_turns(), get_rounds(), get_cost()

The conversation itself, and the model shown above the prompt


Git
Git



Claude Code also has what this agent lacks: plan mode, hooks, skills, compaction of long conversations, many more tools, and far more checks around each one. Building the small version is not a reason to use it for real work. It is a way to understand what the big one is doing.






NoteCheck · Reproduce · Record





You can now: explain an agent as a model, a harness and tools in a loop, and build one in R, trusted because you wrote every line that touches your files, and a test you did not write decides whether its change is right.

Check: every write and every run is shown to you before it happens; the Git pane shows what changed; the test runs in a fresh R session.

Reproduce: run_r() runs in a fresh R session, so the agent’s checks do not depend on what is loaded in yours.

Record: chat$get_turns() is the full record of what was sent and received; your AI-use log records the tool, model and what you kept.

Going further (not covered live)
This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you.






TipAdd a run_tests tool





Replace general-purpose run_r() for checking with a tool that can only run the project’s tests, function() testthat::test_dir("tests") run through callr::r(). A narrow tool needs less approval than a general one: you might let it through without asking, and keep asking for run_r().









TipA restricted mode





Change ask_first() so it asks before every call, reads included. You then see every file the agent wants to read before it is sent to the provider, which is the habit Block 4 recommends near confidential data.









TipPackages that do more







btw gives ellmer agents ready-made tools for R: package documentation, your live session’s objects and your project’s files.

mcptools connects R to the Model Context Protocol, so R functions can be tools for other assistants, including Claude Code.










TipAnother provider





ellmer has a chat_*() function for each provider it supports, and the tools and loop stay the same. Tool calling can be much less reliable with small local models, so start with a hosted model.
