E.3 Exploring common geom types
So far we have only made a scatterplot, but ggplot offers many more geoms. This chapter works through some of the most common ones.







Data type
Example geom
Purpose



Continuous–continuous

geom_point(), geom_line(), geom_smooth()

Relationships/trends


Categorical–continuous

geom_boxplot(), geom_violin(), geom_col()

Comparisons


Continuous

geom_histogram(), geom_density()

Distributions

title: Appendix E — ggplot
text:
E.4 Histogram (geom_histogram())
If you want to show the distribution of a continuous variable, you can use a histogram. As with every plot, you need at least 3 layers to create a base version of the plot. geom_histogram() only needs an x variable, because it does the counting “in the background”.
A histogram divides the data into “bins” (i.e., groupings displayed in a single bar). These bins are plotted along the x-axis, with the y-axis showing the count of observations in each bin. It’s basically a barchart for continuous variables.
Let’s have a look at the weight distribution in our dataset.

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_histogram() 






Figure E.1: Default histogram




The default number of bins is 30 (as shown in Figure E.1 above). Changing the number of bins (argument bins) makes the histogram coarser or finer. More bins show more detail.
Perhaps it’s more intuitive to modify the width of each bin using the binwidth argument. For example, binwidth = 1 for the weight category would mean each “weight group” represents 1 g, while binwidth = 50 would group weights into 50 g spans. The plots below show modifications for both bins and binwidth.

#less finetuning
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 10) 

# more fineturning
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 50) 








Figure E.2: Bins vs binwidth arguments




The warning message tells us 2 rows of data were removed due to containing non-finite outside the scale range. Have a look at the body mass column (penguins) to see if you can decipher the warning message.
The rows were removed because 
they fall outside of the plot range
they contain missing values.
Click through each tab to see how you can modify colours, axis labels, margins, and breaks, and apply a different theme.


Colour
Axes labels, margins, and breaks
Themes



We can change the plot colours by adding a fill argument and a colour argument. The fill argument changes the colour of the bars, while the colour argument modifies the outline of the bars. Note that these arguments are added directly to the geom_histogram(), rather than within the overall aes(), because we want every bar to be the same colour rather than mapping colour to a variable.

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 50, fill = "#586cfd", colour = "#FC58BE")













Tip



You could use:

Hex codes for fill and colour, as we did here: geom_histogram(binwidth = 50, fill = "#586cfd", colour = "#FC58BE"). If you want to create your own colours, check out this website.
Pre-defined colour names: geom_histogram(binwidth = 50, fill = "purple", colour = "green"). See the full list here.





Here we removed the label for the y-axis Count (to show you some variety) and modified the breaks. The y-axis is now displayed in increasing steps of 5, and the x-axis has a break every 500 g.
Notice how the breaks = argument changes the labels of the break ticks but not the scale limits. You can adjust the limits of the scale using the limits = argument. To make the effect obvious, we set the limits to 2000 and 7000. See how the values from 2000 to 2500, and 6500 to 7000 do not have labels? You would need to adjust that using the breaks = argument.
The expansion() function removes the gap between the x-axis and the bars.

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 50, fill = "#586cfd", colour = "#FC58BE") +
  labs(x = "Body mass in (g)", # renaming x axis label
       y = "") + # removing the y axis label
  scale_y_continuous(
    # remove the space below the bars (first number), but keep a tiny bit (5%) above (second number)
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05)),
    # changing break points on y axis
    breaks = seq(from = 0, to = 20, by = 5)
    ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    # changing break points on x axis
    breaks = seq(from = 2500, to = 6500, by = 500),
    # Experimenting with the scale limits
    limits = c(2000, 7000)
    )









Let’s experiment with the themes. For this plot we have chosen theme_bw():

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 50, fill = "#586cfd", colour = "#FC58BE") +
  labs(x = "Body mass in (g)", # renaming x axis label
       y = "") + # removing the y axis label
  scale_y_continuous(
    # remove the space below the bars (first number), but keep a tiny bit (5%) above (second number)
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05)),
    # changing break points on y axis
    breaks = seq(from = 0, to = 20, by = 5)
    ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    # changing break points on x axis
    breaks = seq(from = 2500, to = 6500, by = 500),
    # Experimenting with the scale limits
    limits = c(2000, 7000)
    )+
  theme_bw()

title: Appendix E — ggplot
text:
E.5 Scatterplot (geom_point())
Scatterplots are appropriate when you want to plot two continuous variables. We can also add a trendline by using geom_smooth(). The default trendline is loess. If you want a linear trendline, you would need to add method = "lm" inside the geom_smooth() function.

ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x=culmen_length_mm, y=culmen_depth_mm)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth()

ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x=culmen_length_mm, y=culmen_depth_mm)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = lm)








Figure E.3: Default Scatterplot with added trendline - loess (left) and linear (right)




Customising the colour of a scatterplot is slightly different from the other plots we’ve encountered so far. Technically, the point is not a “filled-in black area” but rather an extremely wide outline of a circle. Therefore, we cannot use the usual fill argument and instead need to use the colour argument, similar to how we customised the outline of the histogram.
See the tabs below to learn how to change the colour for all points or how to adjust the colour based on groupings.


Colour for all points
Colour with grouping
Legend title and labels



If we want to change the colour of all the points, we can add the colour argument to the geom_point() function. Likewise, to change the colour of the trendline, we would also use the colour argument. Here, we used pre-defined colour names, but HEX codes would work just as well.

# colour of all points and the trendline
ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x=culmen_length_mm, y=culmen_depth_mm)) +
  geom_point(colour = "darkorange")+
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "darkblue")









If we want the points to change colour based on another grouping variable, the colour argument should go inside the aes(). If you don’t want to define the colours manually, you can use a colour palette like Brewer (scale_colour_brewer()) or Viridis (scale_colour_viridis_d()).

## adding grouping variable species and changing the colour values manually
ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x=culmen_length_mm, y=culmen_depth_mm, colour = species)) +
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")+
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("darkorange", "cyan", "purple"))













ImportantWhat happened to the direction of correlation?





Colouring the points by species reveals a reversal of the apparent correlation.
This is known as Simpson’s Paradox, and is a result of “Omitted Variable Bias”: our original scatterplot did not include the confounder, species.
Omitting important variables can lead to incorrect conclusions.





You can tidy the legend title and group labels using the scale_colour_? function, depending on the palette you’re using (e.g., scale_colour_manual(), scale_colour_brewer and many more).

ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x=culmen_length_mm, y=culmen_depth_mm, colour = species)) +
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")+
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("darkorange", "cyan", "purple"),
                      name = "Species",
                      labels = c("Adelie penguin", "Chinstrap penguin", "Gentoo penguin"))












Your turn


All other layers remain exactly the same as in other plots. Try adding layers to make the plot above prettier:

1. relabel axes x and y
2. move the legend to a different position (either top, left, or bottom)
3. add a theme







NoteMore hints





If you are experiencing issues with the legend position and theme, try modifying the order of the layers.





Solution


ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x=culmen_length_mm, y=culmen_depth_mm, colour = species)) +
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(method = "lm",
              show.legend = FALSE)+ # stop this layer from appearing in the legend.
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("darkorange", "cyan", "purple"),
                      name = "Species",
                      labels = c("Adelie penguin", "Chinstrap penguin", "Gentoo penguin"))+
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Bill depth (mm)")+
  theme_classic() + # place before moving the legend position
  theme(legend.position = "top") # move legend to the top

title: Appendix E — ggplot
text:
E.6 Boxplot (geom_boxplot())
A boxplot is one way to display a continuous variable with a categorical grouping variable.

# default boxplot
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g))+
  geom_boxplot()







Tada! As usual, we can enhance the plot by adding various layers. Click on each tab below to see how.


Colour
Axes labels
Legend and theme



We can change the colour by adding a fill argument inside the aes(). To customise the colours further, we can add a scale_fill_? layer. If you have specific colours in mind, use scale_fill_manual(). If you prefer pre-defined palettes, such as Brewer, you can use scale_fill_brewer().

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species))+
  geom_boxplot()+
  # customise colour
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Dark2")









We need to relabel the axes. The function to use depends on the variable type. Here, we need scale_x_discrete() for the x-axis and scale_y_continuous() for the y-axis. We can also tidy up the group labels and adjust the breaks on the y-axis (e.g., in steps of 500 g) within these same functions.

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species))+
  geom_boxplot()+
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Dark2")+
  scale_x_discrete(
    # changing the label of x
    name = "Species",
    # changing the group labels of the 3 groups
    labels = c("Adelie penguin", "Chinstrap penguin", "Gentoo penguin")) + 
  scale_y_continuous(
    # changing name of the y axis
    name = "Body mass (g)",
    # changing break labels
    breaks = c(seq(from = 3000, to = 6000, by = 500))
  )









The legend is superfluous; best to take it off. We can remove the legend by adding the argument guide = "none" to the scale_fill_? function.
Let’s pick a theme we haven’t used yet: theme_dark().

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species))+
  geom_boxplot()+
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Dark2",
                    guide = "none")+
  scale_x_discrete(
    # changing the label of x
    name = "Species",
    # changing the group labels of the 3 groups
    labels = c("Adelie penguin", "Chinstrap penguin", "Gentoo penguin")) + 
  scale_y_continuous(
    # changing name of the y axis
    name = "Body mass (g)",
    # changing break labels
    breaks = c(seq(from = 3000, to = 6000, by = 500))
  ) +
  theme_dark()

title: Appendix E — ggplot
text:
E.7 Violin plot (geom_violin())
An alternative way to display a continuous variable with a categorical grouping variable is a violin plot.

# default violin plot
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species))+
  geom_violin()









Your turn


Adjusting the violin plot would be exactly the same as the boxplot. Try to add layers to the base plot above to:

change the colours either manually or using a pre-defined colour palette
tidy the axes labels and group names
in case a legend appears, take it off
add a theme



Solution


ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species))+
  geom_violin()+
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Dark2",
                    guide = "none")+
  scale_x_discrete(
    # changing the label of x
    name = "Species",
    # changing the group labels of the 3 groups
    labels = c("Adelie penguin", "Chinstrap penguin", "Gentoo penguin")) + 
  scale_y_continuous(
    # changing name of the y axis
    name = "Body mass (g)",
    # changing break labels
    breaks = c(seq(from = 3000, to = 6000, by = 500))
  )+
  theme_bw()

title: Appendix E — ggplot
text:
E.8 Violin-boxplots
So far, we’ve only added one geom_? layer to our plots. However, thanks to ggplot’s layered system, we can add multiple geoms, for example, when creating a violin-boxplot.
Remember, the order of the layers can sometimes make a difference. We’ve seen this already - adding a theme at the end can override earlier arguments like the legend position. Similarly, ggplot + violinplot + boxplot will look different from ggplot + boxplot + violinplot.

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species))+
  geom_violin()+
  geom_boxplot()


ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species))+
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_violin()








Figure E.4: Default violin-boxplot: Order of the layer matters




See the tabs below to learn how to customise various elements, such as the width of the boxes, and the colour or opacity.


Width of the boxes
Colour



If we want to get any information from the boxplot, we need to place it “on top of” the violin plot. But still, the boxplot is pretty wide and covers important details from the violin plot. To make the information more visible, we can adjust the width of the boxes. Finding an appropriate width might take some trial and error.

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species))+
  geom_violin()+
  geom_boxplot(width = .2)






Figure E.5: Default violin-boxplot: adjusting width of the box






Adding colour should be pretty straightforward by now. The code is no different from what we used for the boxplot or violin plot. We need to add the fill argument within the aes(), along with a scale_fill_? layer.
However, we can further customise the plot by adding an opacity argument using alpha to the violin plot geom.

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species))+
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.4) + # alpha for opacity
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.2) + # change width of the boxes
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Dark2") # customise colour






Figure E.6: Violin-boxplot with a different colour palette









Your turn



Change the x- and y-axis labels
Remove the legend
add a theme



Solution


ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species))+
    geom_violin(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Dark2",
                    guide = "none")+
  scale_x_discrete(
    # changing the label of x
    name = "Species",
    # changing the group labels of the 3 groups
    labels = c("Adelie penguin", "Chinstrap penguin", "Gentoo penguin")) + 
  scale_y_continuous(
    # changing name of the y axis
    name = "Body mass (g)",
    # changing break labels
    breaks = c(seq(from = 3000, to = 6000, by = 500))
  ) +
  theme_classic()














Meyer, F., & Perrier, V. (2025). Esquisse: Explore and visualize your data interactively. https://dreamrs.github.io/esquisse/


Wickham, H., Chang, W., Henry, L., Pedersen, T. L., Takahashi, K., Wilke, C., Woo, K., Yutani, H., Dunnington, D., & van den Brand, T. (2026). ggplot2: Create elegant data visualisations using the grammar of graphics. https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org

title: Appendix F — ggplot2
text:
F.1 Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

title: Appendix F — ggplot2
text:
Control aesthetics and grouping behaviour in multilayered plots.
Use and combine a broad range of geoms, including line and label.
Customise and extend colours, palettes, scales, axes, and legends.
Use facets effectively for multi-dimensional comparisons.
Arrange and enhance plots using patchwork and marginal plots.
Export visualisations with ggsave() and make them interactive with plotly.







Note



Like Appendix E, this appendix uses the penguins data from files/chapter5.RDS, which keeps the original culmen_length_mm and culmen_depth_mm column names (called bill_length_mm and bill_depth_mm in palmerpenguins::penguins and on Day 3).

title: Appendix F — ggplot2
text:
F.2 Colours, palettes and extensions
Colour is one of the strongest visual cues in data visualisation. In ggplot2, colours can mark categories, highlight relationships and guide the viewer’s attention. It is also one of the most common sources of confusion and inaccessibility.

F.2.1 How colour works in ggplot2

ggplot2 applies colour in two main ways:

Mapped colour: controlled by a variable in aes(), such as colour = species or fill = species.
Fixed colour: set manually outside aes(), e.g. geom_point(colour = "blue").


penguins |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=flipper_length_mm, 
             y = body_mass_g,
             colour=species))+ 
  geom_point()









Your turn



Change the code above so that all the points are coloured blue.



Solution


penguins |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=flipper_length_mm, 
             y = body_mass_g))+ 
  geom_point(colour = "blue")








A fixed colour is a setting, not a mapping, so it goes outside aes(), as an argument to the geom (here geom_point()).

title: Appendix F — ggplot2
text:
F.3 Choosing effective palettes






Tip



Choosing palettes and checking them for colour vision deficiency are covered in more depth in Day 3, Block 1 (Colour and Accessibility) and Block 4 (Accessible colour with colorspace and colorBlindness).


Good palettes show contrast and group differences, and stay readable for all audiences.
In ggplot2, colours that are assigned to variables are modified via the scale_colour_* and the scale_fill_* functions. To use colour with your data, the most important thing to know is whether you are dealing with a categorical or continuous variable. Choose the colour palette according to the type of variable:

sequential or diverging colour palettes for continuous variables
qualitative colour palettes for (unordered) categorical variables









You can pick your own sets of colours and assign them to a categorical variable. The number of specified colours has to match the number of categories. You can use a wide range of preset colour names or you can use hexadecimals.

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g, fill = species)) +
geom_histogram(bins = 20, 
               alpha = 0.7, 
               position = "identity") +
scale_fill_manual(values = c("Adelie" = "#1b9e77", 
                             "Chinstrap" = "#d95f02", 
                             "Gentoo" = "#7570b3")) +
theme_minimal()








F.3.1 Using predefined palettes from colorspace
The colorspace Ihaka et al. (2026) package offers curated, perceptually balanced palettes designed for clarity and accessibility.
You can select qualitative, sequential, or diverging palettes using scale_*_discrete_qualitative(palette = "*") or similar functions.

library(colorspace)

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g, fill = species)) +
geom_histogram(bins = 20, alpha = 0.7, position = "identity") +
scale_fill_discrete_qualitative() +
theme_minimal()









Your turn


Explore the palettes available in colorspace:

Run the command hcl_palettes(plot = TRUE)
Choose an appropriate palette and try it for our plot



Solution


library(colorspace)

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g, fill = species)) +
geom_histogram(bins = 20, alpha = 0.7, position = "identity") +
scale_fill_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") +
theme_minimal()











F.3.2 Other palettes

Generate a palette
Wes Anderson palettes
ggokabeito
scico

F.3.3 Accessibility
It’s very easy to get carried away with colour palettes, but your figures must always be accessible. One way to check how accessible your figures are is to use a colour blindness checker, colorBlindness Ou (2021).

## Check accessibility ----

library(colorBlindness)
colorBlindness::cvdPlot() # will automatically run on the last plot you made








F.3.4 Guides to visual accessibility
Using colours to tell categories apart can be useful, but as we can see in the example above, you should choose carefully. Other aesthetics you can use in your geoms include shape and size, and you can combine these with colour to make your plots more accessible. Here is a hierarchy of “interpretability” for different types of data:










Shape
Colour
Colour redundancy




penguins |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=flipper_length_mm, 
             y = body_mass_g,
             shape=species))+ 
  geom_point() +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(21,22,23))










penguins |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=flipper_length_mm, 
             y = body_mass_g,
             colour=species))+ 
  geom_point() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Adelie" = "#1b9e77", 
                             "Chinstrap" = "#d95f02", 
                             "Gentoo" = "#7570b3")) 










penguins |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=flipper_length_mm, 
             y = body_mass_g,
             colour=species,
             shape = species))+ 
  geom_point() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Adelie" = "#1b9e77", 
                             "Chinstrap" = "#d95f02", 
                             "Gentoo" = "#7570b3"))

title: Appendix F — ggplot2
text:
F.4 Grouping logic
When drawing lines with geom_line(), ggplot2 needs to know which points belong together.
If it cannot infer groups, it will connect every point in order of x, producing meaningless zigzags.
Let’s see how grouping works implicitly, explicitly and in summary form.

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = culmen_length_mm, y = flipper_length_mm)) +
    geom_line()








F.4.1 Implicit grouping via colour or fill
Discrete aesthetics such as color, fill, or linetype automatically define groups.

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = culmen_length_mm, y = flipper_length_mm,
color = species)) +
  geom_line()








F.4.2 Explicit grouping
Explicit grouping defines the groups by which lines should be drawn (still in order of x) without relying on other aesthetics or implicit grouping.

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = culmen_length_mm, y = flipper_length_mm,
group = species)) +
  geom_line()







Grouping by individual_id instead joins up the repeat measurements of the same bird, so each line shows how one penguin’s measurements vary between the years it was sampled. Birds that were only measured once have nothing to join to, so they get no line.

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = culmen_length_mm, y = flipper_length_mm,
colour = species, group = individual_id)) +
  geom_line()








F.4.3 Summary trend lines

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = culmen_length_mm, y = flipper_length_mm,
colour = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha =.8)+
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")

title: Appendix F — ggplot2
text:
F.5 Scales, axes and ordering

F.5.1 Axes limits
Now, we’ll use scale_x_continuous() and scale_y_continuous() for setting our desired values on the axes.
The key parameters in both functions are:

“limits” (defined as limits = c(value, value))
“breaks” (which represent the tick marks, specified as breaks = value:value).

Note that “limits” are only two values (the minimum and maximum), while “breaks” are a range of values (for instance, from 0 to 100).

## Set axis limits ----
penguins |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=flipper_length_mm, 
             y = body_mass_g,
             colour=species))+ 
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(method="lm",    
              se=FALSE)+
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Adelie" = "#1b9e77", 
                             "Chinstrap" = "#d95f02", 
                             "Gentoo" = "#7570b3")) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0,240), 
                     breaks = seq(20,240,by = 20))+
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0,7000), 
                     breaks = seq(0,7000,by = 10))









Your turn


Pick a more appropriate set of axis breaks:


Solution

R chooses the limits and breaks for you automatically. But it is useful to know how to override this when needed.

## Set axis limits ----
penguins |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=flipper_length_mm, 
             y = body_mass_g,
             colour=species))+ 
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(method="lm",    
              se=FALSE)+
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Adelie" = "#1b9e77", 
                             "Chinstrap" = "#d95f02", 
                             "Gentoo" = "#7570b3")) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(160,240), 
                     breaks = seq(160,240,by = 20))+
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(2500,6500), 
                     breaks = seq(2500,6500,by = 500))











F.5.2 Zooming in and out
We have seen how we can set the parameters for the axes for both continuous and discrete scales.
It can be useful to zoom in and out of figures, mainly to focus on one section of the plot.
One function we can use to do this is coord_cartesian() in ggplot2, where you can:

Set the limits on the x-axis (xlim = c(value, value))
Set the limits on the y-axis (ylim = c(value, value))
Set whether to add a small expansion to those limits or not (expand = TRUE/FALSE).


penguins |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=flipper_length_mm, 
             y = body_mass_g,
             colour=species))+ 
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(method="lm",    
              se=FALSE)+
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Adelie" = "#1b9e77", 
                             "Chinstrap" = "#d95f02", 
                             "Gentoo" = "#7570b3")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(180,210), 
                  ylim = c(3000,4000), 
                  expand = FALSE)













ImportantLimits vs co-ords





This IS different to setting the axis limits. coord_cartesian is like a zoom, while scale sets the plotting range.
Below we use a shortcut to scale with xlim and ylim - the trendline is now calculated only from the visible/plotted points.

penguins |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=flipper_length_mm, 
             y = body_mass_g,
             colour=species))+ 
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(method="lm",    
              se=FALSE)+
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Adelie" = "#1b9e77", 
                             "Chinstrap" = "#d95f02", 
                             "Gentoo" = "#7570b3")) +
  xlim(180,210) +
  ylim(3000,4000)











F.5.3 Axis ordering
Axis ordering affects how quickly and accurately viewers can interpret data.
For example, ordering categories by value shows which groups have the highest or lowest measurements, while random or inconsistent ordering makes comparisons confusing.
By default R will order categories along the axis in alphabetical order:

penguins |> 
ggplot(aes(x = species)) +
  geom_bar()













NoteQuestion



What makes the default ordering less than suitable for rapid comparisons?



F.5.3.1 Reordering manually
To switch the order, use the scale_x_discrete() function and set the limits within it (limits = c(“category”,“category”)):

penguins |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = species)) +
  geom_bar()+
  scale_x_discrete(limits = c("Adelie", "Gentoo","Chinstrap")) 








F.5.3.2 Reordering by values
Or by using features in the forcats package:

fct_infreq(): orders by frequency
fct_reorder(): orders by another numeric variable (e.g., mean body mass)


penguins |> 
  mutate(species = forcats::fct_infreq(species)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = species)) +
  geom_bar()









Your turn


How could we improve the readability of this plot even further?


Solution


penguins |> 
  mutate(species = forcats::fct_infreq(species)) |> 
  # Species on the y axis gives horizontal bars, which are easier to read
  ggplot(aes(y = species)) +
  geom_bar()+
  # Direct annotation
  geom_label(stat='count', aes(label=after_stat(count)))+
  # reverse order so the most common species is at the top
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev)+
  # Redundant titles removed
  labs(y = "",
       x = "Count")

title: Appendix F — ggplot2
text:
F.6 Facets
When it becomes difficult to see the trends or differences in your plot, we can break up a single plot into sub-plots; this is called ‘faceting’. Facets are commonly used when there is too much data to display clearly in a single plot.

F.6.1 Cluttered plots
In the example below it is hard to see the exact distribution of each histogram:

penguins |> 
  ggplot(aes(body_mass_g,
             fill = species))+
  geom_histogram()+
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("darkorange", "purple", "cyan"))







Facetted panels make side-by-side comparisons easier:

penguins |> 
  ggplot(aes(body_mass_g,
             fill = species))+
  geom_histogram()+
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("darkorange", "purple", "cyan"))+
  facet_wrap(~species) # make facets by species

title: Appendix F — ggplot2
text:
F.7 Highlighting
Plot highlighting, for example with the gghighlight package in R Yutani (2025), lets you:

Emphasise values over certain ranges
Emphasise key groups
Make facetted plots easier to read:


library(gghighlight)

penguins |> 
  ggplot(aes(body_mass_g,
             fill = species))+
  geom_histogram(position = "identity")+
  gghighlight()+
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("darkorange", "purple", "cyan"))+
  facet_wrap(~ species)








F.7.1 Nested facets
The ggh4x::facet_nested() function in the ggh4x van den Brand (2025) package is used for creating nested or hierarchical faceting in ggplot2 plots. Nested faceting lets you subdivide facet panels into smaller panels, creating a hierarchy of facets. Here we group the species by their broad diet: Adelie and Chinstrap penguins eat mainly krill, while Gentoo penguins eat krill and fish.

library(ggh4x)

penguins |> 
  mutate(Nester = ifelse(species == "Gentoo", "Krill and fish", "Mainly krill")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = culmen_length_mm,
             y = culmen_depth_mm,
             colour = species))+
  geom_point()+
  facet_nested(~ Nester + species)+
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("darkorange", "purple", "cyan"))+
  theme(legend.position = "none")

title: Appendix F — ggplot2
text:
F.8 Patchwork
patchwork Pedersen (2025) lets you combine multiple ggplots, side by side or stacked, without exporting to another program.
This keeps everything reproducible inside R.

Use / to stack plots vertically
Use + to align plots horizontally


library(patchwork)

p1 <- penguins |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=flipper_length_mm, 
             y = culmen_length_mm))+
  geom_point(aes(colour=species))+
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("darkorange", "purple", "cyan"))

p2 <- penguins |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=culmen_depth_mm, 
             y = culmen_length_mm))+
  geom_point(aes(colour=species))+
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("darkorange", "purple", "cyan"))


p3 <- penguins |>     
     drop_na(sex) |> 
     ggplot(aes(x=species, 
                fill = sex)) + 
    geom_bar(width = .8,
             position = position_dodge(width = .85))+
  scale_fill_discrete_diverging()

 (p1+p2)/p3+
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") 







You can also add overall titles and adjust layouts:

 (p1+p2)/p3+
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") +
plot_annotation(
title = "Penguin Bill and Body Measurements",
subtitle = "Comparing relationships across species"
)








F.8.1 Marginal plots
A marginal plot augments a two-dimensional plot (usually a scatterplot) with one-dimensional summaries along its margins, typically histograms, density curves, or boxplots.
They let readers inspect the joint relationship and each variable’s distribution simultaneously.
Conceptually:

The main panel shows how x and y relate.
The marginal panels show the univariate spread of each variable.


pal <- c("darkorange", "purple", "cyan")

# density plot of flipper length
marginal_1 <- penguins |>  
  ggplot()+
  geom_density(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, fill = species),
               alpha = 0.5)+
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal)+
  theme_void()+
  theme(legend.position = "none")

# density plot of body mass
marginal_2 <- penguins |>  
  ggplot()+
  # body mass on y, so the density runs vertically beside the scatterplot
  geom_density(aes(y = body_mass_g, fill = species),
               alpha = 0.5)+
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal)+
  theme_void()+
  theme(legend.position = "none")


scatterplot <- penguins |>  
  ggplot(aes(x=flipper_length_mm, 
             y = body_mass_g,
             colour=species))+ ### now colour is set here it will be inherited by ALL layers
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(method="lm",    #add another layer of data representation.
              se=FALSE)+
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal)+
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

# Layout allows us to have total customisation over the position of our plots

layout <- "
AAA#
BBBC
BBBC
BBBC"


marginal_1+scatterplot+marginal_2 +plot_layout(design = layout)

title: Appendix F — ggplot2
text:
F.9 Plotly
plotly Sievert et al. (2026) turns static ggplots into interactive web graphics built on the JavaScript Plotly.js library. It preserves ggplot2’s grammar (via ggplotly()), but turns each layer into a responsive SVG/HTML element with tooltips, zooming, and panning:

library(plotly)
ggplotly(
penguins |> 
    ggplot(
        aes(x = culmen_length_mm,
            y= body_mass_g,
            colour = species)) +
    geom_point(aes(fill = species), shape = 21, colour = "white") +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE,linetype = "dashed", alpha = .4)+
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("darkorange", "purple", "cyan"))+
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("darkorange", "purple", "cyan"))
)

title: Appendix F — ggplot2
text:
F.10 Exporting safely

F.10.1 ggsave







Tip



Saving figures is covered in more depth in Day 3, Block 5 (Saving figures correctly).


One of the easiest ways to save a figure you have made is with the ggsave() function. By default it will save the last plot you made on the screen.
You should specify the output path to your figures folder, then provide a file name. Here I want to save it as a .PNG image file. Always set the width, height, units and resolution (dpi) explicitly: the defaults depend on the size of your plot window, so the same code can produce a different figure each time. dpi 300 is good enough for most purposes.

# OUTPUT FIGURE TO FILE


ggsave("outputs/figures/YYYYMMDD_ggplot_workshop_final_plot.png",
       width = 7, height = 5, units = "in", dpi = 300)


F.10.2 svg

Not exactly programmatic, but occasionally a lifesaver. If you save your ggplot image in .svg format then it becomes vectorised.
What does this mean?
Open your image in a programme like PowerPoint and each element of the plot can be edited, resized or moved!

ggsave("outputs/figures/test-file.svg",
       width = 7, height = 5, units = "in")













Ihaka, R., Murrell, P., Hornik, K., Fisher, J. C., Stauffer, R., Wilke, C. O., McWhite, C. D., & Zeileis, A. (2026). Colorspace: A toolbox for manipulating and assessing colors and palettes. https://zeileis.codeberg.page/colorspace/


Ou, J. (2021). colorBlindness: Safe color set for color blindness. https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.colorBlindness


Pedersen, T. L. (2025). Patchwork: The composer of plots. https://patchwork.data-imaginist.com


Sievert, C., Parmer, C., Hocking, T., Chamberlain, S., Ram, K., Corvellec, M., & Despouy, P. (2026). Plotly: Create interactive web graphics via plotly.js. https://plotly-r.com


van den Brand, T. (2025). ggh4x: Hacks for ggplot2. https://github.com/teunbrand/ggh4x


Yutani, H. (2025). Gghighlight: Highlight lines and points in ggplot2. https://yutannihilation.github.io/gghighlight/

title: Appendix G — Working with larger data
text:
G.1 Why a data frame is sometimes the wrong tool
Throughout this chapter we use the Portal mammals survey data, distributed as both a CSV file and a SQLite database. The CSV is around 35,000 rows: small enough to inspect, large enough to make timing differences visible.
A data.frame (and its tidyverse refinement, the tibble) holds the whole dataset in memory and copies it on most operations. For tens of thousands of rows this is invisible. For tens of millions it becomes the dominant cost of an analysis, and for data larger than available RAM it fails outright.
Two strategies address this. The first keeps the data in memory but uses a structure optimised for speed and low copying: data.table. The second leaves the data on disk in a database and pulls only what each query needs: a SQLite file queried through dbplyr. The rest of this chapter works through each in turn.

title: Appendix G — Working with larger data
text:
Note



The thresholds are approximate and hardware-dependent, but a useful rule of thumb: under ~1 GB, a tibble is fine; from ~1 GB up to the limits of RAM, reach for data.table; beyond RAM, or when the data are already in a database, use a database backend.

title: Appendix G — Working with larger data
text:
G.2 Reading large files: fread()

There are three common ways to read a delimited file: base R’s read.csv(), readr::read_csv(), and data.table::fread(). For small files the choice is immaterial. As files grow past roughly 100 MB the differences become substantial, with fread() and read_csv() typically several times faster than read.csv().

library(microbenchmark)

microbenchmark(
  base  = read.csv(csv_name),
  readr = readr::read_csv(csv_name, show_col_types = FALSE),
  dt    = data.table::fread(csv_name, showProgress = FALSE),
  times = 10,
  unit  = "ms"
)

The return types differ, and this matters. read.csv() returns a data.frame, read_csv() returns a tibble, and fread() returns a data.table. The first two behave identically for our purposes; the data.table is a different object with its own syntax, covered below.

G.2.1 Reading only part of a file
When a file does not fit in memory, the simplest fix is to read less of it. fread() exposes two arguments for this. nrows caps the number of rows read, and skip discards lines from the top of the file.

# First 500 rows only
fread(csv_name, nrows = 500, showProgress = FALSE)

# Skip the header and the first 999 records, so reading starts at record 1000.
# The header line has been skipped too, so we supply the column names ourselves
col_names <- names(fread(csv_name, nrows = 0))
fread(csv_name, skip = 1000, header = FALSE, col.names = col_names,
      showProgress = FALSE)

skip can also be given a string, and fread() then starts at the first line that contains that text anywhere. This is less useful than it sounds. With skip = "1986", the first matching line is record number 1986, which was collected in 1979, not the first record from 1986. Because the header line is skipped as well, the columns come back named V1 to V9. To keep only certain years, read the file and filter it instead.
The select argument restricts which columns are read, which often has a larger effect on memory than restricting rows. drop is its complement.

three_columns <- fread(
  csv_name,
  select       = c("species_id", "sex", "hindfoot_length"),
  showProgress = FALSE
)

readr offers the same controls under different names: n_max for rows, skip for an offset, and col_select for columns. Unlike older versions, col_select now accepts column names directly, so the two packages are close to equivalent here.

readr::read_delim(
  csv_name,
  delim      = ",",
  n_max      = 500,
  col_select = c(species_id, sex, hindfoot_length)
)

title: Appendix G — Working with larger data
section: G.3 data.table syntax in one minute
text:
G.3 data.table syntax in one minute
A data.table is indexed as dt[i, j, by]: filter rows in i, do something to columns in j, grouped by by. It is terse and fast, but the grammar is not dplyr’s.

allData <- fread(csv_name, showProgress = FALSE)

# Filter rows
allData[year > 1988]

# Select columns (note: .() returns a data.table, not a vector)
allData[, .(species_id, year)]

# Aggregate by group
allData[, .(mean_hf = mean(hindfoot_length, na.rm = TRUE)), by = species_id]

You do not have to learn this grammar to get the speed. dtplyr lets you write ordinary dplyr and translates it to data.table code under the hood.

section: G.5 When the data live on disk: databases
text:
G.5 When the data live on disk: databases
data.table still holds everything in memory. Once the data exceed RAM, or when they already sit in a shared database, the better move is to leave them where they are and query across the connection. We use SQLite here because it is a single file with no server to configure, but the same code works against PostgreSQL, MySQL, BigQuery, and others through the common DBI interface.
First download the Portal mammals database (a SQLite file of about 1 MB) with the button below. Save it as portal_mammals.sqlite in a data folder inside your project, so its path is data/portal_mammals.sqlite.



 Download Portal mammals database (SQLite)




library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)

# A connection to a SQLite database file
mammals <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(),
                          here::here("data", "portal_mammals.sqlite"))

DBI::dbListTables(mammals)
# [1] "plots"   "species" "surveys"

dbConnect() opens the connection; RSQLite::SQLite() names the driver. The returned object, mammals, is the handle we query against. Point a tbl() at one of its tables to get something that behaves like a lazy tibble.

surveys <- dplyr::tbl(mammals, "surveys")
surveys
# # Source:   table<`surveys`> [?? x 9]
# # Database: sqlite [.../portal_mammals.sqlite]
#    record_id month   day  year plot_id species_id sex   ...
#        <int> <int> <int> <int>   <int> <chr>      <chr>
#  1         1     7    16  1977       2 NL         M
#  ...

Note the [?? x 9]: R reports nine columns but an unknown number of rows. It has not counted them, because doing so would mean reading the whole table. This laziness is the point: R fetches only what a query needs.

title: Appendix G — Working with larger data
text:
G.6 Querying with dbplyr

dbplyr translates dplyr verbs into SQL automatically. In practice you write the same pipeline you would for a local tibble, with one addition: nothing is fetched until you call collect().

library(dbplyr)

# How many males were recorded in plot 2 in 1978?
surveys |>
  filter(sex == "M", year == 1978, plot_id == 2) |>
  count() |>
  collect()                # <- pulls the result into a local tibble

Without collect(), the pipeline remains a query object and prints only a preview. With it, the SQL runs on the database and the (usually small) result comes back as an ordinary tibble you can plot or model. Filter and aggregate on the database side, where the data are; collect() only the reduced result.






Note



Most dplyr verbs translate, but not all of R is available inside a database. slice_head() and friends are unsupported because database tables have no inherent row order, and any function dbplyr cannot translate will error. When that happens, collect() first and finish the work locally.



G.6.1 Seeing the generated SQL
Learning what dbplyr produces is a low-cost way to learn SQL itself. Pipe any un-collected query into show_query().

surveys |>
  filter(year %in% c(1998, 1999, 2000)) |>
  summarise(n = n(), .by = c(year, species_id)) |>
  show_query()
# <SQL>
# SELECT `year`, `species_id`, COUNT(*) AS `n`
# FROM (
#   SELECT `surveys`.*
#   FROM `surveys`
#   WHERE (`year` IN (1998.0, 1999.0, 2000.0))
# ) AS `q01`
# GROUP BY `year`, `species_id`

This is the real output from dbplyr 2.5.1. dbplyr wraps the filter in a subquery and writes the years as decimals (1998.0), because R numbers are doubles. A person writing the same query by hand would probably write the shorter version in the dbGetQuery() example below, and the database treats the two the same.
If you prefer to write SQL directly, DBI::dbGetQuery() sends a raw query and returns a data frame in one step.

DBI::dbGetQuery(
  mammals,
  "SELECT year, species_id, COUNT(*) AS n
   FROM surveys
   WHERE year IN (1998, 1999, 2000)
   GROUP BY year, species_id"
)


G.6.2 Activity: SQL to dplyr and back


read it, then write it


First, translate this SQL into a dbplyr pipeline:
SELECT record_id, hindfoot_length
FROM surveys
WHERE hindfoot_length > 20
Then, going the other way, write the dbplyr pipeline below, predict the SQL it will generate, and check your prediction with show_query():

surveys |>
  filter(year > 1977, year < 2000, hindfoot_length == 30) |>
  arrange(desc(species_id))





Solution


# SQL -> dbplyr
surveys |>
  select(record_id, hindfoot_length) |>
  filter(hindfoot_length > 20) |>
  collect()

# show_query() on the second pipeline gives (dbplyr 2.5.1):
# <SQL>
# SELECT `surveys`.*
# FROM `surveys`
# WHERE (`year` > 1977.0) AND (`year` < 2000.0) AND (`hindfoot_length` = 30.0)
# ORDER BY `species_id` DESC

Two things to notice. The comma-separated filter() conditions become a single WHERE joined by AND, and arrange(desc(...)) becomes ORDER BY ... DESC. The mapping is close enough that reading SQL and reading dplyr reinforce each other.

title: Appendix G — Working with larger data
section: G.7 Building a database from a CSV
text:
G.7 Building a database from a CSV
If your data start life as a CSV that is too large to load, you can write it into a SQLite file in chunks, then query it lazily as above. Read a block with fread(), append it to the table, and repeat. purrr::walk() drives the loop for its side effect (writing), returning nothing.

library(purrr)

db <- dbConnect(SQLite(), here::here("data", "surveys.sqlite"))

# Read the column names once, from the header line only
col_names <- names(fread(csv_name, nrows = 0))
n <- 5000

# Write one chunk: skip the header plus `skip_rows` data rows, read `n` rows,
# and append them to the table
write_chunk <- function(skip_rows) {
  chunk <- fread(csv_name, skip = skip_rows + 1, nrows = n, header = FALSE,
                 col.names = col_names, showProgress = FALSE)
  dbWriteTable(db, "surveys", chunk, append = TRUE)
}

# Offsets for each chunk (the file has 35,549 data rows), then write them all
skips <- seq(0, by = n, length.out = 8)
walk(skips, write_chunk)

dbDisconnect(db)

Only the first line of the file holds the column names, so we read them once and pass them to every chunk with header = FALSE. Without this, every chunk after the first loses its names and dbWriteTable() refuses to append it. The + 1 in skip steps over that header line. The general pattern is to never hold more than one chunk in memory at a time.






Note



Where this leaves us. We can read selectively with fread(), run dplyr at data.table speed through lazy_dt(), and query on-disk databases through dbplyr while fetching only what we need with collect(). The common thread is that the dplyr grammar carries across all three settings; what changes is where the data sit and when the work actually runs.
